entries.full:
The day began with a summons from Knepp's maid to attend the women's day at the playhouse, and I rewarded her with half-a-crown and a kiss. I then went to St. James's, where the Duke of York asked me to prepare something for better managing the Office, acting on the Lord Keeper's advice.

Later, I visited Lord Burlington's house for the first time, saw Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady, and met Sidney Montagu just arrived from Mount's Bay. There I learned of my Lord's urgent need for money, and I felt duty-bound to supply L500, though I regretted my remissness in writing to him during his voyage.

At Lord Burlington's, I accidentally set my periwig on fire by a candle, causing a strange noise. Afterwards, I walked through Westminster, stopped by my vintner's to admire his handsome wife, and greeted the widow Mrs. Horsfall.

I then went to the King's playhouse, where I saw the silly play "The City Match" with a full house for the women's sake. In the evening, I attended the Queen, who came out with her ladies to hear Italian musicians in a barge, with Seignor Joanni's voice standing out.

I also saw Sidney Montagu kiss the Queen's hand, and the King spoke with him. However, I heard troubling news that Sir W. Coventry is out of favor, and there are designs to make my Lord Arlington Lord Treasurer, which I cannot believe.

The Duke of York also told me of the hot dispute over Gawden, and he stood firmly in his support.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to the office, and before the office did speak with my Lord Brouncker, and there did get his ready assent to T. Hater’s having of Mr. Turner’s place, and so Sir J. Minnes’s also: but when we come to sit down at the Board, comes to us Mr. Wren this day to town, and tells me that James Southern do petition the Duke of York for the Storekeeper’s place of Deptford, which did trouble me much, and also the Board, though, upon discourse, after he was gone, we did resolve to move hard for our Clerks, and that places of preferment may go according to seniority and merit. So, the Board up, I home with my people to dinner, and so to the office again, and there, after doing some business, I with Mr. Turner to the Duke of Albemarle’s at night; and there did speak to him about his appearing to Mr. Wren a friend to Mr. Turner, which he did take kindly from me; and so away thence, well pleased with what we had now done, and so I with him home, stopping at my Lord Brouncker’s, and getting his hand to a letter I wrote to the Duke of York for T. Hater, and also at my Lord Middleton’s, to give him an account of what I had done this day, with his man, at Alderman Backewell’s, about the getting of his L1000 paid; and here he did take occasion to discourse about the business of the Dutch war, which, he says, he was always an enemy to; and did discourse very well of it, I saying little, but pleased to hear him talk; and to see how some men may by age come to know much, and yet by their drinking and other pleasures render themselves not very considerable. I did this day find by discourse with somebody, that this nobleman was the great Major-General Middleton; that was of the Scots army, in the beginning of the late war against the King. Thence home and to the office to finish my letters, and so home and did get my wife to read to me, and then Deb to comb my head....

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Lay long in bed talking with my wife, she being unwilling to have me go abroad, saying and declaring herself jealous of my going out for fear of my going to Deb., which I do deny, for which God forgive me, for I was no sooner out about noon but I did go by coach directly to Somerset House, and there enquired among the porters there for Dr. Allbun, and the first I spoke with told me he knew him, and that he was newly gone into Lincoln’s Inn Fields, but whither he could not tell me, but that one of his fellows not then in the way did carry a chest of drawers thither with him, and that when he comes he would ask him. This put me into some hopes, and I to White Hall, and thence to Mr. Povy’s, but he at dinner, and therefore I away and walked up and down the Strand between the two turnstiles, hoping to see her out of a window, and then employed a porter, one Osberton, to find out this Doctor’s lodgings thereabouts, who by appointment comes to me to Hercules pillars, where I dined alone, but tells me that he cannot find out any such, but will enquire further. Thence back to White Hall to the Treasury a while, and thence to the Strand, and towards night did meet with the porter that carried the chest of drawers with this Doctor, but he would not tell me where he lived, being his good master, he told me, but if I would have a message to him he would deliver it. At last I told him my business was not with him, but a little gentlewoman, one Mrs. Willet, that is with him, and sent him to see how she did from her friend in London, and no other token. He goes while I walk in Somerset House, walk there in the Court; at last he comes back and tells me she is well, and that I may see her if I will, but no more. So I could not be commanded by my reason, but I must go this very night, and so by coach, it being now dark, I to her, close by my tailor’s, and she come into the coach to me, and je did baiser her.... I did nevertheless give her the best council I could, to have a care of her honour, and to fear God, and suffer no man para avoir to do con her as je have done, which she promised. Je did give her 20s. and directions para laisser sealed in paper at any time the name of the place of her being at Herringman’s, my bookseller in the ‘Change, by which I might go para her, and so bid her good night with much content to my mind, and resolution to look after her no more till I heard from her. And so home, and there told my wife a fair tale, God knows, how I spent the whole day, with which the poor wretch was satisfied, or at least seemed so, and so to supper and to bed, she having been mighty busy all day in getting of her house in order against to-morrow to hang up our new hangings and furnishing our best chamber.

levels.sentence: I slipped away under my wife's jealous eye, hunted down Deb through a chain of porters, and stole a dark coach-ride with her before coming home to a lie and a fresh-hung chamber.
levels.paragraph: I lay long in bed while my wife voiced her jealousy, and though I denied it, I was no sooner out than I made straight for Somerset House to trace Dr. Allbun and, through him, Deb. After a day of enquiries, portering, and walking the Strand, a message brought word she was well and willing, and I went to her in the dark, kissed her, counselled her to keep her honour, gave her twenty shillings, and arranged how to reach her through my bookseller. Then I came home and told my wife a fair tale, and she seemed satisfied, busy preparing our best chamber for new hangings.
levels.summary:
Waking late, I found my wife suspicious and jealous, fearing I meant to visit Deb; I denied it, and God forgive me for the lie, for at noon I went straight to Somerset House to find Dr. Allbun, with whom Deb was lodged.

A porter told me Allbun had just moved to Lincoln's Inn Fields, and though I spent the day between White Hall, Povy's, the Strand, and Hercules Pillars, I could not learn his lodging until the chest-carrying porter agreed to carry a message to Mrs. Willet from a friend in London.

At nightfall the porter returned to say she was well and I might see her, and my reason could not hold me back. I rode to her in the dark, she came into the coach, and I kissed her; yet I gave her the best counsel I could—to guard her honour, fear God, and let no man do with her as I had done—which she promised.

I gave her 20s. and a sealed direction to leave news of her whereabouts at Herringman's, my bookseller, and resolved to seek her no more till I heard from her.

Home I went, told my wife a fair tale, and she, poor wretch, seemed satisfied, having been busy all day setting the house in order against to-morrow's hanging of our new hangings.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and at the Office all the morning, with my heart full of joy to think in what a safe condition all my matters now stand between my wife and Deb, and me, and at noon running up stairs to see the upholsters, who are at work upon hanging my best room, and setting up my new bed, I find my wife sitting sad in the dining room; which enquiring into the reason of, she begun to call me all the false, rotten-hearted rogues in the world, letting me understand that I was with Deb. yesterday, which, thinking it impossible for her ever to understand, I did a while deny, but at last did, for the ease of my mind and hers, and for ever to discharge my heart of this wicked business, I did confess all, and above stairs in our bed chamber there I did endure the sorrow of her threats and vows and curses all the afternoon, and, what was worse, she swore by all that was good that she would slit the nose of this girle, and be gone herself this very night from me, and did there demand 3 or L400 of me to buy my peace, that she might be gone without making any noise, or else protested that she would make all the world know of it. So with most perfect confusion of face and heart, and sorrow and shame, in the greatest agony in the world I did pass this afternoon, fearing that it will never have an end; but at last I did call for W. Hewer, who I was forced to make privy now to all, and the poor fellow did cry like a child, obtained what I could not, that she would be pacified upon condition that I would give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb, while I live, as I did before with Pierce and Knepp, and which I did also, God knows, promise for Deb. too, but I have the confidence to deny it to the perjury of myself. So, before it was late, there was, beyond my hopes as well as desert, a durable peace; and so to supper, and pretty kind words, and to bed, and there je did hazer con eile to her content, and so with some rest spent the night in bed, being most absolutely resolved, if ever I can master this bout, never to give her occasion while I live of more trouble of this or any other kind, there being no curse in the world so great as this of the differences between myself and her, and therefore I do, by the grace of God, promise never to offend her more, and did this night begin to pray to God upon my knees alone in my chamber, which God knows I cannot yet do heartily; but I hope God will give me the grace more and more every day to fear Him, and to be true to my poor wife. This night the upholsters did finish the hanging of my best chamber, but my sorrow and trouble is so great about this business, that it puts me out of all joy in looking upon it or minding how it was.

levels.sentence: After my wife somehow discovered I had been with Deb the day before, I confessed the whole wicked business, endured her furious threats and curses all afternoon, and at last bought peace by promising under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again, yet the finished bedchamber gave me no joy.
levels.paragraph: I came upstairs in high spirits to see the upholsterers at work upon my best room, but found my wife sitting sad in the dining room. She soon called me every false, rotten-hearted rogue in the world and let me understand that she knew I had been with Deb yesterday. I denied it for a while, but at last confessed all, to ease my mind and hers and to discharge my heart of this wicked business. All afternoon I endured her threats, vows, and curses, until W. Hewer, who cried like a child, helped obtain a peace upon condition that I give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again. Even after supper and bed, and though the chamber was finished, my heart had no joy in it.
levels.summary:
I went to the Office all morning with a heart full of joy, but when I ran upstairs to see the upholsterers hanging my best room and setting up my new bed, I found my wife sitting sad in the dining room. She called me every false, rotten-hearted rogue in the world and made clear she knew I had been with Deb yesterday.

Though I thought it impossible for her to understand, I denied it for a while and then confessed the whole wicked business, for the ease of my mind and hers and to discharge my heart of it.

All afternoon I endured her threats, vows, and curses. She swore by all that was good that she would slit the girl's nose and be gone that very night, demanding three or four hundred pounds to buy her peace, or else she would make all the world know of my treachery. I feared it would never have an end.

In the greatest agony and shame I called for W. Hewer, who was forced to be privy to all and cried like a child; he obtained what I could not, a pacified wife, on condition that I give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb while I live, as I had formerly done with Pierce and Knepp.

To my own perjury I denied that I had made the same promise for Deb.

Before it was late, beyond my hopes as well as desert, there was a durable peace. We went to supper with pretty kind words and to bed, where I made love to her content. I am absolutely resolved, if ever I can master this bout, never to give her occasion of more trouble of this or any other kind while I live.

That night I began to pray to God on my knees alone, though not yet heartily, and the upholsterers finished my best chamber; but my sorrow and trouble put me out of all joy in looking upon it.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and walked abroad in the garden, and find that Mrs. Tooker has not any of her daughters here as I expected and so walked to the yard, leaving Middleton at the pay, and there I only walked up and down the yard, and then to the Hill-House, and there did give order for the coach to be made ready; and got Mr. Gibson, whom I carried with me, to go with me and Mr. Coney, the surgeon, towards Maydston which I had a mighty mind to see, and took occasion, in my way, at St. Margett’s, to pretend to call to see Captain Allen to see whether Mrs. Jowles, his daughter, was there; and there his wife come to the door, he being at London, and through a window, I spied Jowles, but took no notice of he but made excuse till night, and then promised to come and see Mrs. Allen again, and so away, it being a mighty cold and windy, but clear day; and had the pleasure of seeing the Medway running, winding up and down mightily, and a very fine country; and I went a little out of the way to have visited Sir John Bankes, but he at London; but here I had a sight of his seat and house, the outside, which is an old abbey just like Hinchingbroke, and as good at least, and mighty finely placed by the river; and he keeps the grounds about it, and walls and the house, very handsome: I was mightily pleased with the sight of it. Thence to Maydstone, which I had a mighty mind to see, having never been there; and walked all up and down the town, and up to the top of the steeple, and had a noble view, and then down again: and in the town did see an old man beating of flax, and did step into the barn and give him money, and saw that piece of husbandry which I never saw, and it is very pretty: in the street also I did buy and send to our inne, the Bell, a dish of fresh fish. And so, having walked all round the town, and found it very pretty, as most towns I ever saw, though not very big, and people of good fashion in it, we to our inne to dinner, and had a good dinner; and after dinner a barber come to me, and there trimmed me, that I might be clean against night, to go to Mrs. Allen. And so, staying till about four o’clock, we set out, I alone in the coach going and coming; and in our way back, I ‘light out of the way to see a Saxon monument, as they say, of a King, which is three stones standing upright, and a great round one lying on them, of great bigness, although not so big as those on Salisbury Plain; but certainly it is a thing of great antiquity, and I mightily glad to see it; it is near to Aylesford, where Sir John Bankes lives. So homeward, and stopped again at Captain Allen’s, and there ‘light, and sent the coach and Gibson home, and I and Coney staid; and there comes to us Mrs. Jowles, who is a very fine, proper lady, as most I know, and well dressed. Here was also a gentleman, one Major Manly, and his wife, neighbours; and here we staid, and drank, and talked, and set Coney and him to play while Mrs. Jowles and I to talk, and there had all our old stories up, and there I had the liberty to salute her often, and pull off her glove, where her hand mighty moist, and she mighty free in kindness to me, and je do not at all doubt that I might have had that that I would have desired de elle had I had time to have carried her to Cobham, as she, upon my proposing it, was very willing to go, for elle is a whore, that is certain, but a very brave and comely one. Here was a pretty cozen of hers come in to supper also, of a great fortune, daughter-in-law to this Manly, mighty pretty, but had now such a cold, she could not speak. Here mightily pleased with Mrs. Jowles, and did get her to the street door, and there to her su breasts, and baiser her without any force, and credo that I might have had all else, but it was not time nor place. Here staid till almost twelve at night, and then with a lanthorn from thence walked over the fields, as dark as pitch, and mighty cold, and snow, to Chatham, and Mr. Coney with great kindness to me: and there all in bed before I come home, and so I presently to bed.

levels.sentence: I rode to Maidstone with Gibson and Coney, enjoyed the sights along the way, and on my return spent an evening of free flirtation with Mrs. Jowles, taking liberties but leaving before the final act.
levels.paragraph: I set out for Maidstone with Gibson and Mr. Coney, eager to see a town I had never visited. The ride was cold and windy but the country was fine, and I enjoyed the sight of Sir John Bankes's abbey and later the Saxon stones near Aylesford. In Maidstone I walked the town, climbed the steeple, and watched an old man beating flax. On the way back I stopped again at Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles proved very free with her kindness, allowing me to kiss her and touch her breast at the door, though I lacked time and place to carry her to Cobham.
levels.summary:
I took a coach with Gibson and Mr. Coney, surgeon, toward Maidstone, having a mighty desire to see that town. On the way I stopped at Captain Allen's to give the pretence of calling on him, but really to see if his daughter Mrs. Jowles was about; she was, but I took no notice and promised to return at night.

Riding on, I was pleased with the sight of the Medway and the fine country, and I turned aside to see Sir John Bankes's old abbey, though he was in London. At Maidstone I walked all over the town, climbed the steeple for a noble view, watched an old man beating flax, and bought fresh fish for our dinner at the Bell.

In the afternoon we set back, and I stopped to see a Saxon monument of three stones by Aylesford. Then I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Mr. Coney. Mrs.

Jowles came to us, a fine, proper lady, and we talked over old stories while I took the liberty to salute her often, pull off her glove, and find her hand moist. She was very willing to go with me to Cobham, for I believe she is a whore, but a brave and comely one.

A pretty cousin of hers came to supper, and later I got Mrs. Jowles to the street door, where I touched her breasts and kissed her without force. I might have had all else, but it was neither the time nor the place.

We stayed till almost midnight, then walked over the fields in pitch darkness and snow to Chatham, where I went straight to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to the office, and thence before the office sat to the Excise Office with W. Hewer, but found some occasion to go another way to the Temple upon business, and I by Deb.’s direction did know whither in Jewen Street to direct my hackney coachman, while I staid in the coach in Aldgate Street, to go thither just to enquire whether Mrs. Hunt, her aunt, was in town, who brought me word she was not; thought this was as much as I could do at once, and therefore went away troubled through that I could do no more but to the office I must go and did, and there all the morning, but coming thither I find Bagwell’s wife, who did give me a little note into my hand, wherein I find her para invite me para meet her in Moorfields this noon, where I might speak with her, and so after the office was up, my wife being gone before by invitation to my cozen Turner’s to dine, I to the place, and there, after walking up and down by the windmills, I did find her and talk with her, but it being holiday and the place full of people, we parted, leaving further discourse and doing to another time. Thence I away, and through Jewen Street, my mind, God knows, running that way, but stopped not, but going down Holborne hill, by the Conduit, I did see Deb. on foot going up the hill. I saw her, and she me, but she made no stop, but seemed unwilling to speak to me; so I away on, but then stopped and ‘light, and after her and overtook her at the end of Hosier lane in Smithfield, and without standing in the street desired her to follow me, and I led her into a little blind alehouse within the walls, and there she and I alone fell to talk and baiser la and toker su mammailles, but she mighty coy, and I hope modest.... I did give her in a paper 20s., and we did agree para meet again in the Hall at Westminster on Monday next; and so giving me great hopes by her carriage that she continues modest and honest, we did there part, she going home and I to Mrs. Turner’s, but when I come back to the place where I left my coach it was gone, I having staid too long, which did trouble me to abuse the poor fellow, so that taking another coach I did direct him to find out the fellow and send him to me. At my cozen Turner’s I find they are gone all to dinner to Povy’s, and thither I, and there they were all, and W. Batelier and his sister, and had dined; but I had good things brought me, and then all up and down the house, and mightily pleased to see the fine rooms: but, the truth is, there are so many bad pictures, that to me make the good ones lose much of the pleasure in seeing them. The. and Betty Turner in new flowered tabby gowns, and so we were pretty merry, only my fear upon me for what I had newly done, do keep my content in. So, about five or six o’clock, away, and I took my wife and the two Bateliers, and carried them homeward, and W. Batelier ‘lighting, I carried the women round by Islington, and so down Bishopsgate Street home, and there to talk and sup, and then to bed.

levels.sentence: I spent the day pursuing secret meetings with Bagwell's wife and then Deb., while trying to attend to business and social obligations, leaving me both hopeful and guilt-ridden.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to the office, but my thoughts were elsewhere. Following Deb.'s direction, I tried to visit her aunt in Jewen Street but found her not in town. Later, I met Bagwell's wife in Moorfields, but the holiday crowd forced us to part. Then I saw Deb. on Holborn Hill and led her into a blind alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she stayed coy. I gave her twenty shillings and arranged another meeting, but my mind was full of trouble. I rejoined my wife and friends at Povy's house, but the bad pictures and my own fears spoiled my pleasure.
levels.summary:
's directions to search for her aunt in Jewen Street, only to learn she was away. Back at the office, I found Bagwell's wife waiting, and she slipped me a note asking me to meet her in Moorfields.

I went there after the office rose, but because it was a holiday and crowded, we could only talk briefly and agreed to meet another time.

While riding through the city, I caught sight of Deb. on Holborn Hill. I followed her into a little alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she seemed modest and hesitant. I gave her twenty shillings and we agreed to meet again in Westminster Hall on Monday.

My heart was troubled by what I had done, and even at my cousin Turner's and then at Povy's house, among family and friends, I could not shake my unease. I took my wife and the Bateliers home by way of Islington, and after supper went to bed, carrying my secret with me.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Troubled, about three in the morning, with my wife’s calling her maid up, and rising herself, to go with her coach abroad, to gather May-dew, which she did, and I troubled for it, for fear of any hurt, going abroad so betimes, happening to her; but I to sleep again, and she come home about six, and to bed again all well, and I up and with Mr. Gibson by coach to St. James’s, and thence to White Hall, where the Duke of York met the Office, and there discoursed of several things, particularly the Instructions of Commanders of ships. But here happened by chance a discourse of the Council of Trade, against which the Duke of York is mightily displeased, and particularly Mr. Child, against whom he speaking hardly, Captain Cox did second the Duke of York, by saying that he was talked of for an unfayre dealer with masters of ships, about freight: to which Sir T. Littleton very hotly and foolishly replied presently, that he never heard any honest man speak ill of Child; to which the Duke of York did make a smart reply, and was angry; so as I was sorry to hear it come so far, and that I, by seeming to assent to Cox, might be observed too much by Littleton, though I said nothing aloud, for this must breed great heart-burnings. After this meeting done, the Duke of York took the Treasurers into his closet to chide them, as Mr. Wren tells me; for that my Lord Keeper did last night at the Council say, when nobody was ready to say any thing against the constitution of the Navy, that he did believe the Treasurers of the Navy had something to say, which was very foul on their part, to be parties against us. They being gone, Mr. Wren took boat, thinking to dine with my Lord of Canterbury; but, when we come to Lambeth, the gate was shut, which is strictly done at twelve o’clock, and nobody comes in afterwards: so we lost our labour, and therefore back to White Hall, and thence walked my boy Jacke with me, to my Lord Crew, whom I have not seen since he was sick, which is eight months ago, I think and there dined with him: he is mightily broke. A stranger a country gentleman, was with him: and he pleased with my discourse accidentally about the decay of gentlemen’s families in the country, telling us that the old rule was, that a family might remain fifty miles from London one hundred years, one hundred miles from London two hundred years, and so farther, or nearer London more or less years. He also told us that he hath heard his father say, that in his time it was so rare for a country gentleman to come to London, that, when he did come, he used to make his will before he set out. Thence: to St. James’s, and there met the Duke of York, who told me, with great content, that he did now think he should master our adversaries, for that the King did tell him that he was; satisfied in the constitution of the Navy, but that it was well to give these people leave to object against it, which they having not done, he did give order to give warrant to the Duke of York to direct Sir Jeremy Smith to be a Commissioner of the Navy in the room of Pen; which, though he be an impertinent fellow, yet I am glad of it, it showing that the other side is not so strong as it was: and so, in plain terms, the Duke of York did tell me, that they were every day losing ground; and particularly that he would take care to keep out Child: at all which I am glad, though yet I dare not think myself secure, as the King may yet be wrought upon by these people to bring changes in our Office, and remove us, ere it be long. Thence I to White Hall, an there took boat to Westminster, and to Mrs. Martin’s, who is not come to town from her husband at Portsmouth. So drank only at Cragg’s with Doll, and so to the Swan, and there baiser a new maid that is there, and so to White Hall again, to a Committee of Tangier, where I see all things going to rack in the business of the Corporation, and consequently in the place, by Middleton’s going. Thence walked a little with Creed, who tells me he hears how fine my horses and coach are, and advises me to avoid being noted for it, which I was vexed to hear taken notice of, it being what I feared and Povy told me of my gold-lace sleeves in the Park yesterday, which vexed me also, so as to resolve never to appear in Court with them, but presently to have them taken off, as it is fit I should, and so to my wife at Unthanke’s, and coach, and so called at my tailor’s to that purpose, and so home, and after a little walk in the garden, home to supper and to bed.

levels.sentence: Troubled by my wife's early May-dew outing, I spent the day navigating court rivalries, dining with Lord Crew, hearing from the Duke of York that our adversaries were losing ground, and then fretting over my own ostentatious coach and gold-lace sleeves.
levels.paragraph: I rose troubled at three when my wife went off with her maid to gather May-dew, and though I feared for her safety, she came home well and to bed. The day was taken up with court business, where the Duke of York clashed with Sir T. Littleton over Mr. Child, leaving me anxious about heart-burnings. I dined with Lord Crew, who is much decayed, and heard his curious rule about country families and distance from London. Later the Duke of York assured me our adversaries were losing ground, and that Sir Jeremy Smith would be made Commissioner, which gladdened me, though I remain wary. My pleasure was spoiled by warnings about my fine coach and gold-lace sleeves, so I resolved to have the lace taken off.
levels.summary:
Troubled at three in the morning, I could not rest while my wife went abroad to gather May-dew; she returned safe, but my unease lingered. At White Hall, the Duke of York met the Office, and a hot dispute broke out about Mr. Child: Captain Cox seconded the Duke's hard words, and Sir T.

Littleton replied foolishly, so that the Duke grew angry. I was careful not to be seen to take sides, for fear of breeding heart-burnings.

After a wasted trip to Lambeth with Mr. Wren, I dined with my Lord Crew, who is mightily decayed since his sickness. He entertained me with an old rule about country families lasting longer the farther they lived from London.

Then the Duke of York told me the King was satisfied with the Navy constitution, and that Sir Jeremy Smith would replace Pen as Commissioner. He declared our adversaries were losing ground and that he would keep out Child; I was glad, though I dare not think myself secure.

I stopped at several taverns, kissed a new maid at the Swan, but found Mrs. Martin absent. At the Committee of Tangier, things seemed going to rack. Creed and Povy both noticed my fine coach and gold-lace sleeves in the Park, which vexed me, so I resolved to have the lace taken off and avoid such notice.

I walked briefly in my garden, then supped and went to bed.

I stopped at several taverns, kissed a new maid at the Swan, but found Mrs. Martin absent. At the Committee of Tangier, things seemed going to rack. Creed and Povy both noticed my fine coach and gold-lace sleeves in the Park, which vexed me, so I resolved to have the lace taken off and avoid such notice.

I walked briefly in my garden, then supped and went to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up, and to Westminster Hall, where the term is, and this the first day of my being there, and here by chance met Roger Pepys, come to town the last night: I was glad to see him. After some talk with him and others, and among others Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu, the latter of whom is to set out to-morrow towards Flanders and Italy, I invited them to dine with me to-morrow, and so to Mrs. Martin’s lodging, who come to town last night, and there je did hazer her, she having been a month, I think, at Portsmouth with her husband, newly come home from the Streights. But, Lord! how silly the woman talks of her great entertainment there, and how all the gentry come to visit her, and that she believes her husband is worth L6 or L700, which nevertheless I am glad of, but I doubt they will spend it a fast. Thence home, and after dinner my wife and I to the Duke of York’s playhouse, and there, in the side balcony, over against the musick, did hear, but not see, a new play, the first day acted, “The Roman Virgin,” an old play, and but ordinary, I thought; but the trouble of my eyes with the light of the candles did almost kill me. Thence to my Lord Sandwich’s, and there had a promise from Sidney to come and dine with me to-morrow; and so my wife and I home in our coach, and there find my brother John, as I looked for, come to town from Ellington, where, among other things, he tell me the first news that my is with child, and fat gone, which I know not whether it did more trouble or please me, having no great care for my friends to have children; though I love other people’s. So, glad to see him, we to supper, and so to bed.

levels.paragraph: I began the morning at Westminster Hall, where the term opened and I met Roger Pepys, newly come to town, and later promised Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu that they would dine with me tomorrow. From there I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, fresh from Portsmouth, and lay with her, all while she chattered about the gentry who visited her and her husband's supposed fortune, which I fear they will squander. In the afternoon my wife and I went to the Duke of York's playhouse, but from the side balcony I could only hear 'The Roman Virgin' and the candlelight pained my eyes terribly. That evening, after securing Sidney's promise to dine with me, I found my brother John at home from Ellington; he told me the first news that my sister is with child and far gone — which I hardly know whether to welcome or deplore. We supped, and so to bed.

I also spoke with Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu, and invited them to dine with me tomorrow; Sidney, who sets out for Flanders and Italy, gave his promise when I saw him later.

From the Hall I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, where I had my way with her; she had been a month at Portsmouth with her husband, newly home from the Streights, and talked proudly of the gentry who came to visit her and of her husband being worth six or seven hundred pounds — a sum I suspect they will spend quickly.

My wife and I then went to the Duke of York's playhouse, where we sat in the side balcony over against the music; I could hear but not see the new play, 'The Roman Virgin,' which I thought old and ordinary, and the candlelight nearly destroyed my eyes.

Afterwards I went to Lord Sandwich's and came home to find my brother John arrived from Ellington. He brought the first news that my sister is with child, and far gone. I was uncertain whether this troubled or pleased me, for I have never much cared to see my own friends have children, though I love other people's.

Still, I was glad to see John, and we had supper and went to bed.

entries.subject: today
entries.raw: Up very betimes, and so continued all the morning with W. Hewer, upon examining and stating my accounts, in order to the fitting myself to go abroad beyond sea, which the ill condition of my eyes, and my neglect for a year or two, hath kept me behindhand in, and so as to render it very difficult now, and troublesome to my mind to do it; but I this day made a satisfactory entrance therein. Dined at home, and in the afternoon by water to White Hall, calling by the way at Michell’s, where I have not been many a day till just the other day, and now I met her mother there and knew her husband to be out of town. And here je did baiser elle, but had not opportunity para hazer some with her as I would have offered if je had had it. And thence had another meeting with the Duke of York, at White Hall, on yesterday’s work, and made a good advance: and so, being called by my wife, we to the Park, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman, a friend of hers, being with us. Thence to “The World’s End,” a drinking-house by the Park; and there merry, and so home late. And thus ends all that I doubt I shall ever be able to do with my own eyes in the keeping of my journal, I being not able to do it any longer, having done now so long as to undo my eyes almost every time that I take a pen in my hand; and, therefore, whatever comes of it, I must forbear: and, therefore, resolve, from this time forward, to have it kept by my people in long-hand, and must therefore be contented to set down no more than is fit for them and all the world to know; or, if there be any thing, which cannot be much, now my amours to Deb. are past, and my eyes hindering me in almost all other pleasures, I must endeavour to keep a margin in my book open, to add, here and there, a note in short-hand with my own hand. And so I betake myself to that course, which is almost as much as to see myself go into my grave: for which, and all the discomforts that will accompany my being blind, the good God prepare me! May 31, 1669. END OF THE DIARY. PREFACE First issue of this edition June, 1896. Reprinted 1897. In the present volume the Diary is completed, and we here take leave of a writer who has done so much to interest and enlighten successive generations of English readers, and who is now for the first time presented to the world as he really drew his own portrait day by day. No one who has followed the daily notes of Samuel Pepys from January, 1660, to May, 1669, but must feel sincere regret at their abrupt conclusion, more particularly as the writer lays down his pen while in an unhappy temper. It is evident from the tone of his later utterances that Pepys thought that he was going blind, a belief which was happily falsified. The holiday tour in which Charles II. and James, Duke of York, took so much interest appears to have had its desired effect in restoring the Diarist to health. The rest of his eventful life must be sought in the history of the English Navy which he helped to form, and in his numerous letters, which on some future occasion the present editor hopes to annotate. The details to be obtained from these sources form, however, but a sorry substitute for the words written in the solitude of his office by Pepys for his own eye alone, and we cannot but feel how great is the world’s loss in that he never resumed the writing of his journal. All must agree with Coleridge when he wrote on the margin of a copy of the Diary: “Truly may it be said that this was a greater and more grievous loss to the mind’s eye of posterity than to the bodily organs of Pepys himself. It makes me restless and discontented to think what a Diary equal in minuteness and truth of portraiture to the preceding from 1669 to 1688 or 1690 would have been for the true causes, process and character of the Revolution.” Most works of this nature are apt to tire when they are extended over a certain length of time, but Pepys’s pages are always fresh, and most readers wish for more. For himself the editor can say that each time he has read over the various proofs he has read with renewed interest, so that it is with no ordinary feelings of regret that he comes to the end of his task, and he believes that every reader will feel the same regret that he has no more to read. In reviewing the Diary it is impossible not to notice the growth of historical interest as it proceeds. In the earlier period we find Pepys surrounded by men not otherwise known, but as the years pass, and his position becomes more assured, we find him in daily communication with the chief men of his day, and evidently every one who came in contact with him appreciated his remarkable ability. The survival of the Diary must ever remain a marvel. It could never have been intended for the reading of others, but doubtless the more elaborate portraits of persons in the later pages were intended for use when Pepys came to write his projected history of the Navy. The only man who is uniformly spoken well of in the Diary is Sir William Coventry, and many of the characters introduced come in for severe castigation. It is therefore the more necessary to remember that many of the judgments on men were set down hastily, and would probably have been modified had occasion offered. At all events, we know that, however much he may have censured them, Pepys always helped on those who were dependent upon him. H. R. W. ETEXT EDITOR’S BOOKMARKS, DIARY OF SAMUEL PEPYS, 1969 N.S. levels.sentence: On this last day of my journal, I set my accounts in order, kissed Mrs. Michell, saw the Duke of York, laughed with my wife and friends at The World's End, and then resolved that my failing eyes must force me to lay down my pen and have my diary kept by others.
levels.paragraph: I rose very early and spent the morning with W. Hewer on my accounts, trying to put my affairs in order for going abroad; my weak eyes made the work difficult, but I made a satisfactory beginning. After dining at home I went by water to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's to kiss Mrs. Michell, and then met again with the Duke of York and advanced yesterday's business. In the evening I went to the Park with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman, and we finished merrily at The World's End. But this is the last entry I can write with my own eyes; I must henceforth have the journal kept in long-hand by others, and I feel as if I am going into my grave.
levels.summary:
Today I rose very early and spent the morning with W. Hewer, examining and stating my accounts so that I might fit myself to go abroad. My eyes have been so ill and my neglect of a year or two has left me behindhand, and this work was difficult and troublesome to my mind; still, I made a satisfactory entrance into it.

After dining at home, I went by water to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's, where I saw her mother, knew her husband was out of town, and kissed Mrs. Michell, though I had no opportunity for more. I then met again with the Duke of York about yesterday's work and made a good advance.

My wife called me, and we went to the Park with Mary Batelier and a Dutch gentleman, her friend. From there we went to The World's End, a drinking-house by the Park, and were merry before coming home late. But the real burden of this day is the realisation that I can no longer keep my journal with my own eyes.

Almost every time I take a pen in hand I undo my eyes, and so I must forbear.

I have resolved that from this time forward my journal shall be kept by my people in long-hand, and that I must set down no more than is fit for them and all the world to know. If there be anything, which cannot be much now that my amours to Deb.

are past, I must keep a margin in my book to add a note in short-hand with my own hand. This feels almost like seeing myself go into my grave; and for all the discomforts that will accompany my being blind, I pray God to prepare me.

The preface tells me that I was happily mistaken, and that my holiday tour restored me, yet still the world lost the daily private words that I never resumed.

periods.label: Week of Jan 18

levels.sentence: Mr. Downing's claim that he had made me a Clerk of the Council left me more suspicious than grateful, and the day was spent in errands, a feast, and rumors that all the other clerks were turned out.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was sent for to Mr. Downing, who told me he had got me to be one of the Clerks of the Council. I was stumbled and could not tell whether to thank him, fearing he did it only to ease himself of the salary he gives me. Later I met with Sir Ant. Cooper and got leave to keep the lodgings, so Mr. Sheply could go into the country. I waited at Downing's, read the Dutch Ambassador's answer contradicting my Lord's reasons, and then dined on turkey with Mrs. Jem and Moore. In the evening I observed Downing feasting Sir Arth. Haselrigge, delivered notes to invite members, and heard that all the other Clerks of the Council were turned out except the two Leighs.
levels.summary:
Mr. Downing told me at his bedside that he had made me a Clerk of the Council, but I was not heartily thankful, fearing he only wanted to escape paying me the salary I already received. After that I went with Mr. Sheply and Mr. Pierce to the Harp and Ball, then to Whitehall, where Sir Ant.

Cooper allowed us to keep the lodgings, so Sheply decided to go into the country the next day.

I spent the rest of the morning at Downing's, waiting for someone to read writings who never came, and instead read the Dutch Ambassador's answer to our State, which argued against my Lord's reasons for coming home. After dining on a turkey with Mrs.

Jem and Moore, I went to the French Ordinary, where Downing feasted Sir Arth. Haselrigge and many Parliament members; he gave me a note to invite more members to dinner the next day.

At Whitehall I heard from the Clerks of the Council that all of them were turned out, except the two Leighs, and that my name had been mentioned, but nothing decided.

periods.label: Week of Aug 8

levels.sentence: I went from the Privy Seal to my tailor, heard Sir Samuel Morland's secret history of serving the King, dined with my father, settled my brother's allowance and my M.A. fee, and finished the day merrily with my servants combing my head.
levels.paragraph: I began at the Privy Seal, where I agreed with Mr Pim for a velvet coat and heard Sir Samuel Morland tell how Thurloe's bad usage drove him to serve the King, discovering Sir R. Willis and sinking his own fortune. The King has now given him a £500 yearly pension and the benefit of two baronets, which makes me think better of him. Back at the Tower, my father dined with me, and I paid him for my brother John and settled with Mr Fairbrother for my Master of Arts degree. Captain Cuttance brought a firkin of butter for my wife, and at night, after White Hall, I had good sport with the girl and boy combing my head in the kitchen.
levels.summary:
This day was full of business and small reckonings. I went to the Privy Seal, where I settled with Mr Pim for a velvet coat, and there Sir Samuel Morland stayed with me a great while, telling me the whole manner of how he had served the King in the time of the Protector.

He spoke of Thurloe's bad usage, how he discovered Sir R. Willis, how he had sunk his fortune for the King, and how the King now gives him £500 a year out of the Post Office for life and the benefit of two baronets. This makes me begin to think he is not so much a fool as I took him to be.

At the Tower, my father, Mr Fairbrother, and Cooke dined with me. Young Captain Cuttance of the Speedwell brought me a firkin of butter for my wife, which was very welcome. After dinner my father took leave, after I had given him 40s.

for the last half-year for my brother John at Cambridge; and I made even with Mr Fairbrother for my degree of Master of Arts, costing about £9 16s. My wife and I went by water to White Hall, where I was busy at the Privy Seal all afternoon.

At night we returned home, and I made good sport having the girl and the boy comb my head before I went to bed in the kitchen.

periods.label: Week of Sep 4

levels.sentence: A day of farewells, family dinner, a heated quarrel with Antony Joyce, and evening rope-dancing, all shadowed by my wife's mysterious appointment and a dying aunt's summons.
levels.paragraph: This morning I took leave of my mother, who set off for Brampton with my sister Pall, and saw them into the waggon, Pall crying bitterly. After a merry dinner at my uncle Fenner's, I was summoned to attend my dying aunt Kite, but instead found myself quarrelling with Antony Joyce, whose meddling made me very angry. Later I took my wife to the fair, where we watched Italian rope-dancers and women tumbling, yet my mind remained vexed by Antony's words and by the secret message my wife received from a French footman.
levels.summary:
I began the day by attending to business at the Privy Seal, then took leave of my mother as she set out for Brampton with my sister Pall, whom I had given twenty shillings and good counsel.

At my uncle Fenner's I found my wife and Pall, and I saw the two women off from Beard's, Pall crying bitterly as the waggon pulled away. We then drank with my aunt Bell and Charles Pepys before sitting down to a merry family dinner.

After dinner, word came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, lay dying and asked my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.

Before I could respond, Antony Joyce picked a quarrel with me that grew into high words, and though he spoke even worse to his father, the whole company was offended and we parted angry.

I took my wife to the fair, where we saw Italian rope-dancers and women doing strange tumbling tricks, but I walked home vexed about Antony and troubled by a private message a French footman had delivered to my wife, who promised to go somewhere tomorrow morning without telling me what it was.

periods.label: Week of May 28

levels.sentence: I set my private and public affairs in order—paying debts, trimming my beard, auditing my estate, and noting the kingdom's unsettled news—and I am the better for it.
levels.paragraph: I rose late and caught up on my journal, then dealt with Anthony Joyce's dunning before dining with my father and talking over family business. In the evening I had Sarah comb my head, cut off my beard, and wash my feet, resolving to keep my hair unpowdered and my face smooth with pumice. The month ends with fair weather and news of the Queen at Hampton Court, a peace with Algiers, and my own estate worth £530. I have sworn off wine and plays, and find it does me good.
levels.summary:
Today I began with my journal, but was soon vexed by Anthony Joyce, who came dunning me for money I owed for tallow; I promised to pay him next. I went to White Hall looking for Sir G. Carteret, missed him, and instead brought my father home to dinner, where we talked over our dealings with uncle Thomas and T. Trice.

After the office met, I did errands at my brother's and the Wardrobe, then came home to Sarah, who combed my head.

I was disgusted to find it so foul from powdering, so I resolved to try keeping my head dry without powder; and in a sudden fit I cut off all my beard, planning to shave my whole face with pumice-stone to save time. She washed my feet in a herb bath, and I went to bed.

The month ends with fine weather and my health pretty good, though wind torments me. The Queen has come to Hampton Court and is much praised as handsome and discreet; the King seems pleased with her, which I fear will put Madam Castlemaine's nose out of joint.

There is good news of a peace with Algiers, and my Lord Sandwich has arrived safely with the Queen, in good repute. My father is in town, and though his visit costs money, I am pleased with the alterations at Brampton. My audit shows I am worth about £530 clear.

The Act for Uniformity has just been printed and is expected to make mad work among the Presbyterian ministers. People on all sides are discontented—some think they are used too hardly contrary to promise, others that the King has not rewarded them enough. God keep us all.

I have taken a late oath to abstain from wine and plays, and I already find good effect from it.

periods.label: Week of Dec 31

levels.sentence: I closed 1662 in high mirth at the King's ball, yet with sober thoughts on my health, purse, servants, family, and the kingdom's quietness.
levels.paragraph: I spent New Year's Eve at White Hall, first dining at Mrs. Pierce's and then dancing at the King's ball, where the King led out the Duchess of York and all the Court followed. Yet my mind was as full of reckonings as of revels: I reviewed my family, my savings of £650, the oaths that had kept me orderly, and the troubles with Uncle Thomas's estate. Public matters also weighed on me, from the King's open dalliance with Lady Castlemaine to fears about Monmouth and the Duke of York. Still, I thanked God for my health, my wife, and the quiet state of the nation.
levels.summary:
The day began quietly, with my morning draft at the Swan and Mr. Bowyer's gossip about his cousin Butler and Colonel Dillon, who had broken off after letters were opened and knavery discovered. Then I dined at Mrs. Pierce's with Dr. Clerke and Mr. Knight, where I found myself less admiring of Mrs.

Pierce's beauty and Mrs. Clerke's wit than I once had been, though the company was merry. After dinner I attended the Tangier Committee with the Duke of York, and later went with Mr. Povy and Mr. Gauden to Mr. Bland's to discuss the delays in sending boats and provisions to Tangier, where I was pleased to hear Mrs.

Bland talk like a merchant.

The evening brought the greatest pleasure: Mr. Povy carried me to White Hall and into the King's ball, crammed with the finest ladies of the Court. " I watched with infinite content, noting the Duke of Monmouth's mistress, Lady Castlemaine, and Sir Harry de Vicke's daughter as the best dancers.

I left weary but happy, and ended the year in great mirth with my wife.

Looking back, I counted my blessings: good health, a convenient home at the Navy-office, a purse worth about £650, and the orderly life I have led under my oaths against wine and plays. But I also had cares—my maid Jane growing proud, my boy Wayneman to be turned away, and Sarah going to live with Sir W.

Pen, which troubled me. The greatest weight was my uncle Thomas's business, which threatened to pull back my fortune. In public matters, I noted the King's open dalliance with Lady Castlemaine, the splendour of Monmouth, the danger to Lord Chancellor, and the Bishops pressing uniformity.

Yet the nation being quiet, I gave thanks to God for all.

periods.label: Week of Jul 15

levels.sentence: After a morning of scant business, I spent the afternoon dallying with Mrs. Lane and flirting with Mrs. Howlett's daughter, then towzed Mrs. Lane at the Crown in Palace Yard, for which I am heartily ashamed and fear I have caught cold.
levels.paragraph: I rose and did a little business with Sir J. Minnes, then went about town to my bookseller and the instrument maker to bespeak a pocket ruler. In Westminster Hall I waited on Mrs. Lane for my bands, and while she went to the starchers I flirted with Mrs. Howlett's daughter, buying a pair of gloves to talk with her. When Mrs. Lane returned, we met at the Crown and ate a chicken, where I had my full liberty of towzing her, though the last thing leaves me ashamed and resolved never to do so again. She talked much of marriage and fortune, and I pleased her by saying what she wished to hear. I came home all in a sweat, fearful of having taken cold.
levels.summary:
Up early, I did only a little business at the office with Sir J. Minnes, then went to my bookseller's and to Thomson the instrument maker's, where I bespoke a ruler for my pocket for timber measuring. From there I went to the Temple, the Wardrobe, and lastly Westminster Hall, expecting bands from Mrs. Lane.

While Mrs. Lane went to the starchers, I stayed at Mrs. Howlett's shop and bought a pair of gloves to talk with her daughter, whom I call my wife. She is a pretty spoken girl and will prove a mighty handsome wench, and I could love her very well. Then Mrs.

Lane and I met at the Crown in Palace Yard, ate a chicken, drank, and were merry; I towzed her freely and did what I would, but the last thing I am heartily ashamed of and resolve never to do again.

She showed me her hands for fortune-telling, always asking whom and when she would marry, and I pleased her by saying what she wanted. I stayed late until my bands were done, then walked home in a sweat, fearful of having taken cold.

periods.label: Week of Jul 22

levels.sentence: After seeking our lost dog, I enjoyed music with citizens at the Wells, witnessed the King's assent and prorogation at Westminster, spent a pleasant evening with Creed at the Spring Garden, and came home to worry about a swelling that may be a rupture.
levels.paragraph: I rode out to the Wells this morning hoping to recover our dog, and found instead a day of music and ceremony: a knot of citizens singing beautifully under a tree, three cupps with them, and a hard ride home. I then crowded into the Lords' House to see the King give his assent to the subsidies and prorogue the Parliament, his plain speech read lamely from a paper. The evening brought the Spring Garden, codlin tarts, and a tumbling boy, but also a strange moment when one of the Duke's footmen looked me in the face. Now, weary and well pleased, I am troubled by a small swelling near my anus that makes me fear a rupture.
levels.summary:
I rode to the Wells to look for our dog, but could hear nothing; yet the warmer day brought great store of gallant company.

A company singing under a tree, which I at first took for the Waits, proved to be citizens who sang in four or five parts excellently, and I was as pleased with that snapp of musique as ever in my life.

We drank three cupps, rode to Yowell for a breakfast of hashed remains, and after shoeing Creed's horse rode hard home, observing Mr. Gauden's house on the way.

At Westminster I crowded in with the Speaker to the Lords' House and stood close behind him while he made his plain, uneloquent speech to the King in robes.

The King, with his crown on, gave his royal assent to four subsidies and about twenty smaller acts, but the Lord's day bill was lost and the bills against Conventicles and Papists were not passed.

His own speech, read from a paper in his lap, was plain and imperfect, with no spirit; he thanked them for the subsidies, promised care against tumults in the interval, and prorogued the Parliament to 16 March.

I spoke with my Lord Sandwich in the Painted Chamber, who will hasten down into the country once money is settled on the Wardrobe.

Afterwards Creed and I went to the new Spring Garden, where we liked the codlin tarts and saw an idle boy's extraordinary tumbling. We missed Mr. Coventry at St. James's, and one of the Duke's footmen ran up and looked us in the face, which made me fearful.

I came home weary and well pleased, though the ride has raised a swelling just by my anus, about the bigness of a silkworm's bag; it frightens me of a rupture, and I must speak to Mr. Hollyard.

periods.brief: After seeking our lost dog, I enjoyed music with citizens at the Wells, witnessed the King's assent and prorogation at Westminster, spent a pleasant evening with Creed at the Spring Garden, and came home to worry about a swelling that may be a rupture.
periods.full:
I rode to the Wells to look for our dog, but could hear nothing; yet the warmer day brought great store of gallant company.

A company singing under a tree, which I at first took for the Waits, proved to be citizens who sang in four or five parts excellently, and I was as pleased with that snapp of musique as ever in my life.

We drank three cupps, rode to Yowell for a breakfast of hashed remains, and after shoeing Creed's horse rode hard home, observing Mr. Gauden's house on the way.

At Westminster I crowded in with the Speaker to the Lords' House and stood close behind him while he made his plain, uneloquent speech to the King in robes.

The King, with his crown on, gave his royal assent to four subsidies and about twenty smaller acts, but the Lord's day bill was lost and the bills against Conventicles and Papists were not passed.

His own speech, read from a paper in his lap, was plain and imperfect, with no spirit; he thanked them for the subsidies, promised care against tumults in the interval, and prorogued the Parliament to 16 March.

I spoke with my Lord Sandwich in the Painted Chamber, who will hasten down into the country once money is settled on the Wardrobe.

Afterwards Creed and I went to the new Spring Garden, where we liked the codlin tarts and saw an idle boy's extraordinary tumbling. We missed Mr. Coventry at St. James's, and one of the Duke's footmen ran up and looked us in the face, which made me fearful.

I came home weary and well pleased, though the ride has raised a swelling just by my anus, about the bigness of a silkworm's bag; it frightens me of a rupture, and I must speak to Mr. Hollyard.

periods.paragraph: I rode out to the Wells this morning hoping to recover our dog, and found instead a day of music and ceremony: a knot of citizens singing beautifully under a tree, three cupps with them, and a hard ride home. I then crowded into the Lords' House to see the King give his assent to the subsidies and prorogue the Parliament, his plain speech read lamely from a paper. The evening brought the Spring Garden, codlin tarts, and a tumbling boy, but also a strange moment when one of the Duke's footmen looked me in the face. Now, weary and well pleased, I am troubled by a small swelling near my anus that makes me fear a rupture.

periods.label: Week of Sep 2

levels.sentence: On September 4th, I practiced the viol, ran errands, dined at Povy's magnificent house, took my wife to Bartholomew Fair to see strange sights and a clockwork sea spectacle, and read a proclamation for apprehending Lord Bristoll.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with music, then went to Westminster and bought L'Estrange's first newsbook. After an uneasy visit with Mrs. Lane and finding a modest maid for my wife, I dined at Povy's, where I admired his new cellars and grotto yet found his pride a little troublesome. Later I carried my wife to Bartholomew Fair, where we saw dirty monkey sport, odd animals, and a beautiful clockwork sea scene. I finished the evening at the office and read a proclamation against Lord Bristoll.
levels.summary:
After an early hour of viol practice, I went by water to Westminster, where I bought the first newes-books of L'Estrange and spoke with Mrs. Lane, whose eagerness for my company struck me as immodest after my rough handling of her. At Mrs.

Harper's I found a modest-looking maid for my wife and sent her to speak with her.

Creed and I dined at Mr. Povy's with his lady, and I admired his magnificent new cellars, grotto, and fountain, though his self-satisfaction grew a little troublesome.

Later I took my wife to Bartholomew Fair, where we saw monkeys dancing, strange deformed animals, and a delightful clockwork sea scene with Neptune, Venus, mermaids, and a figure on a dolphin. I read a proclamation for apprehending Lord Bristoll, then supped and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 23

levels.sentence: Though I attended to Navy business with Sir Philip Warwick, I strayed to seek Mrs. Lane, yet was denied the main thing, and returned home with guilt and a firm resolution to sin no more.
levels.paragraph: This morning I parted with my brother John and went to Sir Philip Warwick, who assured me the King owes nothing to the Navy and that Sir G. Carteret may owe the King, leaving me doubtful of my own gravity. Later, pretending to my wife I was going to Deptford, I instead met Mrs. Lane at Westminster Hall and took her to Lambeth, where I did everything but the main thing, for which I thank God. After tiring of her, I came home to find my poor wife hard at work, which grieved me to see that I abuse so good a wretch, and I resolved before God never to do the like again.
levels.summary:
This morning I took leave of my brother John and went by water to Sir Philip Warwick's, where we discussed the Navy debt. He made it appear that the King cannot owe the Navy L5,000, and that Sir G. Carteret may actually owe the King money while the Navy debt is fully paid.

I parted with doubts about my own gravity in speaking to so great a man, though I hoped his haste—other important persons waiting—explained it. Then I went to the office, where we sat doing little without Mr. Coventry, and I vexed myself to see what coxcombs we are when he is absent.

In the afternoon, I told my wife I was going to Deptford, but instead took water to Westminster Hall, found Mrs. Lane, and brought her to Lambeth. There I did what I would with her, but she would not consent to the main thing, for which God be praised. I resolved never to do the like again while I live.

After tiring of her company, I landed her at Whitehall and returned home, writing letters at my office until nearly midnight. When I came to bed, I found my poor wife hard at work, which grieved my heart to see that I should abuse so good a wretch.

I saw it was just for God to make her bad with me for my wronging of her, but I resolved never to do the like again.

periods.label: Week of Nov 4

levels.sentence: I held my ground against Sir W. Pen at the office, chased and missed Howlett's daughter, flirted with a pretty lodger at Unthank's, consulted Dr. Turner about freight, and came home with a cold and a plate from Captain Taylor.
levels.paragraph: This morning at the office I opposed Sir W. Pen over a purser's mulct, and he went out in a huff like an ass; I was not sorry, for I will not let him think I am afraid to oppose him. After dinner I rode out on business, followed Howlett's daughter through Westminster Hall but could not overtake her, and at Unthank's I turned my vexation at my wife's unfinished work into a little flirtation with a pretty lodger, taking her hand and laughing at myself. I consulted Dr. Turner about freight due from East India ships, then spent the evening writing letters, and went to bed with a cold from last night. Captain Taylor had brought me a small state plate, and I mean to help him get his demurrage allowance for the William.
levels.summary:
This morning at the office I had a showdown with Sir W. Pen. He pressed me to excuse a fine laid on the purser of the James, who was absent by his order; I refused, and he stormed out looking like a discontented ass. I felt no regret, because I would not have him think I dare not oppose him when I see reason for it.

After dinner I went on several errands about town. In Westminster Hall I saw Howlett's daughter leaving and followed her, hoping to talk and dally a little, but she got away.

Then at Unthank's, when a pretty little lodger came out to tell me my wife's work was not done, I took her by the hand and found ways to stretch the talk; I laughed at myself when I saw how my anger melted at such a messenger. Later I consulted Dr.

Turner at Doctors' Commons about the freight we demand from the East India ships.

I finished the evening writing letters in my office, then went home to supper and bed, nursing a scurvy cold from sleeping cold-headed last night. This day Captain Taylor brought me a little plate, expecting me to help him get demurrage for his ship William, which stayed long at Tangier; I shall and may justly do it.

periods.label: Week of Dec 30

levels.sentence: On this last night of 1663 I sit alone over my accounts, take stock of my growing fortune and many cares, and resolve to keep to business in the year ahead.
levels.paragraph: I spent the day at the office with a throbbing head, then came home to a quiet Christmas dinner with my wife on turkey and mince pie. That night I sat up till four in the morning making up my accounts and writing this last journal of the year. I blessed God to find myself worth above £800, and resolved to live frugally, mind my business, and do my duty to the King in the year to come.
levels.summary:
At the office Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W. Batten at the open table, and though Sir W. Pen took him up like a counterfeit rogue, I knew he was as pleased as any of us. I came home to a quiet Christmas dinner with my wife alone—a fine turkey and a mince pie—and then back to business.

That night, with a good fire in my chamber, I sat till four o'clock in the morning making up my accounts and writing this last journal of the year.

I thanked God to find myself worth above £800 in money, with £700 in my Lord Sandwich's hand, and lived frugally at the Navy Office with my wife and three maids. My health is pretty good, though troubled with a costiveness I am labouring to cure.

At the office I am well, though Batten envies me to the devil and Pen is a false knave to me. My father and mother are well in the country, and the young ladies of Hinchingbroke are with them because of smallpox.

The Queen is recovered, the King minds his mistress too much, and the Duchess of York is sick of the measles but growing well again.

My cares are many: my wife's brother has fallen into unhappiness through his wife, my cousin Angier has broken his trade and I am sending his rogue son John to sea, my brother Tom I know not what to think of, my brother John at Cambridge gives little hope, and Pall grows old with nothing yet to spare her.

The talk is all of the King of France, and the Turk is very far entered into Germany. Yet I bless God I am in a good way, and I resolve to stick to my business, get a little money, and do the best service I can to the King. So ends the old year.

periods.label: Week of May 11

levels.sentence: After a day of worsening pain, I was reduced to crying and roaring in bed until, by chance, kneeling brought me a gradual easing that left me pain-free and sleeping well.
levels.paragraph: I woke full of pain and went to the office, but by dinner it had grown so severe that I took to my bed. For a couple of hours I suffered an agony as great as any stone fit, with pain in my belly and back, unable to break wind. A glyster gave little help, and I cried and roared in anguish. At last, while tumbling about, I got on my knees, and the pain began to lessen, until within an hour I was almost easy, though still unable to break wind or make water, and I slept well all night.
levels.summary:
I rose on May 14th already full of pain, likely from the cold I had gotten the day before. I managed to sit through the office, but by dinner the pain forced me to bed, where it swelled into a fit as terrible as any stone I have known, gripping my lower belly and back.

I could not break wind, and a glyster brought little relief; for two hours I lay crying and roaring in the most extraordinary anguish.

Then, chancing among my tumblings to get upon my knees in bed, the pain began to ease, and within an hour it had subsided to almost nothing. I still could not break wind or make water, yet I slept well all night, thankful for the respite.

periods.label: Week of Oct 19

levels.sentence: I spent the day at the office, dined with my uncle, caressed Bagwell's wife with promises of a place for her husband, heard troubling news about Tangier from Mr. Cholmely, and bought silver tumblers.
levels.paragraph: I rose early and attended the office all morning. At noon my uncle Thomas came to dine with me, and I gave him some money. Back in my office, I caressed Bagwell's wife, finding her more responsive to my good words and promises to get her husband a place. Afterwards I visited Lord Sandwich, and went with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street, where he told me that Tangier is likely in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, a man of no honour or honesty. I returned home, having bought two silver tumblers, worked late, then supped and went to bed.
levels.summary:
At the office all morning, I dined with my uncle Thomas, who came to collect some money from me. The transaction was routine, and I felt the usual obligation to family. Later, I took Bagwell's wife into my office and caressed her, finding her every day more amenable to my advances.

I promised to get her husband a place, which I intend to fulfil, though I know it is a bargain of sorts.

In the afternoon I visited my Lord Sandwich and then walked with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street. Cholmely told me that Tangier is in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, who is dishonourable, dishonest, and works to raise the Irish interest at the expense of the English, offending everyone and accomplishing nothing.

This news grieved me. I bought two silver tumblers on my way home, worked late at the office, and then had supper and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Dec 14

levels.sentence: After walking to Deptford and being kindly entertained by the Bagwells, I found a way to send Bagwell abroad and enjoyed my will with his wife, then returned home to dine with friends and spent the rest of the day at the office.
levels.paragraph: I walked to Deptford and after some yard business I went unnoticed to Bagwell's house, where the poor people gave me a dinner in their fashion and I ate very well. After dinner I found occasion to send Bagwell abroad, and then alone with his wife I attempted what I desired and, against her resistance, accomplished it to my contentment. I walked home, dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, and then spent the afternoon and evening at the office, finishing late and going to bed.
levels.summary:
I set out on foot to Deptford, and after handling some business at the yard I slipped away to Bagwell's house without being observed. The Bagwells were very kind and gave me a meal, and once I had sent Bagwell out on an errand, I was left alone with his wife and pressed my advantage to my full satisfaction.

Afterward I walked home and dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, though I soon left them to the office, where I sat all afternoon and into the evening. I took supper, returned to the office again very late, and then at last went home to bed.

The day mixed a private pleasure with the usual round of work and company, leaving me contented but weary.

periods.label: Week of Dec 28

levels.sentence: On a hard frosty morning I pursued my lewd pleasures, dined nobly at Lord Brunker's, and returned home to find my wife's pointed reading on jealousy stinging my guilty conscience.
levels.paragraph: This morning I walked toward Whitehall and, being overtaken by Sir W. Pen's coach, rode with him to wait on the Duke. After paying my fees, I stopped at my barber's to speak privately with Jane, who promised me a place to meet on Sunday. I then sported with Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan, and later lay with Mrs. Martin at her poor lodgings in Bow Street, though I soon grew sick of her impudence. A noble French dinner at Lord Brunker's lifted my spirits, but at home my wife maliciously made me read a letter about jealousy, which pricked my conscience, and the sight of a dog covering our bitch stirred my own jealousy again.
levels.summary:
After a fine frosty walk, I joined Sir W. Pen's coach to Whitehall and conducted our usual business with the Duke.

Forced to pay out money in basins, I then went to my barber Gervas and found a moment alone with Jane, giving her something; she modestly told me where I might come to her on Sunday, which I shall not fail. Later I sported with Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan, and then agreed with Mrs.

Martin, going to her new lodgings in Bow Street, where I had my will of her for 2s. in wine and cake, though I left sick of her impudence.

At Lord Brunker's in Covent Garden, I made much mirth with a ballad I had brought, pretending it came from the seamen to their ladies, and naming Sir W. Pen, Sir G. Ascue, and Sir J. Lawson as the authors. We had the noblest French dinner I have seen in many a day.

I then bespoke Hooke's book of the Microscope at my bookseller's, and after a short office meeting, went late to Sir Ph. Warwicke's, but he had company.

At home, thinking to be merry, I was vexed because my wife had found a letter in Sir Philip Sidney about jealousy and made me read it; my conscience told me it was apt, and though I read it out frankly, it stuck in my stomach.

I was further vexed by the immodest sight of a dog brought to line our little bitch, which stirred my jealousy again. We played cards a good while, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jan 18

levels.sentence: From Jane's threatened match to a kiss at the Swan, from Doll's mysterious departure to the wondrous hare's foot that eased my belly, I ended a day of odd fancies and small comforts, with Hooke's book in hand.
levels.paragraph: I went to Westminster and spoke with Sir Ph. Warwicke, then to Jervas's, where Jane's mistress told me Jane had pledged herself to a fiddler and they were plotting to marry her to Hayes. I advised Jane privately, though I doubt she will avoid being undone by this fellow. At noon I dined at the Swan and had a kiss from the girl there, but nothing more. I took home Hooke's book of microscopy, a most excellent piece, and later learned that pretty Doll had gone away, which I fear means something worse. On the way home, a hare's foot from Mr. Batten cured my colic by mere fancy, and I ended the day at home with supper, reading, and cards.
levels.summary:
At Jervas's house this morning, I found the household in disorder over Jane. Her mistress told me secretly that Jane had bound herself to a fellow who fiddles for a living, and that they were trying to get her to marry one Hayes instead.

I seemed to go along with the plan and got leave to advise Jane privately, which gave me a chance to be with her. I doubt she will be happy if she marries this fellow, but I gave her my advice and let her do as she pleases, so I may still enjoy her company now and then.

From there I dined at the Swan, where I had a kiss from the girl of the house but nothing more. Then I went to my Lady Sandwich's and took home Hooke's book of microscopy, which I am very proud to own.

In the afternoon, my wife and I met at the New Exchange and found that our pretty Doll had gone away, supposedly to her father in the country, but I suspect something worse. On the way home, a conversation with Mr.

Batten led me to buy a hare's foot; he showed me my mistake about the joint and assured me it cured his colic. Strange as it seems, merely handling his foot eased my belly at once, and I have been well ever since.

At home I did some office work, then supped, read, played cards, and so to bed.
