periods.label: Week of Feb 15

levels.sentence: I spent a painful but busy day tending to office affairs, dining with Sir W. Batten and later discoursing with Mr. Wayth about ticket abuses, then passed the evening with Lady Sandwich, who shared court gossip about Lord Castlemayne's expected return and the Maids of Honour's mad pranks, while Lord Sandwich wrote that he expects to be in town this week.
levels.paragraph: I woke with a mighty pain in my forefinger from last night's struggle with the woman I mentioned, yet I went to the office and was busy till noon. My wife, being long kept indoors in the dirt, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe and now pretends to a resolution of being very clean, though I can guess how long it will hold. I dined with Sir W. Batten and his lady, who are now very fond of me, and later discoursed with Mr. Wayth about the abuse in tickets and Mr. Fen's great profit from his place. Lord Brunkerd then carried me to Lincoln's Inn Fields, where I had innocent discourse with Lady Sandwich about housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, and she told me the latest court gossip.
levels.summary:
I began the day in pain from a strained forefinger, but still attended to office business until noon. My wife, having been confined indoors, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe and now talks of being very clean, though I know how long such resolutions last. I dined with Sir W.

Batten and his lady, who are very fond of me these days, and later went to the Change and then with Mr. Wayth to a cook's shop, where we discussed the growing abuse of tickets and Mr. Fen's profitable place—he demands but five per cent of all he pays, yet is little pleased with anyone who gives him no more.

After more office business, Lord Brunkerd carried me to Lincoln's Inn Fields, where I talked with good Lady Sandwich about housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times.

She told me that Lord Castlemayne is coming over from France and is believed likely to be made friends with his lady again. She also told me of the mad freaks of the Maids of Honour at Court: Mrs.

Jennings recently dressed like an orange wench and cried oranges up and down, until her fine shoes were discerned after a fall in the evening, putting her to great shame. Lady Castlemayne merrily says that her own daughter, not above a year or two old, will be the first maid in Court that will be married.

Lord Sandwich also wrote me word from the Downs that he is like to be in town this week, which will bring more business and news. The whole day left me with a sense of the world's vanity and folly, yet also the comforts of friendship and innocent conversation.

periods.paragraph: I woke with a mighty pain in my forefinger from last night's struggle with the woman I mentioned, yet I went to the office and was busy till noon. My wife, being long kept indoors in the dirt, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe and now pretends to a resolution of being very clean, though I can guess how long it will hold. I dined with Sir W. Batten and his lady, who are now very fond of me, and later discoursed with Mr. Wayth about the abuse in tickets and Mr. Fen's great profit from his place. Lord Brunkerd then carried me to Lincoln's Inn Fields, where I had innocent discourse with Lady Sandwich about housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, and she told me the latest court gossip.

periods.label: Week of Aug 2

levels.sentence: After indulging in a moment of improper fondness with my little girle, I forced myself to quit that dangerous game and spent the day quietly putting my papers in order before riding through the rain to Woolwich.
levels.paragraph: This morning I dressed and let my little girle comb my head, but I found myself being too free with her, touching her breast, and I had to stop myself before I stumbled into some real trouble. To steady myself, I turned to my chamber and spent the day going through my papers, getting more settled than I had managed in the past two days. In the evening, with the rain coming down hard, I took myself off to Woolwich, chatted a little, and went to bed.
levels.summary:
I began the day in a dangerous mood, letting my little girle comb my head and growing too familiar with her, even putting my hands on her breast. I caught myself and resolved to leave off such behavior, fearing it might lead to some major inconvenience.

To keep myself honest, I buried myself in my business, sorting and settling more papers than I had been able to in the previous two days. When evening came, the rain was pouring, so I rode down to Woolwich, exchanged a few words, and went straight to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 9

levels.sentence: As the plague deaths mounted and Alderman Bence's tale proved both false and troubling, I went to dinner, then came home to redraw my will, for the town was so unhealthy I could not count on living two days.
levels.paragraph: This morning my she-cozen Porter begged my help after her husband was taken to the Tower for buying the King's powder, but I dared not involve myself. At the office the mortality bill rose past 4,000, with over 3,000 dead of the plague, and we heard a strange tale of Alderman Bence stumbling over a corpse only to have his pregnant wife die of fright. At dinner Bence denied the story, yet admitted his wife is ill and that he has left her, which troubled me deeply. I went home to redraw my will, bound by oath to finish it by tomorrow night, for the town is so unhealthy that no man can count on living two days.
levels.summary:
This morning my she-cozen Porter came early to tell me her husband had been taken to the Tower for buying some of the King's powder. She begged my help, but I dared not appear in that business again, having had too much trouble lately.

At the office we sat all morning, grieving to see the bill rise so high — above 4,000 dead in all, more than 3,000 of them from the plague.

We also heard an odd story of Alderman Bence stumbling over a dead corpse in the street at night; when he told his wife, she, being with child, took fright, fell sick, and died of the plague.

Later we dined at Sir G. Smith's by invitation — Lord Brunker, Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Batten and I — with good company and good cheer. Captain Cocke and Jacke Fenn were there, and to our great wonder Alderman Bence himself came, insisting that not a word of that story was true.

Yet by his own account his wife is ill, and he has been forced to leave his house and will not go near her; this troubled me all the time I sat there.

After writing letters at the office, I went home to draw over anew my will, which I had sworn to finish by tomorrow night, for the town is grown so unhealthy that a man cannot depend on living two days to an end. So, having done something toward it, I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 27

levels.sentence: After sailing all night, I inspected Chatham Yard, put a wasteful team of horses to shame, wrangled a favor from a false Sir W. Pen, flirted with maids at Rochester Castle despite a paralyzing fear of heights, and ended the day happily at Woolwich with my wife.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at Chatham Yard, where I made a point of showing Commissioner Pett how foolish it was to use four horses for a timber one man could carry, and then wrested a concession from the false Sir W. Pen. Later, at Rochester Castle, I dallied with three pretty maids, though my terror of the precipices cut short my pleasure. After viewing the Cathedral and meeting the Mayor, I hurried to Gravesend and boarded an East Indiaman to soothe Lord Bruncker and Sir John Minnes about pillaged goods, hoping myself to profit honestly. I came home to Woolwich, supped cheerfully with my wife, and went to bed in great content.
levels.summary:
I sailed through the night and reached Gillingham at dawn, then walked to Chatham with Commissioner Pett to inspect the Yard. There I was struck by the absurdity of a team of four horses dragging a timber that one man could easily carry, so I had the horses removed and made the men take it up by hand.

Pett saw this and said nothing, but I think he was ashamed. We then visited Sir W. Pen, who lay in bed and made a show of kindness, though I know him for a false rogue; still, I got his consent to have his silk carried away before the money was received, a favor he would not have granted Cocke.

At Rochester, while dinner was being readied, I wandered to the old Castle ruins, and on the stairs overtook three pretty maids or women.

I took them up with me and kissed and touched their hands and necks to my great pleasure, but the dreadful look down the precipices frightened me so much that it spoiled my enjoyment. I then walked about the Cathedral and met the Mayor, Mr. Fowler, a reverend magistrate.

Leaving after a quick bite, I rode to Gravesend and, because the sickness was severe there, took a boat to the East Indiaman at Erith, where Lord Bruncker and Sir John Minnes were full of envious complaints about the pillaging of the ships.

I pacified them and discussed making money from some of the goods, hoping to be the better for it honestly. By eight o'clock I was at Woolwich, where I supped mighty pleasantly with my wife, who is now all friends with her maids, and so in great joy and content went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Oct 4

levels.sentence: Amid the plague I went about my business and pleasures, dallied with Sarah and my Valentine, admired Evelyn's gardens, and renewed my neglected vows with the Bill fallen by 740.
levels.paragraph: This morning I lay long talking with my wife about giving sister Pall her £400 portion and marrying her soon, but the sickness makes it unfit to send for her. I went to the Duke on victualling business, read Evelyn's book on libraries, then spent time with Sarah and with my Valentine before Mr. Evelyn showed me his evergreens and holly hedge. The plague is all around, yet the Bill is down by 740. At night I renewed my old vows, for without them my mind had run wool-gathering and my business was neglected.
levels.summary:
Lying long abed, my wife and I talked of my sister Pall; my wife is very willing to give her a £400 portion and have her married soon, but the plague makes it unfit to send for her.

I went to the office and to the Duke of Albemarle, reading Evelyn's present on gathering a library on the way—the book is above my reach, though his epistle to Lord Chancellor is fine. With the Duke I advised on putting the victuallers' business into more hands, and I hope to get a job of work out of it myself.

Afterwards I walked to the Swan and spent time with Sarah, then by water to Deptford to my Valentine; the plague is round about and next door, but I did not value it, and did what I would with her. At Mr.

Evelyn's we discoursed of the confused business of prisoners and sick and wounded seamen, and he showed me his gardens—the variety of evergreens and the holly hedge are the finest things I ever saw. Riding to Greenwich we had fine discourse of trees and the nature of vegetables. I wrote late to Sir W.

Coventry about great concernment, and found my wife gone home to Woolwich. Blessed be God, the Bill is less this week by 740.

Having eaten little all day, I got something at my lodging and went to bed, this night renewing my promises to observe my vows; for since I left them off, my mind has run a-wool-gathering and my business neglected.

periods.label: Week of Oct 11

levels.sentence: On a bitter cold morning I went to Lord Bruncker's ship to see the King's enquiry into the prize-goods, found that my Lord Sandwich's order had been shamefully abused by Sir W. Berkeley and others, and yet by evening heard from Captain Cocke that the Duke had shown an order for all respect to the Earl, so that our goods would be weighed tomorrow and the plague was also lessening.
levels.paragraph: I rose before day in horrid cold and went by water to Lord Bruncker's ship, where the King's command to examine all prize-goods dealings was being enforced without any respect to my Lord Sandwich. I found that extreme ill use had been made of my Lord's order: goods were tossed, spoiled, and broken, with Sir W. Berkeley as chief hand and men saying my Lord Sandwich's back was broad enough to bear it. Though the King and Duke seemed severe, at Captain Cocke's I heard that Seymour had cajoled the Duke into showing an order for all respect to the Earl, and that our goods should be weighed tomorrow. Overjoyed, I wrote letters late, and took comfort that plague deaths had fallen by about six hundred.
levels.summary:
I was called up before day and went in horrid cold to Lord Bruncker's ship. He showed me the King's command to examine most severely all that had been done about the prize-goods, without respect to my Lord Sandwich.

I found one man being examined, and it was plain that extreme ill use had been made of my Lord's order: they had tossed, tumbled, spoiled, and broken goods in the hold, with Sir W. Berkeley as the chief hand, and they said my Lord Sandwich's back was broad enough to bear it.

I learned that the King and Duke were very severe in this point and that the entries at the Customs House would show everything that had been taken.

From Woolwich I went by coach in Captain Cocke's company to Greenwich, taking the young lady home. Cocke told me he had cajoled Seymour, who would be our friend, and above all that the Duke had shown him an order from Court for all respect to be paid to the Earl of Sandwich and for goods delivered by his order.

This overjoyed me, and he doubted not we should have possession tomorrow or next day. I wrote my letters late. Good news too that there were about six hundred less dead of the plague than the last week, and so I went home to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jan 3

levels.sentence: Riding into London with Lord Bruncker, I found the city stirring back to life, dined with Mr. Povy, returned to Greenwich, and ended the day in pleasant company with Mrs. Tooker.
levels.paragraph: I rode into London with Lord Bruncker and Mrs. Williams, and was struck by how the town had filled once more—shops reopening, beggars begging, and people bustling about. After setting Mrs. Williams down, I spoke with Sir G. Carteret about the Act, then dined nobly with Mr. Povy at Sir George Smith's. Returning to Greenwich, I tried in vain to see Mrs. Knipp, but instead enjoyed a discourse on the Thames. At home, little Mrs. Tooker supped with me and I kept her late.
levels.summary:
I came to London with Lord Bruncker and Mrs. Williams, and the sight of the city reviving was delightful—porters bowing, beggars beseeching, and shops opening again, though many still shut. The City end was full, but Covent Garden and Westminster remained empty of gentry. After setting Mrs.

Williams down at my Lord's house, he and I went to White Hall to see Sir G. Carteret, who had come to town for a day, and we talked much about the Act and the credit it brings, though no private talk passed between him and me.

I then went to the Exchange, met Mr. Povy fresh in town, and dined nobly at Sir George Smith's. Povy told me how Lord Bellases complains for want of money, blaming him and me, but I value it not, knowing I do all that can be done. Later, I returned to Greenwich, hoping to see Mrs. ' At Mr.

Boreman's, I read a satisfying discourse about the Thames and its choking by encroachments. Back home, for lack of other company, little Mrs. Tooker came, supped with me, and stayed very late while I had my way with her.

periods.label: Week of Jan 10

levels.phrase: Anxious business and a coach fall
levels.sentence: A day of anxious business—securing a tailor, pressing my Lord's pardon, debating pursers at the office, and taking a tumble when my coach broke—ends with my poor wife working like a horse at our hangings.
levels.paragraph: This day I went by coach to the Duke of Albemarle, where only Sir W. Batten and I met, and my heart was troubled to see how things are ordered without consideration. Afterwards I called at Wotton's, my shoemaker, bespoke shoes, and got him to find me a tailor, Mr. Penny, against St. Dunstan's Church. At the Exchange I met Mr. Moore, newly come to town, and took him home to dinner, where we concluded my Lord's case very bad unless he gets a pardon before going to Spain. The rest of the day was spent in an office meeting over my paper about pursers, and then my coach broke and tumbled me over Lord Bruncker, but I got up again; at home my poor wife works all day like a horse at her hangings.
levels.summary:
I began the day at the Duke of Albemarle's, troubled at heart to see how things are ordered there without consideration or understanding. Then I went to my shoemaker Wotton's, bespoke shoes, and hired a tailor, Mr. Penny, because my own clothes and my Lord Sandwich's tailor are not yet in town.

At the Exchange I met Mr. Moore and dined with him, and we agreed my Lord's case is very bad—he must get a pardon for his doings about prizes and Bergen before he goes for Spain.

I was especially anxious to have him pay my cozen Pepys, since I am bound for my Lord in L1000, so I directed Moore to go to my Lord tomorrow about perfecting the pardon. Later I read my paper about pursers to an office meeting; all approved it except Sir W.

Pen, who objected to everything and remedied nothing, though even he declared it the best thing he had ever heard. My Lord Bruncker and I then took coach, but it broke and tumbled me over him near the Stockes; I rose unhurt.

At home I found my poor wife working like a horse at her hangings for our chamber and bed, and so to supper and to bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 28

levels.sentence: On a dry cold morning I walked to White Hall, talked with Sir Ph. Warwicke about the kingdom's ominous state, did business with the Duke of Yorke, dallied with Mrs. Martin and Mrs. Lane, dined with the pleasant Mrs. Knipp, reconciled with Sir G. Carteret who feared a general catastrophe, and ended the month resolving to apply myself better to business.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with a walk to White Hall, where Sir Ph. Warwicke and I spoke anxiously of the kingdom's snarling state and the new Act that left us without money. Business with the Duke of Yorke followed, then idle talk in Westminster Hall with the Michells and Howletts, and a quick encounter with Mrs. Martin. Home for dinner with the delightful Mrs. Knipp, then visits to Colonel Norwood and Sir G. Carteret, who seemed melancholy and feared all things would come to nothing. The evening brought a risky loan and intimacy with Mrs. Lane, and I went to bed by ten, full of resolve to mend my ways after this backward month.
levels.summary:
This day was a mix of public worry and private indulgence. I walked to White Hall and met Sir Ph. Warwicke in the Pell Mall, where we spoke of the melancholy posture of affairs—everyone snarling, the new Act crippling our power to raise money.

He feared, as I did, that all was ill with the State, and we agreed to meet later about Navy business. After doing our duty with the Duke of Yorke, I idled in Westminster Hall, chatting with Mrs. Michell and her pretty daughter, then was called by Mrs.

Martin, bought bands from her, and went to her chamber for what I would.

Dinner at home with Mrs. Knipp was a bright spot, as she is the pleasantest company in the world, and I gave my wife money to lay out on her. Abroad again, I visited Colonel Norwood and Sir G.

Carteret, with whom I have made things right; he is very melancholy, most afraid of a general catastrophe, thinking all will come to nothing. From the Swan I went to Mrs. Lane's, lent her L5 upon gold, and did what I would—but she is grown very bad and offers anything, so I will avoid her a while.

I returned home, worked at the office, and slept by ten, ending the month with my mind full of resolution to apply myself better to business, having been visibly prejudiced by my idleness these last six or eight days.

periods.label: Week of Mar 14

levels.sentence: After my cold improved, I went to church, sought fair Mrs. Butler in vain, took my pleasure with Mrs. Martin, learned that my old sweetheart Betty Howlet had married, and came home to accounts with Mings back from Hamburg empty-handed.
levels.paragraph: My cold being better, I went to church and then home to dinner, before walking out to St. James's Church hoping to see fair Mrs. Butler, but she was not there—nor, I believe, does she live thereabouts now. I walked on to Westminster in very fine dry weather, though all cry out for lack of rain, drank at Herbert's, and then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I did what I would with her while her husband fetched wine. She told me Betty Howlet, my little sweetheart, is married to young Michell and will live nearer me in Thames Street; glad of that news, I returned home by coach, did accounts, and went to bed.
levels.summary:
My cold being better, I rose, went to church, and dined at home before setting out on foot. At St. James's Church I hoped to see fair Mrs. Butler, but she was not there, and I suspect she no longer lives in that neighbourhood. The weather was very fine and dry, though everyone cries out for lack of rain.

I stopped at Herbert's for a drink, then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I lay with her while her husband stepped out for wine; the poor man would take pains if I can get him a purser's place, and I shall endeavour to do so.

Mrs. Martin told me a secret: Betty Howlet of the Hall, my little sweetheart whom I used to call my second wife, has married the younger son of Mr. Michell—the elder brother, who should have had her, being dead of the plague. I am glad of it, and glad that they are to live nearer me in Thames Street by the Old Swan.

That evening I rode home by coach, went to my chamber to do accounts, and so to bed. I also heard that Sir Christopher Mings is come home from Hamburg without having done anything, saving only bringing home some pipestaves for us.

periods.label: Week of Apr 4

levels.sentence: A rainy struggle to reach White Hall, the Duke's wise settling of a captain's quarrel, grim news of a sudden death and the returning plague, and a dinner with Mrs. Hunt talking of the Protector all made for a full, unsettled day that ended quietly with a psalm.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was in great trouble to get passage, the rain making coaches scarce, so I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to White Hall. There the Duke of Yorke heard the dispute between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr. Wayth and resolved it with rare judgement, chiding both yet encouraging Wayth to keep captains honest for the King. The Court was full of news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death and the plague's increase, which frightened everyone. After missing the sermon in the Chappell, I used Lord Hinchingbroke's coach to carry Mrs. Hunt home for dinner, and we talked of the Protector and his family. Later I tried to hear a Jesuite preach but came too late, so I went home to business and ended with Mercer combing my head and a psalm.
levels.summary:
The day began with vexation: rain had driven away all coaches, so I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to White Hall. There I witnessed the Duke of Yorke settle a quarrel between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr. Wayth with great order and judgement.

Allen's complaint about Wayth's usage at the pay of his ship seemed a sorry occasion, and the Duke chided both while encouraging Wayth to be a check on captains for the King's right. I had never seen the Duke do anything with more judgement.

The Court was heavy with news: Tom Cheffin, the King's closet-keeper, had died suddenly between six and seven that morning, apparently of an imposthume in his breast, and the plague was said to be increasing everywhere.

I had the pleasure of seeing an Archbishop in the pulpit at the Chappell, though I could not get in to hear well. Later I carried Mrs. Hunt home in Lord Hinchingbroke's coach and dined with her, discoursing on old matters of the Protector, who lives in France on about L500 a year.

After returning her, I missed the Jesuite's sermon at St. James's, and so went home to business. At night Mercer combed my head, I sang a psalm, and went to bed.

periods.sentence: A rainy struggle to reach White Hall, the Duke's wise settling of a captain's quarrel, grim news of a sudden death and the returning plague, and a dinner with Mrs. Hunt talking of the Protector all made for a full, unsettled day that ended quietly with a psalm.
periods.paragraph: This morning I was in great trouble to get passage, the rain making coaches scarce, so I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to White Hall. There the Duke of Yorke heard the dispute between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr. Wayth and resolved it with rare judgement, chiding both yet encouraging Wayth to keep captains honest for the King. The Court was full of news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death and the plague's increase, which frightened everyone. After missing the sermon in the Chappell, I used Lord Hinchingbroke's coach to carry Mrs. Hunt home for dinner, and we talked of the Protector and his family. Later I tried to hear a Jesuite preach but came too late, so I went home to business and ended with Mercer combing my head and a psalm.

periods.label: Week of Jun 6

levels.sentence: I began the day expecting to celebrate a victory, but by evening the news of our grievous defeat had forced me to write a sorrowful letter to Lady Sandwich.
levels.paragraph: I rose early, expecting to congratulate ourselves on the victory I had believed won yesterday. Instead, Lord Bruncker and Sir T. H. brought terrifying news: we were beaten, lost many ships and commanders, and took none of the enemy's. The Prince ran aground on the Galloper and was burned; Sir G. Ascue was captured. At the Exchange, faces were changed, and I spent the afternoon alone with little Mrs. Tooker, doing what I pleased with her. The Duke of York was dampened, and I worked late preparing an abstract of the fleet's needs.
levels.summary:
I woke early, expecting to share in the congratulations for a victory I had taken for granted yesterday. But Lord Bruncker and Sir T. H. brought news that astonished and troubled me: we had been beaten, lost many ships and good commanders, taken no enemy vessels, and could only claim a victory on paper.

Worst of all, The Prince had run aground on the Galloper and was burned by the Dutch, and Sir G. Ascue was taken prisoner to Holland. The town's mood shifted visibly as I went to the Exchange, and my own spirits sank.

The afternoon, however, took a different turn: I was left alone with little Mrs. Tooker and did what I would with her. When Mr. Wayth came, he told me from Captain Page's own mouth that the Dutch had pursued us for two hours before letting us go home — a sad confirmation of our defeat.

At White Hall, the Duke of York seemed damped, gave me letters from the fleet for setting it out again, and I worked on an abstract until midnight. The losses mounted: The Prince lost, Essex carried into Holland, Swiftsure missing, many captains slain, and Sir William Clerke dead of his leg.

The Duke of Albemarle wrote that not above twenty officers behaved like men. I was forced to write a sad letter to my Lady Sandwich instead of the triumphant one I had expected, and so went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 13

levels.sentence: From political quarrels and a fruitless wait at Whitehall to the joy of my father's portrait, a comic lapse over my lobsters, the solemn funeral of Sir Christopher Mings with its extraordinary offer of revenge, and finally a furtive visit to Mrs. Bagwell shadowed by plague, this day was a whirl of contrasts.
levels.paragraph: I began with business before the Duke of York, hearing of jarrs between the Duke of York and Albemarle. Then I fretted over a missing Tangier committee and tried in vain to break tallies at the Exchequer. My spirits rose at Hales's, seeing my father's portrait begun, but a laughable mishap with lobsters at dinner left me merry. The day ended with the funeral of Sir Christopher Mings, an emotional offer of revenge from his men, and a risky visit to Mrs. Bagwell, darkened by news of the plague.
levels.summary:
At St. James's, I attended to business with the Duke and learned of serious discord between the Duke of York and Albemarle over commanders, particularly the French captain Du Tell. Sir W. Coventry's remarks against Albemarle's captains added to the ill blood.

Afterwards, my hopes for a Tangier committee were dashed, and Lord Peterborough seemed intent on obstructing poor Yeabsly's cause; my attempts to break tallies at the Exchequer also failed.

My spirits lifted when I saw my father's portrait begun at Hales's—such a joy to have his likeness, he being so loving and innocent.

But at dinner a comic mishap occurred: I had bought lobsters, then forgot them when my wife and father took the coach, and during grace I cried out about them, sending Balty chasing after the coach in vain. We laughed heartily.

Later, at the Excise Office, we resolved to state our debts and seek help from the Lord Treasurer.

I attended Sir Christopher Mings's funeral, a grand but sad affair. Sir W. Coventry was there out of generosity, and a dozen of Mings's men offered their lives to serve on a fireship in revenge for him—a romantique and moving gesture. I reflected on Mings's humble origins and his untimely death, leaving no estate.

That night, I went to Mrs. Bagwell's house and did what I would, but I was fearful because her servant had died of the plague and she had only just come abroad. I returned home late, stopping to buy eels, and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 20

levels.sentence: Rising with colic and anxious about my father, I spent the day on financial matters, visits, and an unwanted escort of Mrs. Williams and Knipp, then ended quietly at home.
levels.paragraph: I woke with a colic, likely from washing my feet and wearing a thin waistcoat. I gave my father money for a horse and other needs, which he received with great kindness. After attending the Duke of York, I settled some Exchequer business and deducted £25 for myself from a payment to Colonel Fitzgerald. I dined at the Swan, visited Hales's to see my father's picture, and napped, then hurried home only to be waylaid by Mrs. Williams and the pregnant Knipp in Cheapside. That evening I sang in the garden and went to bed.
levels.summary:
Rising with a colic, I blamed my recent habit of washing my feet and wearing only a thin, open-breasted silk waistcoat. With my father leaving tomorrow, I gave him £20 plus other expenses to buy a horse and necessaries, which he took with infinite kindness. Later, at St.

James's, I attended the Duke of York, and on the way spoke with Colonel Fitzgerald about paying him £700-odd, from which he allowed me to deduct £25 for myself. I then went to the Exchequer and finally arranged to break a large tally into smaller ones.

Afterwards, I visited Mrs. Martin at Westminster Hall, dined at the Swan, chose prints at Faythorne's to varnish, and went to Hales's to see my father's portrait, where I napped for an hour. Fearing my father might meet trouble while visiting Mr. Honiwood, I hurried home, but in Cheapside Mrs.

Williams called to me, so I had to accompany her and the heavily pregnant Knipp to Paternoster Row, dreading they'd ask about my father. At last I came home, found my father and wife had never intended to go to Hales's, spent the evening on business, sang in the garden, and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 1

levels.sentence: I settled my accounts to a new high of £5,700, found all business stalled without me at St James's, learned from Sir W. Coventry of the Dutch defeat, and spent the afternoon in amorous play at Mrs Martin's before returning home to my wife's drawing and a pleasant bed.
levels.paragraph: This morning I settled my last month's accounts and blessed God to find myself worth £5,700, the most my book ever showed. I was delayed by Sir W. Pen and came too late to St James's, where everything stood still for want of me. Walking with Sir W. Coventry, I heard that the Dutch lost 5,000 men and De Ruyter is out of favour, though Coventry is not pleased with our Generals. After church I dined at the Swan on a rabbit, then at Mrs Martin's amused myself with Mrs Burroughs, the widow Mrs Eastwood, and Mrs Fenton. I towzed and tumbled the merry widow, then carried them home, fearful of being seen, and returned to find my wife at her drawing, going to supper and bed very pleasant.
levels.summary:
This day I rose early to settle my last month's accounts, and blessed God to find them very clear, my worth now £5,700, the most my book ever showed. I prepared to attend the Duke of York as usual, but Sir W.

Pen, just as I was going out, came home from Sheerness and held me in discourse about public business, so that I came by coach too late to St James's, where everything stood still and nothing was done for want of me.

Thence I walked over the Park with Sir W.

Coventry, who is not thoroughly pleased with the late management of the fight, nor with anything the Generals do; only he is glad to hear De Ruyter is out of favour, and that this fight cost the Dutch 5,000 men as they report, while we had not above 400 or 500 killed and wounded, and as many flag-officers on their side as ordinary captains on ours.

I left him going to chapel, it being the common fast day, and the Duke of York at chapel.

I went to Mrs Martin's, but she was abroad, so I sauntered to the Abbey and then to the parish church, fearful of being seen; after service I dined at the Swan upon a rabbit, then returned to Mrs Martin's, where I found Mrs Burroughs, a pretty widow, one Mrs Eastwood, and one Mrs Fenton, a maid.

There was merry kissing and looking on their breasts, and all the innocent pleasure in the world; the widow dissembled a faint at a jigg her late husband loved, but I made her as merry as possible and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased.

I carried her and her sober kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings, mightily pleased with the afternoon's mirth yet in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So home, where I was much pleased with my wife's drawing, and so to supper and to bed very pleasant.

periods.brief: I settled my accounts to a new high of £5,700, found all business stalled without me at St James's, learned from Sir W. Coventry of the Dutch defeat, and spent the afternoon in amorous play at Mrs Martin's before returning home to my wife's drawing and a pleasant bed.
periods.full:
This day I rose early to settle my last month's accounts, and blessed God to find them very clear, my worth now £5,700, the most my book ever showed. I prepared to attend the Duke of York as usual, but Sir W.

Pen, just as I was going out, came home from Sheerness and held me in discourse about public business, so that I came by coach too late to St James's, where everything stood still and nothing was done for want of me.

Thence I walked over the Park with Sir W.

Coventry, who is not thoroughly pleased with the late management of the fight, nor with anything the Generals do; only he is glad to hear De Ruyter is out of favour, and that this fight cost the Dutch 5,000 men as they report, while we had not above 400 or 500 killed and wounded, and as many flag-officers on their side as ordinary captains on ours.

I left him going to chapel, it being the common fast day, and the Duke of York at chapel.

I went to Mrs Martin's, but she was abroad, so I sauntered to the Abbey and then to the parish church, fearful of being seen; after service I dined at the Swan upon a rabbit, then returned to Mrs Martin's, where I found Mrs Burroughs, a pretty widow, one Mrs Eastwood, and one Mrs Fenton, a maid.

There was merry kissing and looking on their breasts, and all the innocent pleasure in the world; the widow dissembled a faint at a jigg her late husband loved, but I made her as merry as possible and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased.

I carried her and her sober kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings, mightily pleased with the afternoon's mirth yet in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So home, where I was much pleased with my wife's drawing, and so to supper and to bed very pleasant.

periods.label: Week of Sep 12

levels.sentence: I attended to business with the Duke, helped friends prepare for a move, dined with Balty, and after sending off half my goods from Deptford, I gave in to lust with Bagwell, only to feel disgust and hurry home to Sir W. Pen's, where I found him in the same simple humour.
levels.paragraph: Up early, I went with Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen to St. James's to do our usual business with the Duke of Yorke. After that, I spoke with Michell and Howlett about their young ones going to Shadwell's, and promised to counsel the young man whose unkindness to his wife was now over. I later called on Martin and enjoyed her company, then went home to dine with Balty and his wife, and after dinner took Balty to Deptford to load above half my goods on the Bezan and send them away. In the dark I returned to Bagwell and did what I desired, but afterward I hated both her and the deed, so I left when her husband returned and went late to Sir W. Pen's, where I found him in the same simple humour, and so to bed.
levels.summary:
After attending to business with the Duke of Yorke, I went to Westminster and spoke with Michell and Howlett. They told me about their young ones going to Shadwell's, and I heard of the young man's unkindness to his wife, which is now over; I promised to appear as a counsellor to him.

I was glad she would be near us again. I then visited Martin and enjoyed her company before returning home to dine with Balty and his wife.

Later, I took Balty to Deptford and had him help load more than half my goods onto the Bezan to send them away. Afterward, I found an occasion in the dark to go to Bagwell and did all that I desired, though my intended pleasure turned to self-loathing. I made my escape when her husband returned and went home to Sir W.

Pen's, where I found him in the same simple humour, and so went late to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 26

levels.sentence: After Warren balked at our Scotch motion, I completed the ship lists for Parliament and rejoiced with Sir W. Coventry to find our expenses fully justified, then went home to fetch my wife's new gown and slept content.
levels.paragraph: We held our first office meeting since the fire, but Sir W. Warren balked at our Scotch motion, so nothing was resolved. I went on to complete the lists for the Parliament Committee, then hurried to St James's, where Sir W. Coventry and I found to our joy that our declared expenses were justified. He said we must find a better Comptroller if we get over this rub. I fetched my wife and her new flowered tabby gown, set my clerks to extra work, and went to bed in good humour.
levels.summary:
At our first office meeting since the fire, Sir W. Batten, Sir W. Pen, and I met, and then with Sir W. Warren we took up the Scotch motion.

Warren seemed stumbled and had no ready answer, proposing something previous to it that would keep us busy, so we parted without any resolution and I saw plainly he had no mind to it.

Later I finished the lists for the Parliament Committee of the ships, men, and time employed since the war, and carried them to St James's, where Sir W. Coventry waited.

To our great joy, the medium of wages, victuals, and wear and tear came to above L3,000,000, and the extraordinaries would justify our declared expense of L320,000 since the war. Coventry said that if God sent us over this rub, we must take another course for a better Comptroller; I was mightily satisfied.

I then fetched my wife and her new best gowne — coloured tabby, flowered — from Unthanke's, gave my clerks a little more work in writing over the lists in a new method, and went to bed in good humour, glad of the end we had brought this matter to.

periods.label: Week of Oct 10

levels.sentence: A day of political reckoning over naval funds and personal reckonings with a new maid, an old mistress, and unsettled accounts.
levels.paragraph: After seeing my father off on his journey, I walked the halls of Westminster and learned that Parliament had cut our naval wear-and-tear by £150,000, though they would allow 28,000 men next year. The streets were foul, and the Hall buzzed with talk against the Vice-Chamberlain. Later I dined alone at the Swan, played with Sarah, then went to Mrs. Martin's and lay with her; she is big and has named me godfather. At Deptford I saw to my new press for tools, and came home to find my wife had brought a poor, plain maid whose clothes cost me dear and whose voice is furred. The news of tomorrow's Tangier meeting sent me to my chamber to make up my accounts.
levels.summary:
This morning I took leave of my poor father, who was setting out for Brampton by coach, having come to see the burned city and to bring my brother to town. The weather was foul as I went to St. James's, where Sir W.

Coventry told me the House has cut us off £150,000 of our wear and tear, though they are pleased we abated no more and intend to allow 28,000 men for the next year. This is likely to be the great day.

The Hall was mighty full, and people have a mind to fling at the Vice-Chamberlain; I hope he may weather all, though not by any dexterity of his.

I went to the Treasurer's office, got a ticket paid for my little Michell, and then back to Westminster after the House rose. I dined alone at the Swan and played with Sarah, then went to Mrs. Martin's lodging and did what I would with her; she is very big and resolves I must be godfather.

Thence by water with Cropp to Deptford, where I gave directions for a press to hold my turning and joiner's tools. Coming home in the dark, I found my wife had brought our new girl from Mr. Falconbridge's.

She is wretched poor, but ordinary favoured, and we must lay out seven or eight pounds of clothes on her, which goes against my heart. I cannot esteem her as I might have done another, and her voice is furred; but her manner of singing may yet give me pleasure.

I then met with notice of a meeting of the Commissioners for Tangier tomorrow, so I confined myself to my chamber and set to making up my accounts. They prove clear, though with difficulty because I had not done them sooner.

periods.label: Week of Oct 17

levels.sentence: After church and a merry dinner, I begged the King for Tangier money, heard scandalous Court gossip, secured my cash from the damp cellar, and ended the day with Mrs. Martin's sister.
levels.paragraph: This day I went to church with my wife and our new maid Barker, then dined merrily with Lady Pen and Peg. In the afternoon I attended the Cabinet, where the King sat like a statue while I pleaded for Tangier money. Later I heard gossip about Harry Killigrew's banishment and electoral rebuffs to courtiers. I moved my iron chests of money out of the damp cellar, and then visited Mrs. Martin, where her sister Doll proved surprisingly yielding.
levels.summary:
After morning church with my wife and new maid Barker, I enjoyed a merry dinner with Lady Pen and Peg. Then I went to White Hall to attend the Cabinet, where I had to ask the King and his ministers for money for Tangier—a thankless task, since they hate to hear of wants.

The King sat like an image and said nothing, and I was referred to another meeting. Later, walking with Sir H. Cholmly, I learned that Harry Killigrew had been banished for calling Lady Castlemayne a lecherous girl when young, and that both Mr. Williamson and Bab May were rejected by voters who wanted no courtiers.

In the evening I read Stillingfleet on Purgatory, and though I think we are in the right, I found little in the book. Then, with only my boy and Jane, I carried two iron chests of money from the damp cellar into my closet, glad to see my treasure safe. Afterwards I called on Mrs.

Martin and sat with her; contrary to all expectation, I had my will of her sister Doll.

periods.label: Week of Oct 24

levels.sentence: After Captain Guy's grave account of the fleet's decay and our likely defeat, I tumbled women all afternoon, supped merrily with kin, and then noted more disasters in the King's work.
levels.paragraph: Captain Guy dined with me and cried out against the fleet's discipline, saying true English valour is almost spent and that we shall be beaten next year. He assured me the June fight was a defeat, though we made bonefires, and he condemned Holmes while commending Smith. After he left, I went to Mrs. Martin's and tumbled widow Burroughes and Doll all afternoon, then supped merrily with my uncle and aunt Wight, abusing my aunt with Dr. Venner. At night I found the Revenge, Dyamond, and Foresight have all met disasters, which is strange.
levels.summary:
Captain Guy dined with me and spoke gravely of the fleet: he says English valour is spent, few commanders do their duty, and we may well be beaten next year.

He confessed the June fight was a defeat, though the fleet was ashamed of our bonefires, and he condemns Holmes as idle, proud, and conceited, while commending Smith.

He blames the loss of ships on the sands on weather, but I fear something more; he says the Dutch fight in good order and we in none, and that the whole is governed by fools.

After dinner I went to Mrs. Martin's and tumbled widow Burroughes and Doll all afternoon as I pleased, then gave them wine and went home by boat. In the evening my wife and I supped with uncle and aunt Wight, where I saw Woolly's pretty wife and was very merry abusing my aunt with Dr. Venner.

Later I noted more disasters in the King's work: the Revenge's forecastle blown up, the Dyamond overset careening, and the Foresight with another come to grief—all strange marks of how things are now done.

periods.brief: After Captain Guy's grave account of the fleet's decay and our likely defeat, I tumbled women all afternoon, supped merrily with kin, and then noted more disasters in the King's work.
periods.full:
Captain Guy dined with me and spoke gravely of the fleet: he says English valour is spent, few commanders do their duty, and we may well be beaten next year.

He confessed the June fight was a defeat, though the fleet was ashamed of our bonefires, and he condemns Holmes as idle, proud, and conceited, while commending Smith.

He blames the loss of ships on the sands on weather, but I fear something more; he says the Dutch fight in good order and we in none, and that the whole is governed by fools.

After dinner I went to Mrs. Martin's and tumbled widow Burroughes and Doll all afternoon as I pleased, then gave them wine and went home by boat. In the evening my wife and I supped with uncle and aunt Wight, where I saw Woolly's pretty wife and was very merry abusing my aunt with Dr. Venner.

Later I noted more disasters in the King's work: the Revenge's forecastle blown up, the Dyamond overset careening, and the Foresight with another come to grief—all strange marks of how things are now done.

periods.label: Week of Oct 31

levels.sentence: Amid a gift of cake and a housewarming visit, I found disquiet in the King's service, shared Sir W. Coventry's fears of ruin, and sought comfort from my wife.
levels.paragraph: The day began with a noble cake from Burton's wife, which I sent my wife to use for housewarming Betty Michell. My morning at the office was troubled by want of money, leaving me disquieted that my pains serve the King poorly. After dinner, my wife and company went to Shadwell, while I stayed and had my will with Mrs. Bagwell. In the evening, I conferred with Sir W. Coventry, who shared my melancholy that all discipline is lost in the fleet and all will be ruined. I returned home to my wife, whose comfort and talk eased me before bed.
levels.summary:
I rose to a gift of a noble cake from Burton's wife, and resolved my wife should use it to house-warm Betty Michell. The morning at the office was spent answering people about want of money, which brought me much disquiet, for I find little service done the King and great trouble to myself.

At dinner, my wife, brother, W. Hewer, and Barker went off to Shadwell, while I returned to the office, where I took in Mrs. Bagwell and did what I would with her, then stayed until evening.

When my wife returned, I set her at her sick brother's, and went to White Hall, where I found Sir W. Coventry alone and melancholy. He confessed he expects all will be undone and ruined, and agreed that all discipline is lost in the fleet.

He also noted the House goes slowly in finding money, and the discontented party threaten another bout over our accounts. I left him with sad reflections, took up my wife, and went home, where I found comfort in talk with her and my brother, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Nov 21

levels.sentence: I passed a week of petty quarrels and coarse pleasures—with my wife, with Bagwell's wife, with Doll Lane—while news of the French King's insulting vests and my cousin Roger's talk of ruin made me both merry and afraid.
levels.paragraph: On the 22nd I fell out with my wife over a lace handkerchief, yet we were friends again presently; that same day Batelier brought news that the King of France had put all his footmen into vests in defiance of our King, which I thought a monstrous indignity, though it made me merry. I also had my way with Bagwell's wife and pleased myself with Doll Lane on the 26th, a coarse pleasure. At Westminster I heard the great case against Lord Mordaunt and met my cousin Roger, who talks of inevitable ruin and wants me to find him a rich widow. I pray the news from the North proves nothing.
levels.summary:
On the 22nd I was at the office all morning, where my Lord Bruncker showed me Hollar's new print of the City, with a pretty representation of the burnt part. I was glad to hear Hollar is sworn the King's servant and commanded to make a great map like Gombout of Paris.

At noon my wife and I fell out because she had cut a lace handkerchief about her neck down to her breasts almost, thinking it the fashion; we gave one another the lie too much, but were presently friends. That evening Mr.

Batelier came, and we supped and played cards, and he told me how the King of France, in defiance of the King of England, had caused all his footmen to be put into vests.

I thought it the greatest indignity ever done by one Prince to another, and would incite a stone to be revenged; yet it made me mighty merry, and I was angry to see our King so little as to have it offered him. The relator came over with my Lady Fanshaw, who is come over with the dead body of her husband.

Batelier also brought oysters and new French wine, mighty good, though I drank but little.

Earlier that same noon, Bagwell's wife was with me at the office, and I did what I would; at night Mrs. Burroughs came and appointed to meet upon the next holyday and go abroad together.

On the 26th I went by water to Westminster to enquire after my tallies, and at the Swan I drank burnt claret with Doll Lane, who told me her sister was brought to bed and that I am to be godfather. I did tumble Doll, and do almost what I would with her—a coarse pleasure, but I took it.

I went to the New Exchange hoping to meet Mrs. Burroughs, but she was with her old aunt and could not leave; so I bought baubles, then went into the House of Parliament, where I heard the great case against my Lord Mordaunt for arbitrary proceedings against one Taylor.

I was glad to see my old chamber-fellow Sawyer in good play against him.

There I met my cozen Roger Pepys, the first time I have spoken with him this parliament. He promised to come and bring Madam Turner with him, who is come to town to see the City but hath lost all her goods in Salisbury Court; Sir William Turner did not endeavour to save one penny.

Roger bids me help him to some good rich widow, for he is resolved to retire wholly into the country, being confident we shall all be ruined very speedily; and I am much in his mind. Having staid too long at the House, I missed Burroughs again, and being very hungry I went home, ate presently, then to Sir W.

Batten's, where Sir J. Minnes and Captain Cocke were. There was no news from the North at all, and the news-book makes the business nothing, but that they are all dispersed; I pray God it may prove so.

periods.label: Week of Nov 28

levels.sentence: I entertained noble guests, pursued amorous adventures, and tended to business while the kingdom fretted over Scotland.
levels.paragraph: This week I delighted in fine dinners with noble company, the resumed meetings at Gresham College, and the amorous attentions of Pegg and later Mrs. Burroughs and Sarah. Yet I also faced duns for money and the growing fear of the Scottish rebels, though we heard of their defeat near Edinburgh. I entertained Kate Joyce and Mrs. Turner, who mourned her losses, and I resolved to mend my ways and settle my accounts.
levels.summary:
This week I entertained noble guests at a lavish dinner, visited Gresham College, and enjoyed the company of several women—Pegg allowed me intimacies, and later I had my way with Mrs. Burroughs and began a new dalliance with Sarah.

Meanwhile, I attended the Duke of York, faced a dun for money, and heard troubling news about Scotland.

I also comforted Mrs. Turner, who lost everything in the plague and was angry with me for not writing. On the last day, I heard of the Scottish rebels' defeat and the safe arrival of mast ships, and I resolved to settle my accounts and begin the new year afresh.

periods.label: Week of Dec 12

levels.sentence: On this day I learned of poor Batters's drowning, which filled me with fear, yet I went about my business, visited Mrs. Martin and Sarah for merry company, collected more plate, and invited Mr. Andrews to Christmas dinner, though I remained sorry for Batters.
levels.paragraph: I heard this morning that poor Batters, a bred seaman who had brought his ship from sea but yesterday, was drowned as he went down to her in the Thames. The news left me afeard, more than ever I was. I went about my day nonetheless: dined at home, called on Lord Bellasses, and spied Mrs. Martin in Westminster Hall, who is well after her childbed and leaves tomorrow. She told me the child came on the very day it ought, after my being with her before her husband came home. I made merry with Sarah at the Swan, collected more plate, and invited Mr. Thomas Andrews to Christmas dinner, yet went to bed sorry for poor Batters.
levels.summary:
I began the day with the ill news that poor Batters, a seaman born and bred, was drowned in the Thames as he went down to his ship after bringing her in safely yesterday. The accident filled me with a fear I have never felt so strongly, and I could not shake it all day.

Even so, I conducted my usual business: dining at home, calling on Lord Bellasses (who was out), and visiting Westminster Hall, where I saw Mrs. Martin, who is quite well and goes abroad tomorrow after her childbed.

She told me her child came on the very day it ought, after my being with her before her husband returned home.

Later I went to the Swan, where I sent for Sarah and we were mighty merry, and then to Sir Robert Viner's about my plate, bringing home another dozen to make my total two and a half dozen. At home I met Mr. Thomas Andrews and invited him to dine with me at Christmas.

I finished the evening at the office, and went to bed still sorrowing for poor Batters.

periods.label: Week of Dec 19

levels.sentence: After a visit from Mrs. Clerk and her daughter, I granted a promise to help her son-in-law gain command of a pleasure boat while stealing a moment of intimacy with her, then spent the day arranging pictures and accounts.
levels.paragraph: I lay late, and when I rose, Mrs. Clerk of Greenwich and her daughter Daniel came to see me. The daughter's business was to ask my help in getting her husband the command of a new little pleasure boat, and I promised to assist. In my chamber I took the opportunity to kiss her and touch her breasts. Then I went to the office, did a little business, and later spent the afternoon putting pictures in order, including framing Lady Castlemayne's print. In the evening I marshalled my papers of accounts against future need, did some Tangier work, and went to bed.
levels.summary:
Mrs. Clerk of Greenwich and her daughter Daniel visited me this morning. The daughter asked me to help her husband gain command of a new pleasure boat being built, and I agreed. While alone with her in my chamber, I seized the chance to kiss her and fondle her breasts, a small indulgence I noted with pleasure.

After that I attended to business at the office and the Exchange, then dined at home. The rest of the afternoon I spent arranging my pictures, especially framing a fine print of Lady Castlemayne.

In the evening I organized the accounts I had presented to Parliament, so I might use them again if needed, and finished with some Tangier work before going to bed.

periods.label: Week of Dec 26

levels.sentence: After paying his debts and settling his accounts for 1666, Samuel Pepys laments his increased spending and the nation's dire state, though he thanks God for his growing wealth.
levels.paragraph: On the last day of 1666, Pepys rises early to pay his debts and clear accounts, meeting Doll Lane for a drink along the way. He spends the afternoon balancing his books, finding that his income has fallen and his spending risen, though his net worth has increased. He resolves to be more careful. In the evening, he reflects on the public misfortunes of the year—unpaid seamen, powerful enemies, and a negligent court—while counting his blessings. The text ends with a list of editor's bookmarks from the diary.
levels.summary:
On the final day of 1666, Samuel Pepys sets out to settle his year's accounts, paying all his debts around town. Along the way he meets Doll Lane and a companion, and drinks burnt wine with them at the Half Moon Tavern, though he takes 'no more pleasure' in it.

He returns home to balance his books, discovering that his income for the year was L2,986—L573 less than the previous year—while his spending soared to L1,154, L644 more than before.

He is discontented by his prodigality but comforted that his total worth now exceeds L6,200, an increase of L1,800, and he prays to be thankful and more careful.

' He fears ruin for the kingdom. Personally, he reports that his household is well—four maids, a clerk, and his brother—though his eyes are sore from overwork. He also notes with pride that he can now serve guests entirely on silver plate, having two and a half dozen pieces.

The text concludes with a lengthy list of editor's bookmarks—quotable phrases and notable lines culled from Pepys's diary for the year.

periods.label: Week of Jan 2

levels.sentence: Amid fresh alarms of a French descent, I walked to White Hall, heard Parliament wrangle over the Wine Patent, tippled with Doll Lane, then sat through the worst play I ever saw and came home displeased with myself for neglecting my wife.
levels.paragraph: I spent the day at White Hall and Westminster, where everyone was talking of the French having shipped landsmen at Brest and perhaps meaning Ireland; the Houblons laughed at this and said it was only a West Indies convoy dressed up to hurry Parliament's money. George Montagu told me the King has displeased the Commons by turning their Accounts bill into a commission that left out Coventry and me. I heard a good conference on the Wine Patent, then met Doll Lane at the Rose Tavern. In the afternoon I went to the King's House and saw The Custome of the Country, which I thought the worst play ever, though Knipp sang charmingly; I went home much out of humour for having wasted time and disobliged my wife.
levels.summary:
I walked to White Hall to attend the Duke of York, while my wife went with Mrs. Pen to frostbite themselves in the fields. The Court was full of great apprehensions of the French, who had certainly shipped landsmen at Brest, and most guess their design for Ireland.

We have orders to send all possible ships to the Downes; but we can send forth no ships without men, nor will men go without money, and every day brings news of new mutinies among the seamen, so our condition is likely to be very miserable.

At Westminster I met all the Houblons, who laughed at this discourse of the French, saying it was nothing but sending to their plantation in the West Indys, and that we at Court blow up a design of invading us only to make Parliament make more haste in money matters; I do not believe we have any such plot in our heads.

Mr. George Montagu told me all is like to go ill, the King displeasing the House of Commons by evading their Bill for examining Accounts and putting it into a Commission, though he left out Coventry and me and named all the rest the Parliament named.

He finds the enmity almost over for my Lord Sandwich, and that now all is upon the Vice-Chamberlain. In the Painted Chamber I heard a conference between the Lords and Commons about the Wine Patent, exceeding glad because of the good discourses, especially from the Commons, Mr.

Swinfen and Sir Thomas Meres infinitely outdoing the Lords.

Afterwards Doll Lane came to me at the Rose Taverne, and we drank a good deal of wine, and I gave her twelve soldis for some gloves as a New Year's gift. Then with Sir W.

Pen by coach to the Temple, where I ate a bit at an ordinary, and then alone to the King's House, where I saw 'The Custome of the Country' the second time.

Knipp does the Widow well, and sings a little song admirably, but of all the plays that ever I did see it is the worst—no plot, no language, nor anything acceptable.

I went home much displeased for the loss of so much time and disobliging my wife by being there without her, walked by link through the cold, slippery frost, set down my journal, and fell to thinking upon establishing my vows against the next year.

periods.label: Week of Jan 9

levels.sentence: In one diligent week I examined the lost Prince Royall, kissed and touched Mrs. Burroughs, refused Lord Bruncker's play to stick to work, and still found time to worry about shameful Prize Office sales.
levels.paragraph: I kept hard at my office business this week, hosting Lord Bruncker and taking examinations from the master and mates of the lost Prince Royall. I even kissed Mrs. Burroughs, and later touched her breasts when we were alone, though I stayed devoted to my letters and duties. I refused Lord Bruncker's invitation to see Knipp act because I would not abandon my work. At night I went to bed with a mighty light mind, pleased to see my diligence paying off.
levels.summary:
This week I rose early and attended the office all morning, then dined with Lord Bruncker, who joined me in decrying the bad performances of the Controller's and Surveyor's offices.

After dinner, the chief men of the Trinity House met with us to examine the loss of The Prince Royall, and I personally took and kept the examinations of the master and mates. Mrs. Burroughs came to me about business at noon, and I kissed her; later, alone in the office, I touched her breasts, then returned to work.

When Lord Bruncker pressed me to go with him to see Knipp act the great part in The Indian Emperour, I refused because I was so devoted to my business.

That night we were troubled about how to prevent the Prize Office's shameful candle sale of hemp, timber-deals, and other good goods at low prices, knowing we would soon need those same goods and have to buy them back at extraordinary cost.

I went home to supper and to bed with my mind mighty light, seeing the fruits of my diligence in having business go off my hand so merrily.

periods.label: Week of Jan 23

levels.sentence: I delighted in a night of music and dancing with friends at my home, and later stole tender moments with Betty Michell amid a busy week of office duties and London gossip.
levels.paragraph: This week I threw myself into both work and pleasure. After office duties and examining the loss of The Bredagh, I hosted a grand evening at my house, with fiddlers, songs, and a cold supper. I was ravished by Mercer's Italian song, flirted with Knipp in her bed, and finished the night content. A few days later, I found time to see Betty Michell and steal a kiss, then walked with Roger Pepys and heard troubling talk of Parliament.
levels.summary:
On the 24th, I prepared my office for a gathering and entertained a lively company—Mercer and her sister, Mr. Batelier, Pembleton, Lady Pen and Pegg, Captain Rolt, and later Harris, Mrs. Pierce, and Knipp.

We danced to four fiddlers, sang three-part songs, and enjoyed a cold supper; Harris sang a strange Irish song, and Mercer's Italian song ravished me. The night stretched until nearly three, with Knipp feeling ill and my wife putting her to bed.

I went up to Knipp's bed and handled her breasts and kissed her—a merry end to one of the best evenings I could hope for.

On the 27th, my wife went to hear Mr. Frampton but found he had gone to sea. I met the Michells at the Old Swan and had a 'baiser' or two with Betty, whom I love mightily, then took them by sculler to White Hall. The morning was spent with Sir W.

Coventry and Bruncker on office business, and after an anthem and dining with Sir G. Carteret, I met Lord Bellasses about Tangier. Walking in the Pell Mell with Roger Pepys, I heard of Parliament's discontent over the Poll Bill and showed him the Court's liberty, which shocked him.

That night, in warm moonshine, I arranged a boat ride with the Michells and under my cloak got Betty's hand—a sweet end to a busy day.

periods.label: Week of Jan 30

levels.sentence: From settling accounts with gratitude to kissing Mercer in the garden, refusing a gold bribe, and taking liberties with Betty in the dark, this week moved between sober business and private pleasures.
levels.paragraph: This week began tamely with monthly accounts and a thankful small gain, then moved to a pleasant visit with the Michells and an evening in the garden singing with Mercer until my wife reminded me it was a fast-day for the King's death; ashamed, I went to cards and kissed Mercer several times. Later, I refused a box of gold from the flaggmakers, heard good news of the Prince and peace with Spain, and learned of Lord Bellasses's underhand dealings. I saw a good play, admired Mrs. Middleton, gave Betty gifts, and on the dark ride home used a bruise as an excuse to sit beside her and do what I pleased, going to bed glad of my success.
levels.summary:
I began the week with relief, settling my monthly accounts and finding I had saved a little from my salary alone; I thanked God for it. The same afternoon I went with my wife, Mercer, and Barker to visit little Michell and his wife, carrying treats and enjoying their charming house and warm talk.

That evening I lingered in the garden singing with Mercer by moonlight until my wife reminded me it was a fast-day for the King's death; ashamed, I went inside to cards and then kissed Mercer several times before bed.

On the fifth, I refused a box of at least £100 in gold from the flaggmakers Young and Whistler because I did not think them safe men and wanted to be able to say I had refused their offer. I heard the Prince was much better and that Lord Sandwich had perfected peace with Spain, and Sir H.

Cholmly told me of Lord Bellasses's underhand dealings—he had taken near £2000 in gratuities for friendship in the Mole business and then tried to replace him. That evening I saw a good play, heard Knipp sing 'All night I weepe' admirably, and enjoyed the sight of fine ladies, especially Mrs. Middleton.

periods.full:
I began the week with relief, settling my monthly accounts and finding I had saved a little from my salary alone; I thanked God for it. The same afternoon I went with my wife, Mercer, and Barker to visit little Michell and his wife, carrying treats and enjoying their charming house and warm talk.

That evening I lingered in the garden singing with Mercer by moonlight until my wife reminded me it was a fast-day for the King's death; ashamed, I went inside to cards and then kissed Mercer several times before bed.

On the fifth, I refused a box of at least £100 in gold from the flaggmakers Young and Whistler because I did not think them safe men and wanted to be able to say I had refused their offer. I heard the Prince was much better and that Lord Sandwich had perfected peace with Spain, and Sir H.

periods.label: Week of Feb 6

levels.sentence: A day of official business and anxious news turned into a stolen afternoon with Betty Michell, followed by a heart-stopping narrow escape when her husband and my wife nearly caught me out.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with Tangier business at Sir Philip Warwicke's, only to learn that the Poll Bill offered no hope of money. At Westminster I heard encouraging news of Prince Rupert's recovery and that Lord Sandwich was ordered home, though a fresh hunt for prize goods troubled me briefly. That afternoon I contrived a meeting with Betty Michell, bought her a dressing-box, and passed a merry hour watching cabinet-makers work. But coming home, I fell into a terrible fear that her husband had sent to my house for her, and only by rare good fortune did I arrive before my wife could learn anything. The evening ended quietly, teaching Barker a little of my song, my heart full of joy at being safe.
levels.summary:
Up early, I went by water to Sir Philip Warwicke's with Lord Bellasses and Creed about my Tangier warrant, but we were defeated of any hopes from the Poll Bill. Then at Westminster Hall I heard Prince Rupert was better and that he had expressly told Dr. Troutbecke my Lord Sandwich is ordered home.

I also learned that Prince Rupert had begged the stolen prize-goods and was looking after them anew, which troubled me at first until I saw it was only Hayes and his little people. I bought the King's speech, which held some words that promised a possible peace, God send it!

After dinner, I went with Lord Bellasses to Povy's house, where we found Auditor Beale and Vernatty over their endless accounts. Vernatty is certainly the cunningest knave ever born. From there my lord set me down at the New Exchange, where I waited at Pottle's shop for Betty Michell.

She came about five, surprised not to find my wife there. I took her across the water to a cabinet-maker's, bought her a dressing-box for twenty shillings, and while it was being made, I tried to get her into a drinking house, but she would not.

We watched the workmen, and the mistress of the shop took us for man and wife, which I owned, and we were very merry until late.

The trouble began on the way home: I feared her husband might have gone to my house to look for her and would give my wife occasion for strange thoughts. So I stopped the coach and walked her home, only to learn he had already sent his maid after her.

In a cold sweat I hurried back, cudgeling my brain for a likely excuse for my wife. As God would have it, a little woman stumbled up to my door in the dark—it was her maid again—and I told her her mistress was come home, then blessed my fortune that I had got in before my wife had heard anything.

All was well within; my joy was full. I went to the office awhile, then home, and after supper taught Barker a little of my song before going to bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 13

levels.sentence: A week of hot encounters at court, secret pleasures, and anxious talk of peace and Parliament leaves me resolved to mind my business and watch my pleasures.
levels.paragraph: At the Duke of York's council I faced hot opposition over the Ticket Office, and Sir G. Carteret was stark mad at me for my plain honesty. The King's idle jokes and my failure to answer about the St. Patrick galled me, while Betty Michell's coldness sent me home troubled. Yet I found secret pleasure with Mrs Burrows, and a witty masked lady at the theatre delighted me more than the play. Through all this, Captain Cocke's talk of peace and possible civil war left me anxious for the Kingdom, and I resolved to keep to my business.
levels.summary:
On the 17th, I stood firm at the Duke of York's council, declaring without money no fleet could be expected, but only Sir W. Coventry seconded me. Sir G. Carteret was furious at me afterward, and I felt the weight of honesty. Walking with the King and Duke, I was galled by my ignorance about the St.

Patrick and by the King's coarse jokes about marriage. Later, Betty Michell refused me even a touch of her hand, and I went home troubled, yet resolved to make use of it and mind my business.

Captain Cocke's night visit brought grave news of peace negotiations and fears of civil war, and I read a fine answer to 'The Apology for Papists' before bed, noting a false denial about the Queen.

On the 18th, I was mightily pleased to see our Navy expense accounts handsomely bound at the bookbinder's, and at the Exchequer I handled tallies. Meeting Mr. Weaver eased my mind about a legal omission. In the afternoon, I had Mrs Burrows alone in my closet and kissed and touched her breasts, a secret pleasure.

In the evening, after a short stop at the Duke's playhouse, we saw The Mayd's Tragedy at the King's House, but a masked lady of quality, exceeding witty, diverted me more than the play; she gave Sir Charles Sedley leave to find her out without unmasking. I ended the night at the office, then home to supper and bed.

periods.label: Week of Feb 27

levels.phrase: A whirl of business and pleasure
levels.sentence: A day of dockyard inspections, Sir W. Batten's stumble into a stinking tar-drain, a merry dinner with Captain Cocke, a discreet encounter at Bagwell's, unsettling news from Mr. Chaplin, my wife's first notes on the flageolet, and a preposterous translation of Alsted's Templum made this a busy, eventful March 4th.
levels.paragraph: This morning I went by barge with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten to Deptford and Woolwich on business, where Sir W. Batten sprained his foot after falling into a hole meant for tar drainage. We dined merrily at the White Hart with Captain Cocke, and I later visited Bagwell's wife and spoke with her husband about his new shipbuilding post at Harwich. On my way home I met Mr. Chaplin, who shared troubling news about Dutch demands and French movements. In the evening I was pleased to hear my wife begin learning the flageolet, while all day I puzzled over a ridiculous translation of Alsted's Templum that I could barely understand.
levels.summary:
The day began with an early barge trip to Deptford and Woolwich, where I attended to business with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten. At a storehouse, Sir W.

Batten fell into a stinking tar-drain and sprained his foot, though thankfully no worse; after changing his stockings at a strong-water shop, we continued to Woolwich to inspect a ballast wharf that we decided was not worth hiring unless we could buy the fee-simple, which was not possible.

After a merry dinner at the White Hart with Captain Cocke, where Sir J. Minnes told many tales, we returned to Deptford, where I slipped away to Bagwell's and had my way with his wife, then sent for her husband to discuss his new post at Harwich. Later, on Tower Hill, I met Mr.

Chaplin, who reported that the King of France was denied passage through Flanders, that the Dutch insisted on not striking the flag as a precondition for talks, and that Lord Arlington was rumored to become Lord Treasurer—gossip I doubted.

At home, I was delighted by my wife's first attempts at the flageolet, and I spent the day struggling with Berckenshaw's ridiculous translation of Alsted's Templum, understanding barely three consecutive lines.

periods.label: Week of Mar 13

levels.sentence: Though the kingdom seemed on the brink of war and my own desires left me uneasy, I took what joy I could in music, kisses, and the simple duties of my office.
levels.paragraph: These two days have been a whirl of anxiety and small consolations. At court I heard the fearful news that the Council doubts its own policy and that a fleet cannot be victualled, which set me to preparing a statement of our stores. I dined with Sir G. Carteret's ladies and felt shame that my wife has not visited them, while later I stole a kiss from Betty Michell and yearned in vain for Doll Lane. Amidst the gloom of Lady Carteret and Dr. Fuller, I found gladness in Tom's music and little Mis Tooker's visit, and I resolved to commend Sir John Winter's diligence to the Duke.
levels.summary:
I was much troubled by the state of affairs. At court, after presenting myself to the Duke of York with Sir W. Batten, I found Sir G. Carteret quarreling with Lord Bruncker, which pleased me given my fears. But Mr.

Gawden's news alarmed me: the Council is weary of fitting out squadrons, and a Privy-Councillor said a fleet cannot be set out for want of victuals. Since I ought to have represented the state of provisions, I resolved to draw up a true statement of the Victualler's stores.

At the Exchange, letters brought word that the Dutch and the King of France demand high terms in a most braving manner, so that no one knows whether peace or war will come, and merchants are giving themselves over for lost; I was told a man might get L20,000 in a week by buying goods if war were certain.

Lady Carteret could speak of nothing but sorrow, and even Dr. Fuller was gloomy.

Yet I had my small pleasures amid the anxiety. I dined with Sir G. Carteret's ladies, though ashamed that my wife has not visited them; I stopped at Michell's to kiss Betty; and at home I was pleased that Tom has been teaching Barker to sing a third part, which will delight us.

Little Mis Tooker came, grown a little woman, and I had opportunity to kiss her. But my attempt to meet Doll Lane at the Rose tavern failed, and she never came, which troubled me.

Sir John Winter called me up early on the 15th on the King's business about his timber, and I thought him a worthy good man, resolved to tell the Duke. I also heard that Mr. Carcasse might ask me to be godfather to his child with Lord Bruncker, and that the Duke of Buckingham is concluded gone to France.

After a late night preparing a speech for the King, I finished my journals and went to bed, trying to hold onto the cheerful moments while fearing what lies ahead.
