periods.brief: Though the kingdom seemed on the brink of war and my own desires left me uneasy, I took what joy I could in music, kisses, and the simple duties of my office.
periods.full:
I was much troubled by the state of affairs. At court, after presenting myself to the Duke of York with Sir W. Batten, I found Sir G. Carteret quarreling with Lord Bruncker, which pleased me given my fears. But Mr.

Gawden's news alarmed me: the Council is weary of fitting out squadrons, and a Privy-Councillor said a fleet cannot be set out for want of victuals. Since I ought to have represented the state of provisions, I resolved to draw up a true statement of the Victualler's stores.

At the Exchange, letters brought word that the Dutch and the King of France demand high terms in a most braving manner, so that no one knows whether peace or war will come, and merchants are giving themselves over for lost; I was told a man might get L20,000 in a week by buying goods if war were certain.

Lady Carteret could speak of nothing but sorrow, and even Dr. Fuller was gloomy.

Yet I had my small pleasures amid the anxiety. I dined with Sir G. Carteret's ladies, though ashamed that my wife has not visited them; I stopped at Michell's to kiss Betty; and at home I was pleased that Tom has been teaching Barker to sing a third part, which will delight us.

Little Mis Tooker came, grown a little woman, and I had opportunity to kiss her. But my attempt to meet Doll Lane at the Rose tavern failed, and she never came, which troubled me.

Sir John Winter called me up early on the 15th on the King's business about his timber, and I thought him a worthy good man, resolved to tell the Duke. I also heard that Mr. Carcasse might ask me to be godfather to his child with Lord Bruncker, and that the Duke of Buckingham is concluded gone to France.

After a late night preparing a speech for the King, I finished my journals and went to bed, trying to hold onto the cheerful moments while fearing what lies ahead.

periods.sentence: Though the kingdom seemed on the brink of war and my own desires left me uneasy, I took what joy I could in music, kisses, and the simple duties of my office.
periods.paragraph: These two days have been a whirl of anxiety and small consolations. At court I heard the fearful news that the Council doubts its own policy and that a fleet cannot be victualled, which set me to preparing a statement of our stores. I dined with Sir G. Carteret's ladies and felt shame that my wife has not visited them, while later I stole a kiss from Betty Michell and yearned in vain for Doll Lane. Amidst the gloom of Lady Carteret and Dr. Fuller, I found gladness in Tom's music and little Mis Tooker's visit, and I resolved to commend Sir John Winter's diligence to the Duke.

periods.label: Week of Apr 3

levels.sentence: Amid fears of a bad peace and signs of public suffering, I find myself entangled in small quarrels, base lust, and the shame of an under-assessed poll money.
levels.paragraph: This week was full of disquiet. I quarreled with Carcasse, distrusted Pen, and could not resist thinking on Betty Michell. The town cries for peace, but all signs point to a bad one, with tenants and even great lords losing money. Even my poll money shamed me for being so little. Yet I found some content in settling accounts with Viner and reading a good book.
levels.summary:
After a morning quarrel with Mr. Carcasse, I went to Sir W. Pen about Mrs. Turner's son, and was again struck by Pen's falseness—the worst fellow I ever hope to know. Later I drank with Betty and her husband at the Old Swan, but had no chance to kiss her, and saw Mrs.

Howlett back at Westminster Hall after her sickness.

I spent the afternoon settling accounts with Sir Robert Viner, which gave me great content though I found their records poor, and met James Houblon, who saw no hope of peace and expected abuse from the King of France. In the evening Mr.

Young told me how the new churches are placed for the advantage of the Archbishop, Bishop, Chancellor, and City rather than the convenience of the people, and how Moorefields, leased for seven years, now has two-story houses and paved streets—a scheme invented by Alderman Hooker to raise money for Commissioner Taylor and Sir W.

Batten. I also paid my poll money of L40 17s, and was ashamed it was so little, since I chose not to assess myself for my money when the ablest merchants like Sir Andrew Rickard did not.

At the Exchange, the town cried out for peace, but I fear the peace we make will be a bad one. There is real suffering: tenants flinging up lands they cannot pay for, the Duke of Buckingham losing £6000, and my father writes that Jasper Trice has given up housekeeping to board with his brother at Offord.

These are sad signs of the times. In the afternoon I went to the King's house to see "The Tameing of a Shrew," which was mean fare despite some good pieces; only Sawny by Lacy had any life, and even that faltered. My wife came with W. Hewer and others.

Afterward I tried to meet Knipp for some air, but she was gone, which spared me any indiscretion. Then at the Swan I kissed a little miss, and at the Old Swan I found Betty Michell so pretty that my mind ran on her all evening and into the next day—God forgive me. Sir W.

Batten told me his lady's jewels, long lost, were found in her closet under a china cup, after a servant had been imprisoned and arraigned. Mrs. Turner and I suspect my Lady had disposed of them to friends in case she died, and now they are back. I finished the day reading a well-regarded book on Turkish policy.

periods.label: Week of Apr 10

levels.sentence: I spent the morning blocking Pett's trick against Lord Bruncker, sang a little with my wife, wrote to my ailing father, and then let Mrs Lowther willingly tempt me into fondling her breasts and mouth.
levels.paragraph: This morning I sat in the office and was wary of the false Commissioner Pett, who wanted Carcasse's case brought on to-day to spite my Lord Bruncker; I prevented it. After dinner I sang a little alone with my poor wife, with some pleasure, then returned to the office till late at night. My eyes still trouble me after candle-light, which I noted with concern. I wrote to my father, glad he is at ease again, and I long to have him in town so I can do all I can for him. In the afternoon Mrs Lowther came to me, and I touched and kissed her breasts and mouth, and she was very willing.
levels.summary:
I sat at the office all morning, and saw clearly how the false Commissioner Pett tried to force Carcasse's business onto the agenda, hoping to embarrass my Lord Bruncker; I made sure it was not brought on today.

At home I sang a little alone with my poor wife, which gave me some pleasure, then back to the office till late. My eyes still trouble me after candle-light, and that weighs on me.

I wrote to my father, glad to hear he is at ease again, and I long for him to be in town so I can do what I can for him — I want him to live and take pleasure in my doing well.

In the afternoon Mrs Lowther came to me at the office, and I touched and kissed her breasts and mouth, and she was very willing; I let myself enjoy it.

periods.label: Week of Apr 17

levels.sentence: Amid the feasting at White Hall for the Swedish ambassadors, I spent the day at the office, waited anxiously while my wife attended Betty Michell in labour, and rejoiced at the safe birth of a pretty girl, before slipping off to Mrs Martin and then visiting the new mother.
levels.paragraph: Today White Hall kept a feast to show jollity to the Swedish ambassadors before they leave for the treaty abroad. I was at the office all morning, and heard that young Michell had called for my wife to attend his wife's labour. At noon I dined alone, then worked on music papers until my wife came home with the good news that she and the midwife had delivered poor Betty of a pretty girl. Later my wife and I went to her mother's, and I found time to call on Mrs Martin, then we visited little Michell's to see the child, which I like mightily, and so home to bed.
levels.summary:
The day began with a grand feast at White Hall, designed to show jollity to the Swedish ambassadors before they depart for treaty negotiations abroad. I sat at the office all morning, distracted by word that young Michell had summoned my wife to attend Betty Michell in labour.

I waited in expectation, and at noon dined alone before turning to my music papers. My wife returned with the delightful news that she and the midwife had delivered poor Betty of a pretty girl, and I was mighty glad of it.

Later I set my wife down at her mother's and went about business, though I accomplished little. I called on Mrs Martin and did what I would with her, then fetched my wife and went to little Michell's, where we saw the child, which I like mightily, and I asked after Betty, being glad she was well.

The day also saw me openly opposing Sir W. Warren in discourse, as he now applies himself wholly to Lord Bruncker. I came home to the office and then to my chamber, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 15

levels.sentence: A busy day of music lessons, errands about coach-houses, public speculation on the new Treasury commissioners, and private strolls that brought me sight of Betty Michell and a stolen hour with Mrs. Martin, all shadowed by doubts of peace.
levels.paragraph: This morning I learnt a new tune on the flagelet and then went out on business, hearing contradictory reports about the King's new Treasury commissioners. Later, with Mr. Commander, I looked at coach-houses and stables for the project behind our house. I took a broken-day walk through the Minorys and the postern-gate, espying my young mercer and his pretty wife, and at the Old Swan found Betty Michell as pretty as ever. After some idle talk at Westminster Hall, I spent a while with Mrs. Martin before going home to play flagelets with my wife.
levels.summary:
Up betimes and had my flagelette master set me a new tune, which I played presently and shall soon master.

Then to the Commissioners of Excise and Westminster Hall, where the talk was all about the King's naming of the Treasury commissioners yesterday; the names reported differ, but all agree the Duke of Albemarle is among them, and it will be known in a day or two.

In the afternoon, because it was a broken day and my vows allowed me to walk abroad, I went over the Hill to the postern-gate for the first time since the fire pulled down those houses, and spied my young mercer and his pretty little wife in their new place, though I took no notice of them.

At the Old Swan I saw Betty Michell, whom I had not seen since her christening; Lord! how pretty she is, and her child too. I walked a while with Sir W. Doyly, and then to Mrs. Martin's lodging, where I did what I would with her and drank, before going home by coach.

I must note that in the morning I was ashamed at the Swan when tumbling with the little girl her uncle found her neckcloth off, but I let it pass with a laugh.

In the evening I played flagelets with my wife, she still troubled with her cold, and after a little reading went to bed. Everywhere I find it doubted whether we shall have peace: a captain who went with the ambassadors says the seamen of Holland defied us and cried out against peace, though the common people wish it.

periods.label: Week of May 22

levels.sentence: On a sweltering Sunday I chased pleasure at church, read new books, and returned to find my father in a painful fit.
levels.paragraph: I rose early and walked in the garden, feeling the oppressive heat. At church I was distracted, and after dinner I pursued Mrs. Martin, though my plans were thwarted and I was forced to endure the sermon; I did later enjoy her company. Returning home, I found my father in terrible distress from a fallen bowel, which moved me deeply. That evening we discussed building at Brampton, but my heart was troubled by concerns about my family obligations.
levels.summary:
On a sweltering Sunday I rose early, left off my waistcoat, and walked in the garden before church. My wife and I attended, finding the pew full of strangers. At noon we dined at home with little Michell and his pretty wife. Afterwards I went by water alone to Westminster to see Mrs. Martin.

She was going to the parish church with Mrs. Hargrave, and I followed, but Mr. Howlett insisted I join him in the gallery. I endured the whole sermon in pain, though I passed the time with my perspective glass, gazing at many fine women, and sleeping.

After the sermon I went to Mrs. Martin and stayed an hour or two, doing what I would with her. Then I rowed back, reading Mr. Evelyn's new book against Solitude, which I found rather thin, and Mr. Boyle's book of Colours, which made me laugh with its fine observations.

At Barne Elmes I saw gallant ladies supping under the trees, which was mighty pleasant. But at home I found my poor father in an unexpected fit, his bowel fallen down, and W. Hewer helped put it back. My father's patience under his affliction touched me deeply, and I hope a steel truss will relieve him.

That evening we talked of building at Brampton, but I have doubts about my engagement to Uncle Thomas and his son, and fear the obligations of being near Hinchingbroke.

periods.brief: On a sweltering Sunday I chased pleasure at church, read new books, and returned to find my father in a painful fit.
periods.full:
On a sweltering Sunday I rose early, left off my waistcoat, and walked in the garden before church. My wife and I attended, finding the pew full of strangers. At noon we dined at home with little Michell and his pretty wife. Afterwards I went by water alone to Westminster to see Mrs. Martin.

She was going to the parish church with Mrs. Hargrave, and I followed, but Mr. Howlett insisted I join him in the gallery. I endured the whole sermon in pain, though I passed the time with my perspective glass, gazing at many fine women, and sleeping.

After the sermon I went to Mrs. Martin and stayed an hour or two, doing what I would with her. Then I rowed back, reading Mr. Evelyn's new book against Solitude, which I found rather thin, and Mr. Boyle's book of Colours, which made me laugh with its fine observations.

At Barne Elmes I saw gallant ladies supping under the trees, which was mighty pleasant. But at home I found my poor father in an unexpected fit, his bowel fallen down, and W. Hewer helped put it back. My father's patience under his affliction touched me deeply, and I hope a steel truss will relieve him.

That evening we talked of building at Brampton, but I have doubts about my engagement to Uncle Thomas and his son, and fear the obligations of being near Hinchingbroke.

At church I was distracted, and after dinner I pursued Mrs. Martin, though my plans were thwarted and I was forced to endure the sermon; I did later enjoy her company. periods.label: Week of Jun 5

levels.sentence: I spent the day courting favour with Sir W. Coventry, giving maps to Lord Barkeley, dallying with Mrs. Martin, and ended by issuing orders for fire-ships against the Dutch.
levels.paragraph: I went to White Hall and St. James's, where I heard the Duke of Cambridge might recover. I talked long with Sir W. Coventry and gladly gave Lord Barkeley a set of pocket maps. Later I met Creed, went to church, saw Betty Michell, and then visited Mrs. Martin for my pleasure. That evening I read a witty translation and came home to find orders for fire-ships, which I helped issue with Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen.
levels.summary:
I began the day at White Hall and St. James's, learning that the Duke of Cambridge, once given over by doctors, now might live. I made a point of visiting Sir W. Coventry, so the world would see my interest with him, and I gave Lord Barkeley a set of six pocket maps of England when he asked for maps.

I also saw the Duke of Monmouth and his young Hectors, who I fear will only debauch country women.

After chapel with Creed, we went to a crowded church in Southwarke, then home for dinner with my father and wife. Later I delivered the maps to Captain Aldrige for Lord Barkeley, saw Betty Michell at Westminster Church, and then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I had my way with her.

I took a solitary boat ride to Barne Elmes, reading "The Visions," a translation by L'Estrange that I admire greatly. That night, finding an order for fire-ships to annoy the Dutch in the King's Channel, I joined W. Batten and W. Pen in issuing orders before supper and bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 12

levels.sentence: I spent a day troubled by lack of money, visited by cousin Roger Pepys and his silly son, writing a bold letter to Sir W. Coventry, and stealing dalliances with Nell and Mrs. Markham.
levels.paragraph: I spent the day at the office, preparing letters to justify our warnings about the want of money, and entertained my cousin Roger Pepys and his son Talbot, whom I think a silly lad. We dined and talked anxiously about the kingdom's misery and mal-administration, and he told me Lord Arlington had taken up £12,000 in gold. In the afternoon I stayed home while he went to church, and I showed some dalliance to my maid Nell. Later, after Roger returned, I wrote a bold letter to Sir W. Coventry about the lack of money, fearing it might give offence but finally satisfied it was good, though sorry Sir W. Batten signed with me. After Roger left, I dallied alone in the garden with Mrs. Markham, then read and wrote before bed.
levels.summary:
I spent the morning at the office, where several called on business, and I searched out old letters to Sir W. Coventry so the office could justify its repeated warnings about the want of money.

My cousin Roger Pepys came with his son Talbot, whom he had meant to settle at the Temple, but the present stirs made him carry the boy back again this week; I thought Talbot a silly lad. I sent them to church and stayed at my work.

At dinner Roger and I talked much about the misery and mal-administration of the times. He told me Lord Arlington had taken up 12,000 pounds in gold the last week, which seemed likely since all the gold that could be had was taken.

He also promised to show me an old Chancery decree at his house with twenty-six housekeepers of our name in Cottenham in Queen Elizabeth's time. That afternoon, while Roger was at church, I showed some dalliance to my maid Nell, speaking of her sweetheart, silly girl.

When he returned we spent the evening discoursing, much troubled by the evils of our time.

Later I wrote a plain, bold letter to Sir W. Coventry about the lack of money. After it was sent I feared it might give offence, but on reading the copy two or three times I was satisfied it was a good letter; only I wished Sir W. Batten had not signed it with me.

After Roger left, I went into the garden and dallied a while all alone with Mrs. Markham, and then went to my chamber to read and write before supper and bed.

periods.label: Week of Jun 26

levels.sentence: Though everything stands still for want of money and the Dutch are on our coast, I wear my new camelott vest, hear that I alone am well spoken of among our criticized office, dally with Nell, walk in the garden with my wife and Sir W. Pen over cider, and learn that poor Tooker is dead.
levels.paragraph: Today I put on my new silk camelott suit made from my cloak, now a vest, and went to a meeting with W. Pen and Sir T. Harvy—our first since the Dutch came—only to find we can do nothing because we owe money to the owners of the merchantmen and they will not fit their ships without an advance. At noon my wife and Jane went to see Jane's old mistress, whose kindness toward the girl is pleasant to hear. After dinner I dallied a little with my maid Nell in my chamber. In the evening Mrs. Turner walked with me in the garden and told me that the King, Prince, and Duke of Albemarle speak badly of our office, but not of me; I am glad to think I may pass as well as anybody. Then my wife and I walked with Sir W. Pen and drank his cider, though Sir J. Minnes's illness kept us from singing, and I heard that poor Tooker is dead.
levels.summary:
On this July day, with the Dutch still on our coast, our office met for the first time since their coming, but we could do nothing: the owners of six merchantmen we have been taking up for a fortnight will not fit their ships without money, and we owe them for last year's earnings.

I put on my new silk camelott suit made from my cloak into a vest, and felt that the whole business stands still for want of money—even the necessary grapnells we promised ready money for remain unpaid.

At home, my wife and Jane went to see Jane's old mistress, who speaks of the girl with such kindness and would still have her; Jane cried when her old mistress said she would have her back. I dallied a little with my maid Nell. Later Mrs.

Turner walked with me in the garden and told me that the King, Prince, and Duke of Albemarle speak ill of our office, but everyone speaks mightily of me; I am very glad to hear it and think I may pass as well as anybody. My wife and I walked with Sir W. Pen, who gave us a bottle of cider, though Sir J.

Minnes's illness kept us from singing. This day I am told poor Tooker is dead, a very painful poor man as ever I knew.

periods.label: Week of Jul 3

levels.sentence: News of a concluded peace lifts my heart, confirming my hopes and relieving my fears, even as I navigate personal encounters and small omens through the day.
levels.paragraph: Today the long-awaited word arrived: peace is concluded, and Mr. Coventry is coming over to confirm it. My heart lightened at once, for a continuing war must have undone us; now there is a chance to save ourselves. I shared the news with Batten and Pen, then went to Westminster, where I heard Mrs. Martin is not with child—a fear that had troubled me greatly. Even Doll's wild tale of a Dutch captain did not dampen my joy, knowing her as I do. I returned home, wrote letters, and chose not to go to Epsom after all.
levels.summary:
This day began with the glorious news of peace, brought by Creed at dinner. The King's letters said it was concluded, and Mr. Coventry was on his way over. My heart was light, for I knew a continuing war must ruin us, while peace offers a chance to save ourselves. I hurried to tell W. Batten and W.

Pen, then went to Westminster to confirm the tidings with Mr. Williamson at White Hall, who said Coventry was coming with a project of peace for both sides to approve.

At Mrs. Martin's I received the welcome assurance that she is not with child, which set my mind at ease. But her sister Doll came in weeping, accusing Captain Vandener of assaulting her in a stable—a story I cannot fully credit, knowing how freely she has been with me. Later I met Mr.

Rolt, who is off to be a Cornett under Colonel Ingoldsby; his nose bled at parting, which struck me as an ill omen. Sir Alexander Frazier also mistakenly told me Sir J. Minnes was dead, but he is still alive.

I ended the day a little troubled for not going to Epsom, yet glad to hear that my Lady Jemimah has been brought to bed of a boy at Hinchingbroke.

periods.label: Week of Jul 10

levels.sentence: On a hot July day, I took my wife and Mrs. Turner to Epsom for waters, dinner, and countryside walks, delighting in a shepherd and his boy reading the Bible, but came home lame from a sprained foot.
levels.paragraph: Early this morning, my wife, Mrs. Turner, and I set out by coach for Epsom, drinking the waters and enjoying the fine weather despite the dust. We dined, napped, and strolled through the countryside, visiting my cousin Pepys's house and a nearby wood, where I sprained my foot leaping down a bank. The sweetest moment was meeting a shepherd and his little boy reading the Bible on the downs, a scene that moved me deeply. We returned at night, admiring glow-worms, but my foot pained me greatly, and I went to bed with a cerecloth, thankful no business had been missed.
levels.summary:
Up before four with my wife and Mrs. Turner, I had arranged a coach and four for a day at Epsom.

I was vexed that my wife kept us waiting until past five, but we set off pleasantly, drinking the waters at the well—I took four pints and had good stools—and then dined at the King's Head, where we heard that Lord Buckhurst and Nelly were lodged next door, keeping a merry house.

I pitied poor Nelly for her loss at the King's house. In church I met the Houblon brothers, and James Houblon told me I was the only happy man of the Navy, having no bad word spoken of me during all the treasonous talk, which gave me great joy.

After dinner and a nap, we walked to my cousin Pepys's house and into a wood, where I sprained my right foot leaping down a bank, though it eased with walking. The most innocent sight I ever saw was on the downs: a shepherd and his little boy reading the Bible together, far from any houses.

I gave the boy money and talked with the father, who had been a servant at my cousin's; he showed me his iron-shod shoes and told me of his flock of eighteen score sheep. Mrs. Turner gathered a pretty nosegay, and we drank our fill of milk from a poor woman's pail.

Returning at night, we enjoyed the glow-worms, but my foot grew worse, and at eleven I had to be helped home. I went to bed in great pain with a cerecloth, but thanked God no business had been missed.

  - Coach and four with wine, beer, and cold fowle; dusty road

periods.brief: On a hot July day, I took my wife and Mrs. Turner to Epsom for waters, dinner, and countryside walks, delighting in a shepherd and his boy reading the Bible, but came home lame from a sprained foot.
periods.full:
Up before four with my wife and Mrs. Turner, I had arranged a coach and four for a day at Epsom.

I was vexed that my wife kept us waiting until past five, but we set off pleasantly, drinking the waters at the well—I took four pints and had good stools—and then dined at the King's Head, where we heard that Lord Buckhurst and Nelly were lodged next door, keeping a merry house.

I pitied poor Nelly for her loss at the King's house. In church I met the Houblon brothers, and James Houblon told me I was the only happy man of the Navy, having no bad word spoken of me during all the treasonous talk, which gave me great joy.

After dinner and a nap, we walked to my cousin Pepys's house and into a wood, where I sprained my right foot leaping down a bank, though it eased with walking. The most innocent sight I ever saw was on the downs: a shepherd and his little boy reading the Bible together, far from any houses.

I gave the boy money and talked with the father, who had been a servant at my cousin's; he showed me his iron-shod shoes and told me of his flock of eighteen score sheep. Mrs. Turner gathered a pretty nosegay, and we drank our fill of milk from a poor woman's pail.

Returning at night, we enjoyed the glow-worms, but my foot grew worse, and at eleven I had to be helped home. I went to bed in great pain with a cerecloth, but thanked God no business had been missed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 21

levels.sentence: After church and dinner with Pelling, I wandered by water to Westminster, hoped in vain to spy Betty Michell at church, then took a leisurely walk to Barne-Elmes, reading Boyle's Hydrostatics with great delight before supping with W. Hewer.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at church, then hosted Pelling for dinner. Afterwards I went by boat to Westminster, where I kissed Frank at the Swan and attended church hoping to see Betty Michell, but mistook her mother for her. My boat's oar broke, but it was soon mended. I proceeded to Putney, admired the fine folk there, and walked on to Barne-Elmes, delighting in Boyle's Hydrostatics. In the evening I supped with W. Hewer and talked freely about office matters.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to church, then dined with Pelling, whose pleasant discourse made the meal agreeable.

Afterward, I set out by water, dropping Pelling at White Hall and continuing to Westminster, where I kissed Frank at the Swan and went to church in hopes of seeing Betty Michell—but the nose I spied belonged to her mother, which vexed me.

My boat had broken an oar, yet it was quickly repaired, so I rowed up to Putney, stepped into the church there to admire the young ladies, and then walked to Barne-Elmes, savoring Boyle's Hydrostatics as Russel carried it. I strolled among the elms, then returned home by boat with great pleasure, supped with W.

Hewer, and relished our good talk about the Office before going to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 4

levels.sentence: After a lewd morning with Doll Lane and a tiresome dinner at Sir W. Batten’s, I ended my day with my wife at Bartholomew Fair, pitying a crippled dancer and marvelling at a clockwork show, before a near-misadventure with Sam Hartlib in the dirty street.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at the Exchequer and then met Doll Lane at the Swan, where I touched her and drank. Finding my wife gone to Walthamstow, I followed with Mrs. Turner, gossiping about Sir W. Pen’s baseness and the suspicion that his son Lowther has the pox. After an indifferent but clean dinner at Sir W. Batten’s, I was tired of the company and left for Bartholomew Fair with my wife. There I pitied a poor fellow who danced on his hands and crutches, admired a clockwork piece showing man’s ages to a hundred, and nearly lost my wife to a stranger’s coach — Sam Hartlib — before we got home to supper and bed.
levels.summary:
I spent the morning on business at the Exchequer, then slipped away to the Swan with Doll Lane, where I touched her and drank — a secret indulgence I keep from my wife. When I got home I found she had gone to Walthamstow with Sir W. Batten, so I followed with Mrs. Turner, and we talked all the way about Sir W.

Pen’s baseness and how the world suspects his son Lowther, sick with a sore mouth, has the pox.

At Sir W. Batten’s we had an indifferent good dinner — good plain victuals and clean linen, though no fine meat — and I admired the house’s furnishings but grew tired of the company.

On the way home my wife and I stopped at Bartholomew Fair, where I saw a poor fellow dance on his hands and crutches with his legs tied behind him, and gave him money out of pity. We also saw a wonderful English clockwork piece showing every stage of man’s age to 100 years.

Afterwards, while we looked for a coach in the dirty night, a man nearly took up my wife — she was wearing her wizard, and we saw it was Sam Hartlib — but he hurried away as soon as a man came to her. We finally got home, supped, and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Sep 25

levels.sentence: I spent the morning on Navy committees and the King's Council, the afternoon in Westminster with Mrs. Martin, and the evening welcoming the new, grave little maid Willet into my home.
levels.paragraph: I went up to White Hall for a Tangier committee and ended up attending the King's Council, where I spoke well on discharging seamen and saw Lord Anglesey quash Lord Ashly's scheme to borrow credit from the East India Company. After a quiet dinner, I returned to White Hall, heard of tomorrow's musique before the King, then slipped away to Westminster and Mrs. Martin's, where I did all with her and promised my goddaughter her first coat. Back home, I found our new girl Willet, brought by Mr. Batelier—very pretty, grave, and too good for my family, I think. Mr. Turner and his wife came by with news of sending their son Franke to the East India Company, and then we all went to bed.
levels.summary:
At White Hall I attended a Tangier committee that did little, then went to St. James's hoping to speak to the Duke of York about my petition for reward for my war service, but I let it drop. Later, at the Council, we Navy officers discussed discharging seamen by tickets.

I spoke in a way that pleased the King and Council. Lord Ashly moved to hand an assignment for money on the Act to the East India Company or the City of London, but Lord Anglesey opposed it handsomely, arguing it would teach Parliament not to trust the King and to want a kingdom's treasurer separate from the King's.

Anglesey carried it, and I agreed it was mean for the King to borrow their credit.

After a lonely dinner at home—our new girl had not yet come—I went back to White Hall and learned there would be musique before the King tomorrow. Then I headed to Westminster, stopped at the Swan, and visited Mrs. Martin, where I had my pleasure with her and promised my goddaughter her first coat.

Returning by coach, I found the pretty, grave Willet already arrived, brought by Mr. Batelier. She is very well-carriaged, almost too good for my family, and I hope my wife will treat her well. That evening Mr.

Turner and his wife told me they hope to place their son Franke with the East India Company, promised by Sir Andr. Rickard, which I like. Now I begin to think seriously of my journey to Brampton next week.

periods.label: Week of Oct 2

levels.sentence: I attended the Council over Pett's neglect, dined cheaply, saw Mrs. Martin, worried over Lord Sandwich's ruinous expenses, and learned that Sir W. Batten is not expected to live till tomorrow.
levels.paragraph: I spent the morning at White Hall in the Council's long hearing on Commissioner Pett's neglect, where the Chatham attendants contradicted him and he struck me as a weak, silly man. After a hasty dinner and a brief business talk with Lord Ashly about Mr. Yeabsly's abatement, I slipped away to Mrs. Martin's, though her husband has come home sooner than I expected. In the evening I conferred with Lord Crew about Lord Sandwich's desperate state — he has spent prodigious sums and can get neither money nor recall. Returning home, I found Sir W. Batten so ill that it is believed he cannot live till to-morrow, which troubles me for kindness and for the money he owes me.
levels.summary:
At White Hall this morning, the Duke of York and the Navy officers met about Navy business, and Sir W. Coventry generously recommended Sir John Harman and my Lady Minnes for the King's bounty.

Then we attended the Council in a long hearing of Commissioner Pett, where the two Masters Attendant of Chatham denied his claim about bringing up the great ships; I thought him a weak, silly man guilty of horrid neglect. The matter was put off till Monday. , then went to Lord Ashly's to settle Mr.

Yeabsly's business, abating him L1000.

Afterwards I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging and heard her husband is come from sea, which is sooner than I expected; I stayed and drank and touched her, then left.

I spent an hour with Lord Crew, who is distressed that Lord Sandwich can neither be called home nor supplied with money — he has spent L20,000 of the King's money and best part of L10,000 of his own, and the Treasury demands an account. I offered to speak to Sir W.

Coventry, but my Lord would not advise it without Sir G. Carteret's consent. Coming home, I found Sir W. Batten asleep and dangerously ill; word came that he cannot live till to-morrow, which troubles me and my wife mightily, partly from kindness and partly because of the money he owes me from our prize bargain.

periods.label: Week of Nov 13

levels.sentence: I navigated a day of financial assurances, parliamentary discord, and personal vanity, only to end with grim warnings of ruin and a summons about prize goods.
levels.paragraph: I called on Alderman Backewell about remitting £6000 to Tangier, and he boasted of weathering the Sheerness disaster by paying the Swedes' ambassadors and offering tallies to all his creditors. At Westminster, the Lords refused to commit Clarendon without a specific charge of treason, which will surely anger the Commons. Later, I entertained the vain young Pelham Humphreys, just back from France, who mocked all the King's musicians, and we played but mean music. In the evening, Mr. Moore brought me fears that the King's quarrel with his brother will ruin us, and the waterman Poundy told me he was summoned to testify against me in the prize-goods matter.
levels.summary:
At Alderman Backewell's, I arranged the remittance of £6000 to Tangier, and he told me with some vanity how he had survived the Sheerness business by paying £7000 to the Swedes' ambassadors and promising the bankers he would answer all drafts.

He even offered tallies to secure his debts and has since lent the Treasury over £40,000, showing a resilience that will make him greater than ever.

At Westminster, the Lords and Commons clashed over the Earl of Clarendon, the Lords refusing to confine him without a specific treason charge, which will likely breed ill blood between the Houses.

Later, I found Mr. Caesar and Pelham Humphreys, lately returned from France, at my tailor's. Humphreys is an absolute Monsieur, full of confidence and vanity, disparaging all the King's music and musicians, especially Grebus, claiming he will soon supplant him.

We dined on venison pasty and fowl and played theorbo, French lute, and viol, but made but mean music; his arrogance offended me, though he is clearly a good musician.

In the evening, Mr. Moore came to supper and told me of his great fear that all will go to ruin, since the King has said the quarrel is not with my Lord Chancellor but with his brother. Buckingham and Bristol now guide the King, and they may fall upon my Lord Sandwich.

Moore read part of Lord Cooke's chapter on treason, which was instructive. Before bed, the waterman Poundy told me he was summoned to testify against me about prize goods, and I bade him tell all he knew, though I am not much troubled.

periods.label: Week of Nov 20

levels.sentence: I learned how the Lords' obstinacy over Clarendon was really self-protective intrigue, and after being stuck with Creed, I pondered Selden's humble tomb in Temple church before dining at home.
levels.paragraph: I rose early and shared a morning draught with Betty Michell but had no chance to kiss her. At Westminster I heard from Cooling that the Lords' hardness toward Clarendon is not kindness but fear for themselves, and that Clarendon himself would rather be tried by the Lords than be committed by the King to a packed court. He told me the Chancellor's son moved for specific treason charges so his father could come to trial. Afterwards I was stuck with Creed, took him to the Excise Office and Temple church, where I observed how plain Selden's tomb is beside his executor's fancier one, then went home to dinner.
levels.summary:
Rising early, I drank my morning draught of strong water with Betty Michell but found no opportunity to kiss her.

At Westminster I met Creed and, from Cooling, learned the truth behind last night's news: the Lords' stiffness toward my Lord Chancellor is no kindness to him, but fear for themselves, since many have reason to dread what yielding might bring.

Cooling showed me that Clarendon would actually be better off tried before the Lords, where he could get right and make interest, than be committed by the King after Parliament rises and tried by a packed court of Lords who want his head.

Indeed, his own son has moved that if treason is alleged, it should be specified and sent to the Lords so he might come to trial — so full of intrigues this business is.

After this I had a mind to be rid of Creed but could not, and was forced to carry him to the Excise Office and then the Temple. There I walked in the Temple church, observing how plain Selden's tomb is, and how much better one of his executors, buried beside him, is provided for.

I parted with Creed at last, took a coach home, and sat down to dinner.

At Westminster I met Creed and, from Cooling, learned the truth behind last night's news: the Lords' stiffness toward my Lord Chancellor is no kindness to him, but fear for themselves, since many have reason to dread what yielding might bring.

Cooling showed me that Clarendon would actually be better off tried before the Lords, where he could get right and make interest, than be committed by the King after Parliament rises and tried by a packed court of Lords who want his head.

Indeed, his own son has moved that if treason is alleged, it should be specified and sent to the Lords so he might come to trial — so full of intrigues this business is.

After this I had a mind to be rid of Creed but could not, and was forced to carry him to the Excise Office and then the Temple. There I walked in the Temple church, observing how plain Selden's tomb is, and how much better one of his executors, buried beside him, is provided for.

I parted with Creed at last, took a coach home, and sat down to dinner.

At Westminster I heard from Cooling that the Lords' hardness toward Clarendon is not kindness but fear for themselves, and that Clarendon himself would rather be tried by the Lords than be committed by the King to a packed court. He told me the Chancellor's son moved for specific treason charges so his father could come to trial. Afterwards I was stuck with Creed, took him to the Excise Office and Temple church, where I observed how plain Selden's tomb is beside his executor's fancier one, then went home to dinner.

periods.label: Week of Dec 25

levels.sentence: As the year ends, I find myself blessed in my family's health and my own affairs, yet deeply troubled by the kingdom's precarious state, with a discontented Parliament, a misguided King, and the threat of French invasion looming.
levels.paragraph: I spent the last day of 1667 at White Hall and then at my office, dealing with public matters and hearing of the seamen's discontent and their being lured into French service. I also enjoyed some personal pleasures, including a visit to Mrs. Martin, and dined with my uncle Thomas. As I reflect on the year, I am grateful for my family's health and happiness, but I am filled with anxiety about the nation's future—Parliament is dissatisfied, the King is led astray, and foreign dangers threaten us.
levels.summary:
I began the day by going to White Hall, where I waited with Creed for the Duke of York, hearing much talk about the expected removal of the great Lords from council, all stemming from their opposition to the King regarding the Chancellor. At the Tangier committee, I found Lord Middleton a dull but stout soldier.

Returning home, I dined with my uncle Thomas, who is in mourning for his daughter Mary, and we discussed the new Act for accounts, which grants extraordinary power to the people—a thing I have no mind to read for fear of troubling myself.

In the afternoon, I accompanied my wife to Unthanke's, then left her to visit Mrs. Martin, with whom I had my way, and chided her husband's extravagance.

Later, Captain Perryman told me how seamen are being enticed to the French King's service, and advised me on my vessel, the Maybolt, suggesting I sell her rather than engage in the coal trade.

As the year closes, I feel great happiness in my own health and family, but my mind is heavy with thoughts of the kingdom's peril: Parliament dissatisfied, the King misled, divisions with the Duke of York, and the ever-present threat of foreign invasion.

I also cannot shake my fears about being examined by the Parliamentary committee on Navy matters.

periods.label: Week of Jan 1

levels.sentence: After a mix-up over dinner and a costly trip to the playhouse, I hosted a splendid evening of dancing and music, concluding that such pleasures are life's greatest comfort.
levels.paragraph: I spent the day dealing with mistaken dinner arrangements and a costly box at the theatre, but the evening made up for it with a grand party at my house. We had excellent music, dancing, and many guests, including Mr. Harris and Mrs. Pierce. I was mightily pleased, though I found Mrs. Hollworthy less impressive than I had hoped. This night reminded me that true pleasure in life comes from such moments of enjoyment.
levels.summary:
I began the day leaving my wife to prepare for our evening company, and went to White Hall. There I learned from Mr. Pierce that he and his wife, thinking they were invited to dinner, were actually expected for supper. I hurried home and found another guest, Mr.

Harris, with the same mistake, but we made do with a modest dinner, and I was delighted by Harris's excellent conversation. We went to see 'The Tempest' at the Duke's house, where I paid dearly for a box because the pit was full, and afterwards brought everyone home for a night of dancing and music.

At home, I had arranged for the Duke of Buckingham's own musicians, sent by Greeting, which made the evening extraordinary. We danced, sang, and feasted on a great supper and a cake from Jane, and the company grew with neighbours. Mrs.

Hollworthy came in at last, and though I had long wanted to meet her, I found her conceited and not very intelligent. Still, the night was a great pleasure, and as I went to bed, I reflected that such social joys are the truest comfort I can expect in life, and I must enjoy them while I have the health and means.

periods.label: Week of Jan 22

levels.sentence: I spent the day quietly, attending church with my wife, then working late into the evening on my Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter, before supper with W. Hewer and having the girl comb my hair until I fell asleep.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to church with my wife, and at noon we dined at home without strangers. The rest of the afternoon and evening I devoted to serious business, settling my Tangier accounts and reviewing my East India accounts with Mr. Poynter, whom I kept all day transcribing them fairly. After supper, W. Hewer joined us, and I had the girl comb my head until I slept, then went to bed.
levels.summary:
I began the day with my wife at church, then came home for a quiet dinner with no strangers present. The bulk of my day, from afternoon until late evening, was spent on serious business: I worked on my Tangier accounts and examined my East India accounts with Mr.

Poynter, whom I employed the whole day to transcribe them fair.

In the evening I had supper with W. Hewer, and finally had the girl comb my head until I fell asleep. It was a steady, industrious day — one of careful reckoning and simple domestic comfort, with no great events but a sense of order restored to my affairs.

periods.label: Week of Feb 26

levels.sentence: A day of preparing my parliamentary defense, interspersed with visits and domestic plans, yet ending with a troubling confession that left me anxious through the night.
levels.paragraph: This morning I hurried to Sir W. Coventry's to refine our defence on tickets for Thursday's House session. I helped him with the flag-maker's place, and noted the victuals complaint that will fall to me. Returning home, I persuaded my wife to accept a country trip to my father's instead of a coach, to keep peace. After visits to the Michells, Mrs. Martin's (where I enjoyed her and saw the King's starling), and inquiries after the sick, I ended the evening in worry, heightened by Carcasse's confession about the Flying Greyhound.
levels.summary:
I rose early and went to Sir W. Coventry’s, where we went over our whole defence concerning tickets, preparing to answer the House on Thursday. He is deeply anxious about Parliament’s proceedings, especially the sale of places, and I helped him with the flag-maker’s defence.

The complaint about lack of victuals in the 1666 fleet also lies on me to answer, filling my head with care.

, and Jane, to avoid the usual quarrels. In the afternoon I went to St. Margaret’s hoping to see Betty Michell, but missed her; I met her parents and was kindly entertained. Then at Mrs. Martin’s I had my way with her and was delighted by a starling that had been the King’s, which whistled and talked wonderfully.

In the evening I talked with W. Hewer about the House, expecting we might all be turned out. Carcasse came and confessed that he had formerly made a complaint against Sir W. Batten, Sir W.

” I believe the thing is true and hope it will come to nothing, but it weighs on my mind as a fresh trouble and kept me restless all night. I went to bed without supper, my eyes being overwrought.

periods.label: Week of Mar 11

levels.sentence: I weathered parliamentary suspicions and household turmoil, found comfort in company and art, and ended at rest.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to face Parliament and dodged potential embarrassments, only to be warned by my cousin that the House suspected me. After an anxious morning and a poor dinner, I went about my duties and social calls, arranging a merry gathering at my house tomorrow. At home, I dealt with my wife's ailment and a cook crisis, but Mr. Levett's help eased my mind. Two days later, I learned the blame laid on us was little, enjoyed fine company and an afternoon with Mrs. Martin, and was delighted by a painted board that tricked my eyes, letting me sleep soundly.
levels.summary:
On the 13th, I prepared for Parliament with the utmost care, avoiding speeches to protect my reputation. At the door, cousin Roger Pepys warned me that the House suspected me, and although I knew of nothing to answer, the waiting weighed on me.

After a bad dinner at Chatelin's, I attended the Duke of York's money complaints and visited Lord Crew's, where I spoke with Lady Hinchingbroke for the first time and agreed to host a merry gathering.

Back home, my wife was unwell with a breaking-out on her breast, and I hoped it would do her good. I bought pewter, struggled to find a cook, and was relieved when Mr. Levett came himself. On the 15th, I learned the Commissioners of Accounts laid little blame on us, which set my mind at ease.

I dined in excellent company, spent a pleasant afternoon with Mrs. Martin, and was amazed by Hewer's painted board that looked like real wood even when I knew it was painted. I went to bed very sleepy but with my mind at rest.

  - Evening: found wife unwell; bought pewter; secured Mr. Levett as cook

periods.label: Week of Mar 18

levels.sentence: A day of political wrangling at the Council over manning the fleet and signing certificates, a Valentine assignation with Doll Lane, and an evening of reading that strained my bad eyes.
levels.paragraph: I rose early to Westminster, where I walked with cozen Roger and Creed, and afterwards met Doll Lane at the Dog tavern, giving her 20s. as my Valentine. At the Council I stayed silent on the question of entering seamen before the ships were ready, but I spoke up boldly to defend the Office's signing of certificates, angering Duncomb and Clifford yet winning the point. Later I took air in Hyde Park, visited the ailing Sir H. Cholmly, and heard Sir H. Yelverton's talk of the fleet and Captain Smith. At home I read the ridiculous History of my Lord Newcastle, written by his wife, and received Mrs. Turner's visit about Ackworth's business, before going to bed with my eyes troubling me.
levels.summary:
I spent the morning in Westminster, first walking with cozen Roger and Creed, who thought only a new Parliament could save the nation, and then meeting Doll Lane at the Dog tavern, where I gave her 20s. as my Valentine.

After paying debts and buying Montaigne's Essays, I attended the Council in the afternoon, where the King overruled objections to entering volunteers for the fleet, and where I successfully defended my office's signing of certificates against the Treasury, though I angered Duncomb and Clifford.

The King even jested that this would only call for another speech from Mr. Pepys.

In the evening I took a hackney-coach with Sir W. Coventry and W. Pen to Hyde Park, the first time I had been there this year, and then visited Sir H. Cholmly, who was ill, meeting Sir H. Yelverton, who remembered my speech at the bar and spoke of Captain Smith being preferred over Holmes.

Returning home, I read my Lord Newcastle's history written by his wife, finding her ridiculous and him an ass to suffer it; Mrs. Turner then came about Ackworth's impending business, which I feared he could not escape. My eyes were very bad, yet I could not abstain from reading.

In the evening I took a hackney-coach with Sir W. Coventry and W. Pen to Hyde Park, the first time I had been there this year, and then visited Sir H. Cholmly, who was ill, meeting Sir H. Yelverton, who remembered my speech at the bar and spoke of Captain Smith being preferred over Holmes.

Returning home, I read my Lord Newcastle's history written by his wife, finding her ridiculous and him an ass to suffer it; Mrs. Turner then came about Ackworth's impending business, which I feared he could not escape. My eyes were very bad, yet I could not abstain from reading.

periods.paragraph: I rose early to Westminster, where I walked with cozen Roger and Creed, and afterwards met Doll Lane at the Dog tavern, giving her 20s. as my Valentine. At the Council I stayed silent on the question of entering seamen before the ships were ready, but I spoke up boldly to defend the Office's signing of certificates, angering Duncomb and Clifford yet winning the point. periods.label: Week of Mar 25

levels.sentence: In a week of committees and errands, I balanced my public duties with private pleasures: I soothed a quarrel with my wife by silence, visited Mrs. Martin, learned of Lord Sandwich's mission to Tangier, answered Parliament's jealous questions about Harman, inspected a giant bladder stone, and gave good advice to weeping Deb before bed.
levels.paragraph: This week I moved between the court and the streets, the office and the park. I was glad to hear Lord Sandwich would inspect Tangier, and I handled a summons to Parliament with my papers on victuals, though the committee's jealousy about Harman was hard to satisfy. At home I tried silence to calm my wife and it worked, but I still found time for Mrs. Martin, and later Deb wept as she wrote her mistress's instructions. The oddities included a bladder stone the size of my fist and poor Charles Wager remembered by the Moors, while the evenings ended with my song for Mr. Harris and a drive in the park.
levels.summary:
On the twenty-seventh I attended the Committee of Tangier at White Hall and learned that my Lord Sandwich would stop at Tangier on his return from Spain; I was glad, hoping he might set things right. Afterwards I wandered, drank at the Swan, kissed Frank, and showed myself on the Exchange.

At home a small squabble with my wife taught me the worth of silence, for she soon grew calm and fond. I then left her to buy lace, visited Mrs. Martin and had my will with her, and met my wife at Unthanke's; we found no play, so went to Hyde Park, where the dust was troublesome.

That night I finished pricking out my song for Mr. Harris and slept well.

On the thirty-first, after the office and a quarterly dinner with Uncle Thomas, a summons came to attend a Committee of Parliament about victuals for Sir John Harman's fleet. I gave a full account under Sir R.

Brookes, but they were full of jealous suspicion, wanting to lay the failure to improve the first victory upon Brouncker. Later I drove in a hackney with the women about the park, ashamed to go into the tour because they were undressed, yet pleased. At home Mr.

Pelling talked late; afterward I called Deb to write instructions for my wife, and when she cried at her poor writing, her mistress thought it sullenness. As she undressed me for bed, I gave her good advice and kissed her, and she went on weeping.

periods.label: Week of Apr 1

levels.phrase: A week of business and diversion
levels.sentence: Amid office troubles, scientific wonders, theater mirth, and court gossip, I found my week busy and entertaining, yet returning to an empty house made me feel my wife's absence keenly.
levels.paragraph: This week brought a medley of duties and pleasures: I saw my wife off to her father's with a kiss for Deb, argued little at the office and much at the Royal Society, where I subscribed L40 to a new college and marveled at hearing the Thames through a broken bottle. Later I enjoyed a play and Knipp's company, heard gossip about Lady Castlemayne's latest fancy, and came home each night to a house that felt emptier without my wife.
levels.summary:
On April 2nd, I saw my wife and her party off to my father's, kissing Deb after giving her ten shillings to attend her mistress, though a second kiss was denied me when Lord Anglesey met me in Cheapside. The office kept me busy until noon, and after dining with Mr.

Pierce I went to hear the Solicitor-General argue; I held my tongue to keep my reputation, though I believe the business will go against Cocke and his friends unjustly.

At the Royal Society I was forced to subscribe L40 to the new college, which I fear will breed faction, but I was delighted by an otacousticon that let me hear the Thames oars from the water's edge.

That evening, Brouncker and Hooke's explanation of musical concords did not satisfy me, and I came home to an empty house, going to bed without supper.

On April 7th, the office was in a hurry to fit forth a little fleet, but money was so scarce that nothing moved, and people demanded payment beforehand.

My solicitor and the Auditor's men came at noon with my account, and after dining with them I escaped to the King's playhouse, where I saw "The English Monsieur," full of mirth. Afterwards I visited Knipp while she undressed, saw her pretty maid, and heard that Sir W.

Davenant has just died and that eldest Davenport has left the house to be kept by somebody, which I am glad of since she is a bad actor.

I took Knipp to the Park, which was fine after rain, and at the Lodge I kissed her a little, though no more due to her paint.

There she told me the mighty news that Lady Castlemayne is mightily in love with Hart, with Becke Marshall as the privy means of bringing them together—a very odd thing, and by this means she is even with the King's love to Mrs. Davis. After setting Knipp down at Mrs.

Manuel's, I went home to my letters and then to bed, the week's business still weighing on my mind.

periods.label: Week of Apr 15

levels.sentence: I began learning the recorder, then spent the day amid political maneuvering over Sir W. Pen's impeachment, visited Mrs. Martin, consulted with Lord Crew, and wrote to Lady Sandwich before retiring, displeased with my maid's brother.
levels.paragraph: This day I began to learn the recorder with Greeting's book, and spent the morning at the office. After dining with my clerks, I heard Sir W. Pen's impeachment discussed in Westminster Hall; G. Montagu told me the Coventrys are trying to save Pen by laying blame on Lord Sandwich, and I remained silent, believing it may be the only way. I later visited Mrs. Martin and did what I would, then conferred with Lord Crew and G. Carteret, who think our matters look better. I wrote to Lady Sandwich, but was displeased that my maid brought her brother to lie at my house.
levels.summary:
This morning I began learning the recorder, using Greeting's book, and then spent all morning at the office. I dined with my clerks and we were merry over Sir W. Pen's crying to the King that he was his martyr. Going to Westminster Hall, I heard that Pen is ordered to be impeached, and G.

Montagu told me, in company with Creed, how the Coventrys are laboring to save him by laying the blame on Lord Sandwich. Our friends cry out against this, but I am silent, believing they did it as the only way to save him. The attempt to commit him could not be carried, and the House is thought to cool; W.

Coventry's support provoked Sir R. Howard and his party, while the Court is all for Pen.

Afterwards I went to Whitehall, where the Commissioners of the Treasury did not meet, and there I met Mr. Hunt. Thence I went to Mrs. Martin's, where I did what I would; she was troubled for want of employment for her husband, and I spent a shilling on her.

I walked in the Hall, bought a ribbon, and went to Lord Crew's, where G. Carteret and my Lord talked with me, and they look upon our matters as much the better. I returned late to the Temple and came home by water in the moonshine, paying various fees.

I wrote my letters to my Lady Sandwich, and was displeased that my maid had brought her brother, a countryman, to lie there; so I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Apr 22

levels.sentence: I spent the day shuttling between White Hall, Ducke Lane, and the playhouse, troubled by Sir W. Coventry's impending petition, seeking a favour for Mrs. Pett, buying a Spanish book, chasing a woman in vain, hearing hopeful news of Sir W. Pen, and ending with supper at Pen's because my eyes were too bad to read.
levels.paragraph: This day was full of politics and small personal errands. At White Hall I heard the unhappy news that Sir W. Coventry is to be petitioned against, though I hope he will escape. I sought Mr. Wren's favour for Mrs. Pett, and he promised it. Later I browsed Monsieur Fouquet's library, bought a Spanish book, and failed in my timid attempt to renew my acquaintance with the pretty woman I had kissed in the dark. The day ended quietly at Sir W. Pen's, after a play and supper, with my eyes too sore for reading.
levels.summary:
I began the morning at White Hall, where I learned that Hopis and Temple intend to bring a petition against Sir W. Coventry—news that grieved me, though I still hope he will weather it. I also presented Mrs. Pett's condition to Mr. Wren and received his promise of favour.

Lord Brouncker then told me he thinks Parliament's violence and money delays will force the King to hazard everything and perhaps dissolve them.

" I tried to see the pretty woman I had kissed in the dark a while ago, and I found her sofa but lacked the confidence to approach her, so my effort came to nothing. Later I stopped at Michell's and saw Betty, but she seemed either shy or foolish, and I found no chance to see her wife.

At White Hall again, I heard the Duke of York speak kindly of Sir W. Pen, whose impeachment had been brought to the Lords; they would not commit him until finding a precedent, and seemed inclined to favour him.

After seeing part of "Beggar's Bush" at the King's playhouse, I went to Sir W. Pen's, supped, and sat talking late, having nowhere else to go and my eyes too bad to read. So I came home and to bed, weary but with much to ponder.

I sought Mr. Wren's favour for Mrs. Pett, and he promised it. Later I browsed Monsieur Fouquet's library, bought a Spanish book, and failed in my timid attempt to renew my acquaintance with the pretty woman I had kissed in the dark. The day ended quietly at Sir W. Pen's, after a play and supper, with my eyes too sore for reading.

periods.label: Week of May 6

levels.sentence: On May 6, 1668, I went to White Hall too late for the Duke of York, noticed how visibly old Mrs. Washington had grown, dined poorly at Mr. Pierce's, saw 'The Virgin Martyr,' walked in the dusk meeting Mercer and Nell, and sent a salmon-pie home to my wife.

I went about my business—White Hall, Westminster Hall, the Exchange, a poor dinner at Mr. Pierce's—and then to the King's playhouse to hear the music I love. In the evening I wandered through the dark streets, met Mercer and Nell, but could hardly speak. At home I packed things for my wife, including a fine salmon-pie from Mr. Steventon.

Up and to the office, then on to White Hall, but I came too late for the Duke of York, so I went to Westminster Hall. There I heard that my Lord St. John is meant by Mr. Woodcocke in 'The Impertinents,' and I met Mrs.

Washington, an old acquaintance; I had not seen her in eight or nine years, and she has grown visibly old. It struck me that time must be doing the same to me. The House, I learned, passed the City Bill, though I was sorry the churches were not allotted by convenience of the people but to gratify bishops and colleges.

After buying shoe-strings at the New Exchange, I dined at Mr. Pierce's with Knepp and Mrs. Foster, but the dinner was poor and sluttish, so I could not be heartily merry. Later I walked with Brisband at White Hall, then saw 'The Virgin Martyr' at the King's playhouse and heard the music I love.

In the evening I returned to Mrs. Pierce's, where Knepp was, and talked and ate curds and cream. I walked in the dusk through the garden, Tower Hill, and Crutched Friars; I met Mercer with a pretty lady and afterward Nell, Payne's daughter, who walked with me to my back entry, but I said little to them.

At home I packed things for tomorrow's carrier for my wife, among them a fine salmon-pie from Mr. Steventon, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 13

levels.sentence: Between the Office, the Court, playhouses, gardens, and taverns, I filled a week of business and small pleasures—approving a wild ship project, mourning a good man's death, enjoying Knepp on the stage, kissing a pretty maid, and stumbling home from Fox Hall after a broken coach.
levels.paragraph: This week I balanced office business with pleasure: I looked into the Excise, sat on matters of the Guards and Tangier, and heard the Council embrace a ship project I consider folly. I mourned the death of good Sir Thomas Teddiman, and though I could not kiss Mrs Michell with her husband by, I was pleased by Knepp's acting and kissed her pretty maid instead. The last day was a mixed evening of dull play, bad music, pleasant singing, silly Mrs Horsfield, and a broken coach. In the end I went to bed almost midnight, tired but content enough.
levels.summary:
I began the week on business. Sir H. Cholmly was not up, so I talked with Sir W. Coventry and walked with him through the Park to White Hall, where I met Cholmly and went to Sir Stephen Fox's to consider the Excise in relation to the Guards and Tangier.

I attended the Duke of York, and the Council agreed to back Hemskirke's project for a ship that sails two feet for every one of any other ship—to my mind a folly, since the secret cannot be kept, yet they will give him L5000 in hand and L15,000 more in seven years if it proves good.

I also heard that Sir Thomas Teddiman died of a thrush in his mouth; he was a good, stout, able man and is much lamented, though some make mirth and say the business of the Parliament broke his heart.

That evening I went to Michell's but her husband was there, so I did not kiss her; I walked a little in Spring Garden, then went home, played my viall, and had Mrs Turner to sup with me.

" Knepp performed her sorrowful part very well. She was not at home when I called afterward, so I kissed her pretty maid, who is very beautiful, and bought a belt for my new suit. The weather being very hot, I had Nell cut my hair close, and went to bed satisfied with the day's small pleasures.

On the 18th I dined alone on mutton at the Rose Tavern while the King, Queen, and all the Court were at the play; though the house was infinitely full, the play had nothing extraordinary and the King never laughed, and Captain Rolt and I were maddened by the worst-composed music I ever heard.

The company made the rest of the day pleasant: we sang at Kensington Grotto—though I was maddened by Sir Heneage Finch's son beating a poor dog until a servant killed it—and then walked, ate, drank, and sang at Fox Hall.

I found Mrs Horsfield one of the veriest citizen's wives, full of little silly talk and some silly bawdry, such that I believe a man might have his way with her alone.

Our return was troublesome: the coach traces broke near the Minorys, we walked in the dark, the coachman lost his whip, a neighbor held out a candle, and Mercer found it; at almost midnight I set them home and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 20

levels.sentence: I began the day amid mistaken congratulations and town talk of a meteor, then spent the afternoon with Mrs. Martin and the evening singing with friends and tasting the first green peas of the year.
levels.paragraph: I went to the Office, where Sir Richard Ford congratulated me on what he took to be my great purchase — but it was cousin Tom Pepys buying Martin Abbey, a mistake I feared would spread to my prejudice. At noon my clerks told me the whole town was talking of a strange fire that flew over the City on Saturday night, and I remembered seeing such a light myself in my garden, brighter than any rocket, vanishing toward Cheapside. After dinner I went to the Temple and bought a new songbook, then to Westminster, where I did as I wished with Mrs. Martin and she promised me her fine starling that once belonged to the King. In the evening I took Mrs. Turner and Mercer to Mile End, sang, and ate a dish of the first green peas of the season, given me by Mr. Gibson; Sir W. Pen remains ill of the gout.
levels.summary:
At the Office Sir Richard Ford congratulated me on a great purchase, but the purchase was cousin Tom's buying Martin Abbey; I was sorry for the mistake and feared it would spread to my prejudice.

At noon my clerks told me the town was full of talk of a meteor or fire that had flown over the City on Saturday night, and I recalled seeing a sudden bright light in the garden, brighter than any rocket, vanish toward Cheapside.

Many people were apprehensive that the City would be burned and the Papists would cut our throats, which God prevent.

After dinner I went to the Temple and bought a new book of songs set to music by Smith of Oxford, including some of Mr. Cowley's songs, then walked in Westminster Hall and called on Mrs. Martin, where I did what I wished with her and sat drinking with her and her sister.

She promised me her fine starling, which was the King's and speaks finely. On my way I met my sober young cousin Alcocke, newly come to town for employment, but I could not serve him, though he deserves well.

In the evening I took Mrs. Turner and Mercer out to Mile End, drank, sang, and ate a dish of green peas, the first I have seen this year, given me by Mr. Gibson, extraordinary young and pretty. I saw them home and went to bed. Sir W. Pen continues ill of the gout.

periods.label: Week of May 27

levels.sentence: In one week I balanced Navy business and court duties with singing, theatre, taverns, wanton company, and a secret visit to Bagwell's wife.
levels.paragraph: This week I balanced my official work on Tangier and Navy accounts with constant pleasure-seeking. I sang with Mercer and Gayet, went to the theatre in my new black bombazin suit, and spent late nights with rogues and fine ladies. Lord Sandwich's gentle reproach for my silence troubled me, yet I still pursued my private design with Bagwell's wife at Deptford, returning home by midnight.
levels.summary:
This week I kept my official duties before me—Tangier accounts, the Council Chamber, Treasury meetings—yet my heart was bent on pleasure.

I sang with Mercer and Gayet at Fox Hall, bought Marcennus's music book, and rejoiced in my new black bombazin suit when I went to the theatre and remembered the part of Arethusa I once meant to play.

But there were darker threads. Lord Sandwich's letter, gently noticing how I had neglected to write while he was abroad, put me in great difficulty. I found myself in bawdy company at Fox Hall, learned from Harris the meaning of the 'Ballets'—naked dancing at my Lady Bennet's—and spent a late, merry supper at Mr.

Mills's house, a place I had never before entered. I also did what I would with Mrs. Martin, and stole down to Deptford to complete my agreed design with Bagwell's wife, leaving by midnight and laughing with a bargeman over the old woman of Woolwich.

Through it all, I balanced business and licence, reminding myself that a man ought once to know the loose company's manner of talk and lives, yet still returned home to do my office business before bed.
levels.outline:
- Week of May 27: Balancing duty and licence
  - 28 May: Office, petition, music book
    - Set Tangier accounts right and dined at home
    - Kissed a poor woman who petitioned me
    - Bookseller delivered Marcennus's book of music (£3 2s)
    - Afternoon pleasure at Neat-houses and Fox Hall with Mercer and Gayet
    - Sang on a bench, attracted gallants, returned via Old Swan
  - 29 May: Council, King's birthday, Lord Sandwich's letter
    - Morning: Tangier accounts, Council Chamber with Duke of York and Navy Committee
    - Prince Rupert and Sir W. Coventry argued about fleet size
    - Dined at Sir G. Carteret's for the King's birthday
    - Received troubling letter from Lord Sandwich about my neglected correspondence
    - Evening: sang with Mercer and Gayet and Mr. Monteith and Mr. Pelham until 11
    - My planned liaison with Bagwell's wife at Deptford was hindered
  - 30 May: New suit, theatre, and loose company
    - Dressed in new black bombazin suit; barber to keep perriwig for 20s a year
    - At theatre, remembered my boyhood part of Arethusa and laughed
    - Called at Mr. Pierces: saw Knepp and Lady Katherine Montagu (sore eyes)
    - To Fox Hall with Harris, Rolt, and Richards; met Harry Killigrew and others
    - Learned from Harris the meaning of the 'Ballets' — naked dancing with my Lady Bennet
    - Called the company loose, cursed, full of wit; a man ought to see it once
    - Home, office business, bed
  - 1 June: Morning tavern, Treasury, Mrs Martin, Fox Hall, and Mr. Mills's house
    - Up early with Sir J. Minnes to Westminster; met Harris and Rolt
    - First morning in a tavern in over seven years at the Rhenish wine-house
    - Got words of a song from Harris; drank with Mr. Young and Whistler
    - Walked with Sir W. Warren, who told me his difficulties with Commissioners of Parliament
    - Attended Lords of the Treasury and committee with Duke of York on fleet charge
    - Went to Mrs. Martin's and did what I would with her
    - Alone to Fox Hall; saw young Newport and rogues seize on two masked ladies
    - To Mr. Mills's house, where I had never been; supped with Mrs. Hallworthy, Mrs. Andrews, and Mrs. Turner
    - Extraordinary merry until one in the morning
  - 2 June: Honest mirth and a sly assignation
    - Dined at home with my people and W. Batelier; sang with Mercer
    - Mercer brought modest Mrs. Knightly; pleasant country walk to Old Ford and the Gun
    - Bought cherries and set them down, still thirsty for more sport
    - Went to Finch's shop, kissed his handsome wife, picked up my cloak
    - Took boat to Deptford; met Bagwell's wife and fulfilled my agreed design
    - Returned by midnight, battled tide, laughed with a western bargeman over the old woman of Woolwich

  - 1 June: Morning tavern, Treasury, Mrs Martin, Fox Hall, and Mr. Mills's house
    - Up early with Sir J. Minnes to Westminster; met Harris and Rolt
    - First morning in a tavern in over seven years at the Rhenish wine-house
    - Got words of a song from Harris; drank with Mr. Young and Whistler
    - Walked with Sir W. Warren, who told me his difficulties with Commissioners of Parliament
    - Attended Lords of the Treasury and committee with Duke of York on fleet charge
    - Went to Mrs. Martin's and did what I would with her
    - Alone to Fox Hall; saw young Newport and rogues seize on two masked ladies
    - To Mr. Mills's house, where I had never been; supped with Mrs. Hallworthy, Mrs. Andrews, and Mrs. Turner
    - Extraordinary merry until one in the morning
  - 2 June: Honest mirth and a sly assignation
    - Dined at home with my people and W. Batelier; sang with Mercer
    - Mercer brought modest Mrs. Knightly; pleasant country walk to Old Ford and the Gun
    - Bought cherries and set them down, still thirsty for more sport
    - Went to Finch's shop, kissed his handsome wife, picked up my cloak
    - Took boat to Deptford; met Bagwell's wife and fulfilled my agreed design
    - Returned by midnight, battled tide, laughed with a western bargeman over the old woman of Woolwich
periods.sentence: In one week I balanced Navy business and court duties with singing, theatre, taverns, wanton company, and a secret visit to Bagwell's wife.
periods.paragraph: This week I balanced my official work on Tangier and Navy accounts with constant pleasure-seeking. I sang with Mercer and Gayet, went to the theatre in my new black bombazin suit, and spent late nights with rogues and fine ladies. Lord Sandwich's gentle reproach for my silence troubled me, yet I still pursued my private design with Bagwell's wife at Deptford, returning home by midnight.

periods.label: Week of Jun 24

levels.sentence: I spent the day on Tangier coal business, then took my wife and companions to a play and Spring Garden supper, and ended the evening singing with Mercer in the garden, though I felt not very merry.
levels.paragraph: After a morning spent on Tangier coal business with Creed and Colonel Atkins, I went to Westminster but found it a holyday, so no business could be done. I went home for dinner, then took my wife, Mercer, Deb., and W. Hewer to see "The Impertinents" at the Duke of York's playhouse, which was pretty good, and then to Spring Garden for supper. The evening was not very merry, but Mercer and I sat and sang in the garden a good while before going to bed.
levels.summary:
This morning Creed and Colonel Atkins came to me about sending coals to Tangier, and I spent most of the morning on that business. Creed and I then went to Alderman Backewell's over Tangier money matters, and on my way to Westminster I stopped at Michell's for a drink, though I did not kiss her.

Since it was a holyday, no business was done at Westminster; I only went to Martin's and then home again by water.

, and W. Hewer to the Duke of York's playhouse, where we saw "The Impertinents," a pretty good play. From there we went by water to Spring Garden and supped, but I was not very merry. When we came home, Mercer and I sat and sang in the garden for a good while, and so I went to bed.

periods.label: Week of Jul 22

levels.sentence: After a busy morning at the office, I dined and went to my bookseller's, where a pretty woman caught my eye and I followed her until I lost her, then visited Lord Crew, saw my wife's nearly finished portrait, took the family to Spring Garden where rude gallants troubled me, and returned home to receive my four new plates that both vex and please me.
levels.paragraph: I spent the morning at my office, then dined and went to my bookseller's in Duck Lane, but his wife was not at home; as I stood there, a pretty woman with a wanton look passed by, and I followed her round the streets to Newgate Market until she turned back and I lost her. I then waited on my Lord Crew, whose face is sore but mending, and from there to Cooper's, where my wife's picture is almost done and mighty fine. Crossing the water with my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, we ate and walked, but I was troubled to see young gallants rudely forcing themselves into arbours where women were without men. We returned home by water with much pleasure, and that day my plate-maker brought four little plates of the four Yards, costing me L5, which troubles me yet pleases me too.

I then visited my Lord Crew, whom I found up, and his face is sore but he hopes to do well again.

At Cooper's, my wife's picture is almost done and mighty fine indeed. , and Mercer to Spring Garden, where we ate and walked.

I was troubled to see how rude some young gallants of the town are become, going into arbours where there are no men and almost forcing the women—a confidence in the vice of this age that disturbed me. We returned home by water with much pleasure.

That day my plate-maker came with my four little plates of the four Yards, costing me L5. They trouble me for the cost, yet they please me as well.
