periods.label: Week of Aug 5

levels.sentence: After attending to business with lords and merchants, I took pride in a compliment from Lord Orrery, oversaw the completion of my wife's portrait, and ended the evening with a servant combing my hair as I fondled her.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with calls on Sir W. Coventry and Lord Arlington, where I was received with respect and warmly complimented by Lord Orrery. After transacting business at the Exchange and dinner at home, I sought out the book vendor's wife in Duck Lane but found no opportunity to be intimate. I then joined my wife at Cooper's studio to see her portrait finished, which pleased me though I had hoped for a closer likeness. The evening closed with my wife reading a silly book, while Deb combed my hair and I touched her with great pleasure.
levels.summary:
This morning I went by water to White Hall, only to find Sir W. Coventry had left town. I then visited Lord Arlington at his new home, Goring House, where he received me with great respect in front of several lords, and I gave an account of my journey.

While waiting, Lord Orrery engaged me in discourse on hangings and shipping, and paid me a mighty compliment on my abilities and ingenuity, which made me very proud.

After doing business at the Exchange and dining at home, I went to Duck Lane hoping to catch the book vendor's wife, but had no opportunity to have my way with her. I then spent the afternoon at Cooper's studio with my wife and girl, watching him finish her portrait.

He charged £30 for the work, plus £8 3s 4d for the crystal, case, and gold case, which I sent him that night to clear my debt. Though the painting was most rare, I was not fully satisfied with the resemblance or the blue garment.

In the evening I returned to Westminster Hall on a small errand, then home to supper. My wife read a ridiculous book about the Tailors' Company while Deb combed my head, and I fondled her with my hand to great pleasure, and so to bed.

periods.label: Week of Aug 26

levels.sentence: Amid my official duties, I indulged in theater, the fair, and several flirtations—some delightful, some merely curious.
levels.paragraph: I kept busy with office and Exchequer business, but found time for many pleasures. I saw a superb Hamlet, visited the fair twice, and had several encounters with women, from a kiss at the Swan to a forward wench in a coach. My wife received a spaniel, and I was left puzzled by a bookseller's wife in tears.
levels.summary:
On August 31, after attending to my office and Exchequer business, I stopped at the Swan to kiss the girl there, did some shopping, and dined alone while my shoe was mended. In the evening I joined Mary Mercer, Batelier, and W. Hewer to see Hamlet, and I was mightily pleased, especially with Betterton's acting.

Afterwards we visited the Fayre to see Polichinelle. I also saw Mrs. Batelier's newly hung chamber and accepted, with some reservation, a spaniel bitch for my wife.

The next day, after the office, I tried to see Betty Michell but her husband was home, so I found no pleasure there. At the Fair, I saw the famous money-telling mare, which picked me out and earned me a kiss from a pretty girl. Later, I found the bookseller's wife in tears but could not learn why.

On my way home in a coach, a naughty wench attempted to join me; I gave her a shilling and left her. Earlier, Mrs. Martin had dined with us.

periods.label: Week of Sep 23

levels.sentence: I spent a day juggling official duties, lending my lord money, setting my periwig alight, and enjoying the Queen's Italian music.
levels.paragraph: This day was a whirl of obligations and pleasures. I attended to business with the Duke of York, visited Lord Burlington's house, and was forced to supply L500 for my Lord. Amidst it all, I set my periwig on fire and later enjoyed the women's day play and Italian music with the Queen. Political rumors about Sir W. Coventry's fall troubled me as I returned home.
levels.summary:
The day began with a summons from Knepp's maid to attend the women's day at the playhouse, and I rewarded her with half-a-crown and a kiss. I then went to St. James's, where the Duke of York asked me to prepare something for better managing the Office, acting on the Lord Keeper's advice.

Later, I visited Lord Burlington's house for the first time, saw Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady, and met Sidney Montagu just arrived from Mount's Bay. There I learned of my Lord's urgent need for money, and I felt duty-bound to supply L500, though I regretted my remissness in writing to him during his voyage.

At Lord Burlington's, I accidentally set my periwig on fire by a candle, causing a strange noise. Afterwards, I walked through Westminster, stopped by my vintner's to admire his handsome wife, and greeted the widow Mrs. Horsfall.

I then went to the King's playhouse, where I saw the silly play "The City Match" with a full house for the women's sake. In the evening, I attended the Queen, who came out with her ladies to hear Italian musicians in a barge, with Seignor Joanni's voice standing out.

I also saw Sidney Montagu kiss the Queen's hand, and the King spoke with him. However, I heard troubling news that Sir W. Coventry is out of favor, and there are designs to make my Lord Arlington Lord Treasurer, which I cannot believe.

The Duke of York also told me of the hot dispute over Gawden, and he stood firmly in his support.

periods.label: Week of Oct 7

levels.sentence: I spent the day pulling strings to get Turner's place for Hater and to settle other preferments, while hearing a sober discourse on the Dutch war from old Major-General Middleton.
levels.paragraph: This morning I got Lord Brouncker's ready assent for Hater to have Turner's place, and hoped for Sir J. Minnes's too, but at the Board we learned James Southern is petitioning for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford, which troubled us. We resolved to push for our own clerks, insisting that preferment follow seniority and merit. After dinner I went with Mr. Turner to see the Duke of Albemarle, who took kindly my speaking for Turner. Then I stopped at Brouncker's for his sign on a letter to the Duke of York, and at Lord Middleton's to report on his L1000 payment, where he talked well against the Dutch war.
levels.summary:

periods.label: Week of Nov 18

levels.sentence: When my wife discovered I had secretly visited Deb, I confessed, swore never to see the girl again, and bought peace with a promise I intended to keep, though the shame left me praying alone and unable to enjoy my new hangings.
levels.paragraph: I lied to my wife about Deb, spent the day finding her, kissed her in a coach, and gave her counsel and money, then came home with a fair tale. The next day my wife knew everything and raged at me until W. Hewer helped make peace on my written oath never to see Deb again. We were reconciled in bed, but I was so ashamed that I began to pray on my knees, and even the finished hangings gave me no joy.
levels.summary:
On Monday I woke late to my wife's jealousy: she feared I meant to visit Deb, and I denied it, God forgive me. That afternoon I hunted for Deb through Somerset House, Lincoln's Inn Fields, White Hall, the Strand, and Hercules Pillars before a porter carried a message to her.

At nightfall I rode to her, kissed her in the coach, counseled her to guard her honour, gave her 20s. and a direction to leave word at Herringman's, and resolved to seek her no more. I went home and told my wife a fair tale.

On Tuesday she confronted me, calling me a false, rotten-hearted rogue, and I confessed the whole wicked business. She swore to slit the girl's nose, leave me, demand hundreds of pounds, or expose me. W.

Hewer came and cried like a child, but he obtained peace on condition I give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again.

Before late a durable peace was made. We went to supper with kind words and to bed, and I made love to her content. I resolved never to give her such occasion again, and I began to pray to God on my knees alone, though not yet heartily.

Even with my best chamber newly hung, my sorrow and trouble put me out of all joy in looking upon it.

periods.label: Week of Mar 24

levels.sentence: I rode to Maidstone with Gibson and Coney, enjoyed the sights along the way, and on my return spent an evening of free flirtation with Mrs. Jowles, taking liberties but leaving before the final act.
levels.paragraph: I set out for Maidstone with Gibson and Mr. Coney, eager to see a town I had never visited. The ride was cold and windy but the country was fine, and I enjoyed the sight of Sir John Bankes's abbey and later the Saxon stones near Aylesford. In Maidstone I walked the town, climbed the steeple, and watched an old man beating flax. On the way back I stopped again at Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles proved very free with her kindness, allowing me to kiss her and touch her breast at the door, though I lacked time and place to carry her to Cobham.
levels.summary:
I took a coach with Gibson and Mr. Coney, surgeon, toward Maidstone, having a mighty desire to see that town. On the way I stopped at Captain Allen's to give the pretence of calling on him, but really to see if his daughter Mrs. Jowles was about; she was, but I took no notice and promised to return at night.

Riding on, I was pleased with the sight of the Medway and the fine country, and I turned aside to see Sir John Bankes's old abbey, though he was in London. At Maidstone I walked all over the town, climbed the steeple for a noble view, watched an old man beating flax, and bought fresh fish for our dinner at the Bell.

In the afternoon we set back, and I stopped to see a Saxon monument of three stones by Aylesford. Then I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Mr. Coney. Mrs.

Jowles came to us, a fine, proper lady, and we talked over old stories while I took the liberty to salute her often, pull off her glove, and find her hand moist. She was very willing to go with me to Cobham, for I believe she is a whore, but a brave and comely one.

A pretty cousin of hers came to supper, and later I got Mrs. Jowles to the street door, where I touched her breasts and kissed her without force. I might have had all else, but it was neither the time nor the place.

We stayed till almost midnight, then walked over the fields in pitch darkness and snow to Chatham, where I went straight to bed.

periods.label: Week of Apr 14

levels.sentence: I spent the day pursuing secret meetings with Bagwell's wife and then Deb., while trying to attend to business and social obligations, leaving me both hopeful and guilt-ridden.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to the office, but my thoughts were elsewhere. Following Deb.'s direction, I tried to visit her aunt in Jewen Street but found her not in town. Later, I met Bagwell's wife in Moorfields, but the holiday crowd forced us to part. Then I saw Deb. on Holborn Hill and led her into a blind alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she stayed coy. I gave her twenty shillings and arranged another meeting, but my mind was full of trouble. I rejoined my wife and friends at Povy's house, but the bad pictures and my own fears spoiled my pleasure.
levels.summary:
's directions to search for her aunt in Jewen Street, only to learn she was away. Back at the office, I found Bagwell's wife waiting, and she slipped me a note asking me to meet her in Moorfields.

I went there after the office rose, but because it was a holiday and crowded, we could only talk briefly and agreed to meet another time.

While riding through the city, I caught sight of Deb. on Holborn Hill. I followed her into a little alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she seemed modest and hesitant. I gave her twenty shillings and we agreed to meet again in Westminster Hall on Monday.

My heart was troubled by what I had done, and even at my cousin Turner's and then at Povy's house, among family and friends, I could not shake my unease. I took my wife and the Bateliers home by way of Islington, and after supper went to bed, carrying my secret with me.

periods.label: Week of May 5

levels.sentence: Troubled by my wife's early May-dew outing, I spent the day navigating court rivalries, dining with Lord Crew, hearing from the Duke of York that our adversaries were losing ground, and then fretting over my own ostentatious coach and gold-lace sleeves.
levels.paragraph: I rose troubled at three when my wife went off with her maid to gather May-dew, and though I feared for her safety, she came home well and to bed. The day was taken up with court business, where the Duke of York clashed with Sir T. Littleton over Mr. Child, leaving me anxious about heart-burnings. I dined with Lord Crew, who is much decayed, and heard his curious rule about country families and distance from London. Later the Duke of York assured me our adversaries were losing ground, and that Sir Jeremy Smith would be made Commissioner, which gladdened me, though I remain wary. My pleasure was spoiled by warnings about my fine coach and gold-lace sleeves, so I resolved to have the lace taken off.
levels.summary:
Troubled at three in the morning, I could not rest while my wife went abroad to gather May-dew; she returned safe, but my unease lingered. At White Hall, the Duke of York met the Office, and a hot dispute broke out about Mr. Child: Captain Cox seconded the Duke's hard words, and Sir T.

Littleton replied foolishly, so that the Duke grew angry. I was careful not to be seen to take sides, for fear of breeding heart-burnings.

After a wasted trip to Lambeth with Mr. Wren, I dined with my Lord Crew, who is mightily decayed since his sickness. He entertained me with an old rule about country families lasting longer the farther they lived from London.

Then the Duke of York told me the King was satisfied with the Navy constitution, and that Sir Jeremy Smith would replace Pen as Commissioner. He declared our adversaries were losing ground and that he would keep out Child; I was glad, though I dare not think myself secure.

I stopped at several taverns, kissed a new maid at the Swan, but found Mrs. Martin absent. At the Committee of Tangier, things seemed going to rack. Creed and Povy both noticed my fine coach and gold-lace sleeves in the Park, which vexed me, so I resolved to have the lace taken off and avoid such notice.

I walked briefly in my garden, then supped and went to bed.

levels.sentence: A day of legal term business, a planned dinner, a quick affair with Mrs. Martin, a straining play at the Duke's house, and my brother's news that my sister is with child left me restless and unsure.
levels.paragraph: I began the morning at Westminster Hall, where the term opened and I met Roger Pepys, newly come to town, and later promised Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu that they would dine with me tomorrow. From there I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, fresh from Portsmouth, and lay with her, all while she chattered about the gentry who visited her and her husband's supposed fortune, which I fear they will squander. In the afternoon my wife and I went to the Duke of York's playhouse, but from the side balcony I could only hear 'The Roman Virgin' and the candlelight pained my eyes terribly. That evening, after securing Sidney's promise to dine with me, I found my brother John at home from Ellington; he told me the first news that my sister is with child and far gone — which I hardly know whether to welcome or deplore. We supped, and so to bed.
levels.summary:
The first day of term brought me to Westminster Hall, where I was glad to meet Roger Pepys, just in from the country. I also spoke with Sir Charles Harbord and Sidney Montagu, and invited them to dine with me tomorrow; Sidney, who sets out for Flanders and Italy, gave his promise when I saw him later.

From the Hall I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging, where I had my way with her; she had been a month at Portsmouth with her husband, newly home from the Streights, and talked proudly of the gentry who came to visit her and of her husband being worth six or seven hundred pounds — a sum I suspect they will spend quickly.

My wife and I then went to the Duke of York's playhouse, where we sat in the side balcony over against the music; I could hear but not see the new play, 'The Roman Virgin,' which I thought old and ordinary, and the candlelight nearly destroyed my eyes.

Afterwards I went to Lord Sandwich's and came home to find my brother John arrived from Ellington. He brought the first news that my sister is with child, and far gone. I was uncertain whether this troubled or pleased me, for I have never much cared to see my own friends have children, though I love other people's.

Still, I was glad to see John, and we had supper and went to bed.

periods.label: Week of May 26

levels.sentence: On this last day of my journal, I set my accounts in order, kissed Mrs. Michell, saw the Duke of York, laughed with my wife and friends at The World's End, and then resolved that my failing eyes must force me to lay down my pen and have my diary kept by others.
levels.paragraph: I rose very early and spent the morning with W. Hewer on my accounts, trying to put my affairs in order for going abroad; my weak eyes made the work difficult, but I made a satisfactory beginning. After dining at home I went by water to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's to kiss Mrs. Michell, and then met again with the Duke of York and advanced yesterday's business. In the evening I went to the Park with my wife, Mary Batelier, and a Dutch gentleman, and we finished merrily at The World's End. But this is the last entry I can write with my own eyes; I must henceforth have the journal kept in long-hand by others, and I feel as if I am going into my grave.
levels.summary:
Today I rose very early and spent the morning with W. Hewer, examining and stating my accounts so that I might fit myself to go abroad. My eyes have been so ill and my neglect of a year or two has left me behindhand, and this work was difficult and troublesome to my mind; still, I made a satisfactory entrance into it.

After dining at home, I went by water to Whitehall, stopping at Michell's, where I saw her mother, knew her husband was out of town, and kissed Mrs. Michell, though I had no opportunity for more. I then met again with the Duke of York about yesterday's work and made a good advance.

My wife called me, and we went to the Park with Mary Batelier and a Dutch gentleman, her friend. From there we went to The World's End, a drinking-house by the Park, and were merry before coming home late. But the real burden of this day is the realisation that I can no longer keep my journal with my own eyes.

Almost every time I take a pen in hand I undo my eyes, and so I must forbear.

I have resolved that from this time forward my journal shall be kept by my people in long-hand, and that I must set down no more than is fit for them and all the world to know. If there be anything, which cannot be much now that my amours to Deb.

are past, I must keep a margin in my book to add a note in short-hand with my own hand. This feels almost like seeing myself go into my grave; and for all the discomforts that will accompany my being blind, I pray God to prepare me.

The preface tells me that I was happily mistaken, and that my holiday tour restored me, yet still the world lost the daily private words that I never resumed.

periods.label: January 1660

levels.sentence: Mr. Downing's claim that he had made me a Clerk of the Council left me more suspicious than grateful, and the day was spent in errands, a feast, and rumors that all the other clerks were turned out.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was sent for to Mr. Downing, who told me he had got me to be one of the Clerks of the Council. I was stumbled and could not tell whether to thank him, fearing he did it only to ease himself of the salary he gives me. Later I met with Sir Ant. Cooper and got leave to keep the lodgings, so Mr. Sheply could go into the country. I waited at Downing's, read the Dutch Ambassador's answer contradicting my Lord's reasons, and then dined on turkey with Mrs. Jem and Moore. In the evening I observed Downing feasting Sir Arth. Haselrigge, delivered notes to invite members, and heard that all the other Clerks of the Council were turned out except the two Leighs.
levels.summary:
Mr. Downing told me at his bedside that he had made me a Clerk of the Council, but I was not heartily thankful, fearing he only wanted to escape paying me the salary I already received. After that I went with Mr. Sheply and Mr. Pierce to the Harp and Ball, then to Whitehall, where Sir Ant.

Cooper allowed us to keep the lodgings, so Sheply decided to go into the country the next day.

I spent the rest of the morning at Downing's, waiting for someone to read writings who never came, and instead read the Dutch Ambassador's answer to our State, which argued against my Lord's reasons for coming home. After dining on a turkey with Mrs.

Jem and Moore, I went to the French Ordinary, where Downing feasted Sir Arth. Haselrigge and many Parliament members; he gave me a note to invite more members to dinner the next day.

At Whitehall I heard from the Clerks of the Council that all of them were turned out, except the two Leighs, and that my name had been mentioned, but nothing decided.

periods.label: August 1660

levels.sentence: I went from the Privy Seal to my tailor, heard Sir Samuel Morland's secret history of serving the King, dined with my father, settled my brother's allowance and my M.A. fee, and finished the day merrily with my servants combing my head.
levels.paragraph: I began at the Privy Seal, where I agreed with Mr Pim for a velvet coat and heard Sir Samuel Morland tell how Thurloe's bad usage drove him to serve the King, discovering Sir R. Willis and sinking his own fortune. The King has now given him a £500 yearly pension and the benefit of two baronets, which makes me think better of him. Back at the Tower, my father dined with me, and I paid him for my brother John and settled with Mr Fairbrother for my Master of Arts degree. Captain Cuttance brought a firkin of butter for my wife, and at night, after White Hall, I had good sport with the girl and boy combing my head in the kitchen.
levels.summary:
This day was full of business and small reckonings. I went to the Privy Seal, where I settled with Mr Pim for a velvet coat, and there Sir Samuel Morland stayed with me a great while, telling me the whole manner of how he had served the King in the time of the Protector.

He spoke of Thurloe's bad usage, how he discovered Sir R. Willis, how he had sunk his fortune for the King, and how the King now gives him £500 a year out of the Post Office for life and the benefit of two baronets. This makes me begin to think he is not so much a fool as I took him to be.

At the Tower, my father, Mr Fairbrother, and Cooke dined with me. Young Captain Cuttance of the Speedwell brought me a firkin of butter for my wife, which was very welcome. After dinner my father took leave, after I had given him 40s.

for the last half-year for my brother John at Cambridge; and I made even with Mr Fairbrother for my degree of Master of Arts, costing about £9 16s. My wife and I went by water to White Hall, where I was busy at the Privy Seal all afternoon.

At night we returned home, and I made good sport having the girl and the boy comb my head before I went to bed in the kitchen.

periods.label: September 1661

levels.sentence: A day of farewells, family dinner, a heated quarrel with Antony Joyce, and evening rope-dancing, all shadowed by my wife's mysterious appointment and a dying aunt's summons.
levels.paragraph: This morning I took leave of my mother, who set off for Brampton with my sister Pall, and saw them into the waggon, Pall crying bitterly. After a merry dinner at my uncle Fenner's, I was summoned to attend my dying aunt Kite, but instead found myself quarrelling with Antony Joyce, whose meddling made me very angry. Later I took my wife to the fair, where we watched Italian rope-dancers and women tumbling, yet my mind remained vexed by Antony's words and by the secret message my wife received from a French footman.
levels.summary:
I began the day by attending to business at the Privy Seal, then took leave of my mother as she set out for Brampton with my sister Pall, whom I had given twenty shillings and good counsel.

At my uncle Fenner's I found my wife and Pall, and I saw the two women off from Beard's, Pall crying bitterly as the waggon pulled away. We then drank with my aunt Bell and Charles Pepys before sitting down to a merry family dinner.

After dinner, word came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, lay dying and asked my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.

Before I could respond, Antony Joyce picked a quarrel with me that grew into high words, and though he spoke even worse to his father, the whole company was offended and we parted angry.

I took my wife to the fair, where we saw Italian rope-dancers and women doing strange tumbling tricks, but I walked home vexed about Antony and troubled by a private message a French footman had delivered to my wife, who promised to go somewhere tomorrow morning without telling me what it was.

periods.sentence: A day of farewells, family dinner, a heated quarrel with Antony Joyce, and evening rope-dancing, all shadowed by my wife's mysterious appointment and a dying aunt's summons.
periods.paragraph: This morning I took leave of my mother, who set off for Brampton with my sister Pall, and saw them into the waggon, Pall crying bitterly. After a merry dinner at my uncle Fenner's, I was summoned to attend my dying aunt Kite, but instead found myself quarrelling with Antony Joyce, whose meddling made me very angry. Later I took my wife to the fair, where we watched Italian rope-dancers and women tumbling, yet my mind remained vexed by Antony's words and by the secret message my wife received from a French footman.

periods.label: May 1662

periods.label: December 1662

levels.sentence: I closed 1662 in high mirth at the King's ball, yet with sober thoughts on my health, purse, servants, family, and the kingdom's quietness.
levels.paragraph: I spent New Year's Eve at White Hall, first dining at Mrs. Pierce's and then dancing at the King's ball, where the King led out the Duchess of York and all the Court followed. Yet my mind was as full of reckonings as of revels: I reviewed my family, my savings of £650, the oaths that had kept me orderly, and the troubles with Uncle Thomas's estate. Public matters also weighed on me, from the King's open dalliance with Lady Castlemaine to fears about Monmouth and the Duke of York. Still, I thanked God for my health, my wife, and the quiet state of the nation.
levels.summary:
The day began quietly, with my morning draft at the Swan and Mr. Bowyer's gossip about his cousin Butler and Colonel Dillon, who had broken off after letters were opened and knavery discovered. Then I dined at Mrs. Pierce's with Dr. Clerke and Mr. Knight, where I found myself less admiring of Mrs.

Pierce's beauty and Mrs. Clerke's wit than I once had been, though the company was merry. After dinner I attended the Tangier Committee with the Duke of York, and later went with Mr. Povy and Mr. Gauden to Mr. Bland's to discuss the delays in sending boats and provisions to Tangier, where I was pleased to hear Mrs.

Bland talk like a merchant.

The evening brought the greatest pleasure: Mr. Povy carried me to White Hall and into the King's ball, crammed with the finest ladies of the Court. " I watched with infinite content, noting the Duke of Monmouth's mistress, Lady Castlemaine, and Sir Harry de Vicke's daughter as the best dancers.

I left weary but happy, and ended the year in great mirth with my wife.

Looking back, I counted my blessings: good health, a convenient home at the Navy-office, a purse worth about £650, and the orderly life I have led under my oaths against wine and plays. But I also had cares—my maid Jane growing proud, my boy Wayneman to be turned away, and Sarah going to live with Sir W.

Pen, which troubled me. The greatest weight was my uncle Thomas's business, which threatened to pull back my fortune. In public matters, I noted the King's open dalliance with Lady Castlemaine, the splendour of Monmouth, the danger to Lord Chancellor, and the Bishops pressing uniformity.

Yet the nation being quiet, I gave thanks to God for all.

periods.label: July 1663

levels.sentence: I spent two July weeks mixing business, Westminster flirtation and music, witnessing the King's prorogation, and riding home to find a troubling swelling that I mean to ask Mr. Hollyard about.
levels.paragraph: This fortnight I did my small errands, bought a pocket ruler for timber, and waited on Mrs. Lane at Westminster. I dallied with her and then with Mrs. Howlett's pretty daughter, though afterward I was heartily ashamed of my liberties. I also heard citizens sing excellently under a tree, rode hard to the Wells, and stood behind the Speaker while the King prorogued Parliament. But the ride has left a swelling near my anus, and I am fearful it may be a rupture.
levels.summary:
Early in the week I did business with Sir J. Minnes and ordered a timber-measuring ruler from Thomson's, then went to Westminster Hall expecting bands from Mrs. Lane. While she went to the starchers, I lingered at Mrs.

Howlett's shop, bought gloves, and talked with her daughter, whom I call my wife; she is pretty-spoken and will make a handsome wench, and I could love her well. Mrs.

Lane and I then met at the Crown in Palace Yard, ate a chicken, and were merry; I towzed her freely and did what I would, though the last thing I am ashamed of and resolve never to do again. She showed me her hands for fortune-telling, asking when she would marry, and I pleased her as she wished.

On the following week I rode to the Wells in search of our dog but found none, though the warm day brought gallant company. A group of citizens sang in four or five parts under a tree, and I was as pleased with that snapp of musique as ever in my life.

I drank three cupps, breakfasted at Yowell, and rode hard home, taking note of Mr. Gauden's house on the way.

At Westminster I crowded in with the Speaker to the Lords' House, stood close behind his plain, uneloquent speech, and watched the King in robes give royal assent to four subsidies and some twenty smaller acts, though the Lord's day bill was lost and the bills against Conventicles and Papists did not pass.

The King's own speech, read from a paper, was plain and imperfect, with no spirit; he thanked them and prorogued Parliament to 16 March.

I spoke with my Lord Sandwich in the Painted Chamber, who will hasten into the country once the money is settled on the Wardrobe. Afterwards Creed and I went to the new Spring Garden, where we liked the codlin tarts and saw an idle boy's extraordinary tumbling. We missed Mr.

Coventry at St James's, and one of the Duke's footmen ran up and looked us in the face, which made me fearful. I came home weary and well pleased, but the ride has raised a swelling just by my anus, about the bigness of a silkworm's bag; it frightens me of a rupture, and I must speak to Mr. Hollyard.

periods.label: September 1663

levels.sentence: In September 1663 I enjoyed fairs and fine dinners, but after twice pursuing Mrs. Lane and deceiving my wife, I found my wife working late and felt deep grief, resolving never to abuse her again.
levels.paragraph: This month I balanced public duties and private pleasures. I visited Westminster, dined at Mr. Povy's, and took my wife to Bartholomew Fair. Yet I also deceived my wife to meet Mrs. Lane, and though I did not go all the way with her, I was filled with remorse when I returned home to find my wife hard at work. I resolved to reform, though I had made such resolutions before.
levels.summary:
At the beginning of September, I rose early for viol practice and went by water to Westminster, where I bought L'Estrange's news-books and spoke with Mrs. Lane, whose forwardness I found immodest. I found a modest maid for my wife, dined at Mr.

Povy's magnificent house with Creed and his lady, and later took my wife to Bartholomew Fair, where we saw dancing monkeys, strange animals, and a clockwork sea scene. I also read a proclamation for apprehending Lord Bristoll.

Later in the month, I took leave of my brother John and met with Sir Philip Warwick about the Navy debt, where I felt doubts about my own gravity. Back at the office without Mr. Coventry, I was vexed by our coxcombry. In the afternoon, I lied to my wife about going to Deptford, and instead met Mrs.

Lane at Westminster Hall and took her to Lambeth. I did what I would with her but she would not consent to the main thing, for which I thanked God. I resolved never to do the like again. Returning home, I wrote letters until near midnight and then found my poor wife hard at work, which grieved my heart.

I saw God's justice in making her bad with me for my wronging her, and I resolved again never to do the like.

Povy's magnificent house with Creed and his lady, and later took my wife to Bartholomew Fair, where we saw dancing monkeys, strange animals, and a clockwork sea scene. I also read a proclamation for apprehending Lord Bristoll.

Later in the month, I took leave of my brother John and met with Sir Philip Warwick about the Navy debt, where I felt doubts about my own gravity. Back at the office without Mr. Coventry, I was vexed by our coxcombry. In the afternoon, I lied to my wife about going to Deptford, and instead met Mrs.

Lane at Westminster Hall and took her to Lambeth. I did what I would with her but she would not consent to the main thing, for which I thanked God. I resolved never to do the like again. Returning home, I wrote letters until near midnight and then found my poor wife hard at work, which grieved my heart.

I saw God's justice in making her bad with me for my wronging her, and I resolved again never to do the like.

periods.sentence: In September 1663 I enjoyed fairs and fine dinners, but after twice pursuing Mrs. Lane and deceiving my wife, I found my wife working late and felt deep grief, resolving never to abuse her again.
periods.paragraph: This month I balanced public duties and private pleasures. I visited Westminster, dined at Mr. Povy's, and took my wife to Bartholomew Fair. Yet I also deceived my wife to meet Mrs. Lane, and though I did not go all the way with her, I was filled with remorse when I returned home to find my wife hard at work. I resolved to reform, though I had made such resolutions before.

periods.label: November 1663

levels.sentence: I held my ground against Sir W. Pen at the office, chased and missed Howlett's daughter, flirted with a pretty lodger at Unthank's, consulted Dr. Turner about freight, and came home with a cold and a plate from Captain Taylor.
levels.paragraph: This morning at the office I opposed Sir W. Pen over a purser's mulct, and he went out in a huff like an ass; I was not sorry, for I will not let him think I am afraid to oppose him. After dinner I rode out on business, followed Howlett's daughter through Westminster Hall but could not overtake her, and at Unthank's I turned my vexation at my wife's unfinished work into a little flirtation with a pretty lodger, taking her hand and laughing at myself. I consulted Dr. Turner about freight due from East India ships, then spent the evening writing letters, and went to bed with a cold from last night. Captain Taylor had brought me a small state plate, and I mean to help him get his demurrage allowance for the William.
levels.summary:
This morning at the office I had a showdown with Sir W. Pen. He pressed me to excuse a fine laid on the purser of the James, who was absent by his order; I refused, and he stormed out looking like a discontented ass. I felt no regret, because I would not have him think I dare not oppose him when I see reason for it.

After dinner I went on several errands about town. In Westminster Hall I saw Howlett's daughter leaving and followed her, hoping to talk and dally a little, but she got away.

Then at Unthank's, when a pretty little lodger came out to tell me my wife's work was not done, I took her by the hand and found ways to stretch the talk; I laughed at myself when I saw how my anger melted at such a messenger. Later I consulted Dr.

Turner at Doctors' Commons about the freight we demand from the East India ships.

I finished the evening writing letters in my office, then went home to supper and bed, nursing a scurvy cold from sleeping cold-headed last night. This day Captain Taylor brought me a little plate, expecting me to help him get demurrage for his ship William, which stayed long at Tangier; I shall and may justly do it.

periods.label: December 1663

levels.sentence: On this last night of 1663 I sit alone over my accounts, take stock of my growing fortune and many cares, and resolve to keep to business in the year ahead.
levels.paragraph: I spent the day at the office with a throbbing head, then came home to a quiet Christmas dinner with my wife on turkey and mince pie. That night I sat up till four in the morning making up my accounts and writing this last journal of the year. I blessed God to find myself worth above £800, and resolved to live frugally, mind my business, and do my duty to the King in the year to come.
levels.summary:
At the office Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W. Batten at the open table, and though Sir W. Pen took him up like a counterfeit rogue, I knew he was as pleased as any of us. I came home to a quiet Christmas dinner with my wife alone—a fine turkey and a mince pie—and then back to business.

That night, with a good fire in my chamber, I sat till four o'clock in the morning making up my accounts and writing this last journal of the year.

I thanked God to find myself worth above £800 in money, with £700 in my Lord Sandwich's hand, and lived frugally at the Navy Office with my wife and three maids. My health is pretty good, though troubled with a costiveness I am labouring to cure.

At the office I am well, though Batten envies me to the devil and Pen is a false knave to me. My father and mother are well in the country, and the young ladies of Hinchingbroke are with them because of smallpox.

The Queen is recovered, the King minds his mistress too much, and the Duchess of York is sick of the measles but growing well again.

My cares are many: my wife's brother has fallen into unhappiness through his wife, my cousin Angier has broken his trade and I am sending his rogue son John to sea, my brother Tom I know not what to think of, my brother John at Cambridge gives little hope, and Pall grows old with nothing yet to spare her.

The talk is all of the King of France, and the Turk is very far entered into Germany. Yet I bless God I am in a good way, and I resolve to stick to my business, get a little money, and do the best service I can to the King. So ends the old year.

periods.label: May 1664

levels.sentence: After a day of worsening pain, I was reduced to crying and roaring in bed until, by chance, kneeling brought me a gradual easing that left me pain-free and sleeping well.
levels.paragraph: I woke full of pain and went to the office, but by dinner it had grown so severe that I took to my bed. For a couple of hours I suffered an agony as great as any stone fit, with pain in my belly and back, unable to break wind. A glyster gave little help, and I cried and roared in anguish. At last, while tumbling about, I got on my knees, and the pain began to lessen, until within an hour I was almost easy, though still unable to break wind or make water, and I slept well all night.
levels.summary:
I rose on May 14th already full of pain, likely from the cold I had gotten the day before. I managed to sit through the office, but by dinner the pain forced me to bed, where it swelled into a fit as terrible as any stone I have known, gripping my lower belly and back.

I could not break wind, and a glyster brought little relief; for two hours I lay crying and roaring in the most extraordinary anguish.

Then, chancing among my tumblings to get upon my knees in bed, the pain began to ease, and within an hour it had subsided to almost nothing. I still could not break wind or make water, yet I slept well all night, thankful for the respite.

periods.label: October 1664

levels.sentence: I spent the day at the office, dined with my uncle, caressed Bagwell's wife with promises of a place for her husband, heard troubling news about Tangier from Mr. Cholmely, and bought silver tumblers.
levels.paragraph: I rose early and attended the office all morning. At noon my uncle Thomas came to dine with me, and I gave him some money. Back in my office, I caressed Bagwell's wife, finding her more responsive to my good words and promises to get her husband a place. Afterwards I visited Lord Sandwich, and went with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street, where he told me that Tangier is likely in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, a man of no honour or honesty. I returned home, having bought two silver tumblers, worked late, then supped and went to bed.
levels.summary:
At the office all morning, I dined with my uncle Thomas, who came to collect some money from me. The transaction was routine, and I felt the usual obligation to family. Later, I took Bagwell's wife into my office and caressed her, finding her every day more amenable to my advances.

I promised to get her husband a place, which I intend to fulfil, though I know it is a bargain of sorts.

In the afternoon I visited my Lord Sandwich and then walked with Mr. Cholmely to Fleet Street. Cholmely told me that Tangier is in a bad condition under Fitzgerald, who is dishonourable, dishonest, and works to raise the Irish interest at the expense of the English, offending everyone and accomplishing nothing.

This news grieved me. I bought two silver tumblers on my way home, worked late at the office, and then had supper and went to bed.

periods.label: December 1664

levels.sentence: After walking to Deptford and being kindly entertained by the Bagwells, I found a way to send Bagwell abroad and enjoyed my will with his wife, then returned home to dine with friends and spent the rest of the day at the office.
levels.paragraph: I walked to Deptford and after some yard business I went unnoticed to Bagwell's house, where the poor people gave me a dinner in their fashion and I ate very well. After dinner I found occasion to send Bagwell abroad, and then alone with his wife I attempted what I desired and, against her resistance, accomplished it to my contentment. I walked home, dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, and then spent the afternoon and evening at the office, finishing late and going to bed.
levels.summary:
I set out on foot to Deptford, and after handling some business at the yard I slipped away to Bagwell's house without being observed. The Bagwells were very kind and gave me a meal, and once I had sent Bagwell out on an errand, I was left alone with his wife and pressed my advantage to my full satisfaction.

Afterward I walked home and dined with Dr. Fayrebrother and Luellin, though I soon left them to the office, where I sat all afternoon and into the evening. I took supper, returned to the office again very late, and then at last went home to bed.

The day mixed a private pleasure with the usual round of work and company, leaving me contented but weary.

periods.label: January 1665

levels.phrase: Lust, jealousy, and a hare's foot
levels.sentence: After a fortnight of illicit pleasures and jealous torments, I find comfort in a superstitious hare's foot and take pride in Hooke's book while meddling in my maids' lives.
levels.paragraph: I spent the fortnight in a whirl of pleasure and vexation. From assignations with Jane and Mrs. Martin to bawdy ballads at Lord Brunker's, I indulged my appetites, yet my wife's reading on jealousy pricked my conscience. The sight of a dog mating with our bitch stirred my own jealous fears, and the disappearance of our pretty Doll added to my suspicions. A superstitious hare's foot from Mr. Batten cured my colic, and I took pride in owning Hooke's book of microscopy, even as I meddled in Jane's marriage plans.
levels.summary:
During this January fortnight, I indulged my wandering appetites with little restraint. After a frosty walk to Whitehall with Sir W. Pen, I paid out money and stole a moment with Jane at my barber's, where she promised me a meeting on Sunday.

I sported with Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan, and then had my will of Mrs. Martin at her new lodgings for two shillings' worth of wine and cake, though her impudence left me sick. At Lord Brunker's I made great mirth with a ballad I passed off as from the seamen, naming Sir W.

Pen and others as authors, over the noblest French dinner I had seen in days.

Back at home, my conscience was pricked when my wife made me read a passage in Sir Philip Sidney about jealousy, for it struck home. The immodest sight of a dog covering our little bitch stirred my jealousy anew.

In the second week, I found Jervas's household in disorder over Jane, who had bound herself to a fiddler; I feigned compliance and got to advise her privately, hoping to keep her company. At the Swan I had a kiss but no more.

My wife and I missed our pretty Doll, who had supposedly gone to her father, though I suspect worse. Yet a hare's foot from Mr. Batten, which he said cured his colic, eased my belly merely by handling it, and I have been well since. I also took home Hooke's book of microscopy, which I am proud to own.

These weeks were a tangle of pleasure and vexation. I pursued my lusts while my wife's reading on jealousy gnawed at me, and I suspected the worst of those around me. Even as I meddled in Jane's marriage plans to suit my own convenience, I felt the sting of conscience.

But superstition and curiosity gave me some comfort, and I continued my daily rounds of office and cards, going to bed each night with these thoughts churning.

    - Paid basins, visited barber Gervas, met Jane, she promised a Sunday meeting
    - Sported with Herbert's kinswoman at the Swan

periods.brief: After a fortnight of illicit pleasures and jealous torments, I find comfort in a superstitious hare's foot and take pride in Hooke's book while meddling in my maids' lives.
periods.full:
During this January fortnight, I indulged my wandering appetites with little restraint. After a frosty walk to Whitehall with Sir W. Pen, I paid out money and stole a moment with Jane at my barber's, where she promised me a meeting on Sunday.

I sported with Herbert's young kinswoman at the Swan, and then had my will of Mrs. Martin at her new lodgings for two shillings' worth of wine and cake, though her impudence left me sick. At Lord Brunker's I made great mirth with a ballad I passed off as from the seamen, naming Sir W.

Pen and others as authors, over the noblest French dinner I had seen in days.

Back at home, my conscience was pricked when my wife made me read a passage in Sir Philip Sidney about jealousy, for it struck home. The immodest sight of a dog covering our little bitch stirred my jealousy anew.

In the second week, I found Jervas's household in disorder over Jane, who had bound herself to a fiddler; I feigned compliance and got to advise her privately, hoping to keep her company. At the Swan I had a kiss but no more.

My wife and I missed our pretty Doll, who had supposedly gone to her father, though I suspect worse. Yet a hare's foot from Mr. Batten, which he said cured his colic, eased my belly merely by handling it, and I have been well since. I also took home Hooke's book of microscopy, which I am proud to own.

These weeks were a tangle of pleasure and vexation. I pursued my lusts while my wife's reading on jealousy gnawed at me, and I suspected the worst of those around me. Even as I meddled in Jane's marriage plans to suit my own convenience, I felt the sting of conscience.

But superstition and curiosity gave me some comfort, and I continued my daily rounds of office and cards, going to bed each night with these thoughts churning.

periods.label: February 1665

levels.sentence: I spent a painful but busy day tending to office affairs, dining with Sir W. Batten and later discoursing with Mr. Wayth about ticket abuses, then passed the evening with Lady Sandwich, who shared court gossip about Lord Castlemayne's expected return and the Maids of Honour's mad pranks, while Lord Sandwich wrote that he expects to be in town this week.
levels.paragraph: I woke with a mighty pain in my forefinger from last night's struggle with the woman I mentioned, yet I went to the office and was busy till noon. My wife, being long kept indoors in the dirt, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe and now pretends to a resolution of being very clean, though I can guess how long it will hold. I dined with Sir W. Batten and his lady, who are now very fond of me, and later discoursed with Mr. Wayth about the abuse in tickets and Mr. Fen's great profit from his place. Lord Brunkerd then carried me to Lincoln's Inn Fields, where I had innocent discourse with Lady Sandwich about housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times, and she told me the latest court gossip.
levels.summary:
I began the day in pain from a strained forefinger, but still attended to office business until noon. My wife, having been confined indoors, went with her woman to a hot-house to bathe and now talks of being very clean, though I know how long such resolutions last. I dined with Sir W.

Batten and his lady, who are very fond of me these days, and later went to the Change and then with Mr. Wayth to a cook's shop, where we discussed the growing abuse of tickets and Mr. Fen's profitable place—he demands but five per cent of all he pays, yet is little pleased with anyone who gives him no more.

After more office business, Lord Brunkerd carried me to Lincoln's Inn Fields, where I talked with good Lady Sandwich about housewifery, husbands for her daughters, and the luxury and looseness of the times.

She told me that Lord Castlemayne is coming over from France and is believed likely to be made friends with his lady again. She also told me of the mad freaks of the Maids of Honour at Court: Mrs.

Jennings recently dressed like an orange wench and cried oranges up and down, until her fine shoes were discerned after a fall in the evening, putting her to great shame. Lady Castlemayne merrily says that her own daughter, not above a year or two old, will be the first maid in Court that will be married.

Lord Sandwich also wrote me word from the Downs that he is like to be in town this week, which will bring more business and news. The whole day left me with a sense of the world's vanity and folly, yet also the comforts of friendship and innocent conversation.

periods.label: August 1665

levels.sentence: Amid the plague's mounting toll, I fought off my own dangerous desires, declined to entangle myself in a cousin's trouble, and hastened to draw up my will before death could claim me.
levels.paragraph: In early August 1665, I caught myself growing too familiar with my little girle and resolved to abandon such behavior, burying myself in business instead. The plague raged on, with deaths above four thousand, and I heard a disturbing tale of Alderman Bence, who stumbled over a corpse only to have his pregnant wife die of fright and plague. At a dinner he denied the story, yet admitted his wife was ill and he had left her, which troubled me deeply. Fearing for my own life in the unhealthy town, I went home to draw over my will.
levels.summary:
This August the plague bore down on London with more than four thousand dead, and I felt the weight of mortality everywhere. I began the month in a dangerous mood, letting my little girle comb my head and touching her breast, but I caught myself and resolved to stop for fear of consequences.

To keep honest, I threw myself into settling papers and rode through the rain to Woolwich.

My she-cozen Porter came asking help for her husband, taken to the Tower for buying the King's powder, but I dared not appear in that business again.

At the office we grieved over the rising bill, and heard the strange tale of Alderman Bence, who stumbled over a corpse and then lost his wife to plague after she took fright. At Sir G.

Smith's dinner, Bence himself denied the story, yet admitted his wife was ill and he had left the house, which sat heavily on me all evening. I went home and began drawing over my will, for the town was so unhealthy that a man could not count on living two days.

periods.label: October 1665

levels.sentence: Through plague-stricken weeks I balanced dockyard business and dodgy prize dealings with stolen pleasures and quiet domestic joys, all while hoping to profit honestly and protect my Lord Sandwich.
levels.paragraph: I traveled between Chatham, Woolwich, and Deptford, inspecting the Yard and haggling over prize-goods. I kissed maids at Rochester and dallied with Sarah and my Valentine, yet the plague raged around me. Business with Lord Bruncker and Captain Cocke gave me hopes of profit and of clearing Lord Sandwich. My wife and I were close and happy, and the death bill was falling, which gave me comfort.
levels.summary:
At Chatham I inspected the Yard with Commissioner Pett and made the men carry a timber by hand to shame the absurd waste of four horses. Sir W. Pen played the kind friend but I know him for a false rogue; still I got him to let me carry away his silk.

At Rochester I took pleasure with three maids on the castle stairs, but the hideous precipice spoiled my delight. The plague was everywhere, yet I kept to my business and my small enjoyments.

In the next week I talked with my wife about giving my sister Pall four hundred pounds to marry, though the plague kept her away. I counselled the Duke of Albemarle on the victuallers and did what I would with Sarah and my Valentine, caring little that the sickness was next door. Mr.

Evelyn showed me his lovely evergreens and holly hedge, and I wrote late to Sir W. Coventry. The plague bill fell by 740, and I renewed my vows, for since I had left them off my mind had wool-gathered.

Then came the King's strict command to examine the prize-goods, and I found my Lord Sandwich grossly abused by Sir W. Berkeley and others, who spoiled and broke goods and said my Lord's back was broad enough.

Captain Cocke told me the Duke had shown an order for all respect to be paid to Sandwich, and that Seymour would be our friend; this overjoyed me. And the plague deaths were about six hundred fewer, so I went home to bed content.

periods.label: January 1666

levels.sentence: Amid London's revival, I attended to business, survived a coach mishap, and indulged in a late supper with Mrs. Tooker.
levels.paragraph: I came to London with Lord Bruncker and Mrs. Williams to find the city stirring back to life, with shops reopening and the streets fuller, though the West End remained empty. I attended to business with Sir G. Carteret, met Povy at the Exchange, and dined nobly at Sir George Smith's. After returning to Greenwich, I read a discourse on the Thames and enjoyed the company of little Mrs. Tooker, who stayed very late. The next week I faced the Duke of Albemarle's disordered affairs, ordered new shoes and a tailor, and read my paper on pursers to a meeting, with Sir W. Pen objecting but offering nothing better. Even after my coach broke and toppled me over Lord Bruncker, I found my wife hard at work on our hangings, and we supped and went to bed.
levels.summary:
I came to London with Lord Bruncker and Mrs. Williams to find the city reviving—porters bowing, beggars beseeching, shops opening again, though Covent Garden and Westminster remained empty. I went with my Lord to White Hall to see Sir G. Carteret and spoke of the Act, then to the Exchange where I met Mr.

Povy, and dined nobly at Sir George Smith's. Povy told me of Lord Bellases's complaints about money, which I did not value.

The next week began at the Duke of Albemarle's, where I was troubled to see things ordered without understanding. I bespoke shoes and hired a tailor, and at the Exchange met Mr. Moore to discuss my Lord's need for a pardon before the Spain voyage. I directed Moore to perfect it.

At an office meeting I read my paper on pursers; all approved except Sir W. Pen, who objected to everything and remedied nothing. Later my coach broke and tumbled me over Lord Bruncker near the Stockes, but I rose unhurt.

Personal matters were not forgotten: I read a satisfying discourse on the Thames's encroachments, and little Mrs. Tooker came to supper and stayed very late, while I had my way with her. At home I found my wife working like a horse on her hangings, so to supper and to bed.

The next week began at the Duke of Albemarle's, where I was troubled to see things ordered without understanding. I bespoke shoes and hired a tailor, and at the Exchange met Mr. Moore to discuss my Lord's need for a pardon before the Spain voyage. I directed Moore to perfect it.

At an office meeting I read my paper on pursers; all approved except Sir W. Pen, who objected to everything and remedied nothing. Later my coach broke and tumbled me over Lord Bruncker near the Stockes, but I rose unhurt.

Personal matters were not forgotten: I read a satisfying discourse on the Thames's encroachments, and little Mrs. Tooker came to supper and stayed very late, while I had my way with her. At home I found my wife working like a horse on her hangings, so to supper and to bed.

I attended to business with Sir G. Carteret, met Povy at the Exchange, and dined nobly at Sir George Smith's. periods.label: February 1666

levels.sentence: On a dry cold morning I walked to White Hall, talked with Sir Ph. Warwicke about the kingdom's ominous state, did business with the Duke of Yorke, dallied with Mrs. Martin and Mrs. Lane, dined with the pleasant Mrs. Knipp, reconciled with Sir G. Carteret who feared a general catastrophe, and ended the month resolving to apply myself better to business.
levels.paragraph: I began the day with a walk to White Hall, where Sir Ph. Warwicke and I spoke anxiously of the kingdom's snarling state and the new Act that left us without money. Business with the Duke of Yorke followed, then idle talk in Westminster Hall with the Michells and Howletts, and a quick encounter with Mrs. Martin. Home for dinner with the delightful Mrs. Knipp, then visits to Colonel Norwood and Sir G. Carteret, who seemed melancholy and feared all things would come to nothing. The evening brought a risky loan and intimacy with Mrs. Lane, and I went to bed by ten, full of resolve to mend my ways after this backward month.
levels.summary:
This day was a mix of public worry and private indulgence. I walked to White Hall and met Sir Ph. Warwicke in the Pell Mall, where we spoke of the melancholy posture of affairs—everyone snarling, the new Act crippling our power to raise money.

He feared, as I did, that all was ill with the State, and we agreed to meet later about Navy business. After doing our duty with the Duke of Yorke, I idled in Westminster Hall, chatting with Mrs. Michell and her pretty daughter, then was called by Mrs.

Martin, bought bands from her, and went to her chamber for what I would.

Dinner at home with Mrs. Knipp was a bright spot, as she is the pleasantest company in the world, and I gave my wife money to lay out on her. Abroad again, I visited Colonel Norwood and Sir G.

Carteret, with whom I have made things right; he is very melancholy, most afraid of a general catastrophe, thinking all will come to nothing. From the Swan I went to Mrs. Lane's, lent her L5 upon gold, and did what I would—but she is grown very bad and offers anything, so I will avoid her a while.

I returned home, worked at the office, and slept by ten, ending the month with my mind full of resolution to apply myself better to business, having been visibly prejudiced by my idleness these last six or eight days.

periods.label: March 1666

levels.sentence: After my cold improved, I went to church, sought fair Mrs. Butler in vain, took my pleasure with Mrs. Martin, learned that my old sweetheart Betty Howlet had married, and came home to accounts with Mings back from Hamburg empty-handed.
levels.paragraph: My cold being better, I went to church and then home to dinner, before walking out to St. James's Church hoping to see fair Mrs. Butler, but she was not there—nor, I believe, does she live thereabouts now. I walked on to Westminster in very fine dry weather, though all cry out for lack of rain, drank at Herbert's, and then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I did what I would with her while her husband fetched wine. She told me Betty Howlet, my little sweetheart, is married to young Michell and will live nearer me in Thames Street; glad of that news, I returned home by coach, did accounts, and went to bed.
levels.summary:
My cold being better, I rose, went to church, and dined at home before setting out on foot. At St. James's Church I hoped to see fair Mrs. Butler, but she was not there, and I suspect she no longer lives in that neighbourhood. The weather was very fine and dry, though everyone cries out for lack of rain.

I stopped at Herbert's for a drink, then went to Mrs. Martin's, where I lay with her while her husband stepped out for wine; the poor man would take pains if I can get him a purser's place, and I shall endeavour to do so.

Mrs. Martin told me a secret: Betty Howlet of the Hall, my little sweetheart whom I used to call my second wife, has married the younger son of Mr. Michell—the elder brother, who should have had her, being dead of the plague. I am glad of it, and glad that they are to live nearer me in Thames Street by the Old Swan.

That evening I rode home by coach, went to my chamber to do accounts, and so to bed. I also heard that Sir Christopher Mings is come home from Hamburg without having done anything, saving only bringing home some pipestaves for us.

periods.label: April 1666

levels.sentence: A rainy struggle to reach White Hall, the Duke's wise settling of a captain's quarrel, grim news of a sudden death and the returning plague, and a dinner with Mrs. Hunt talking of the Protector all made for a full, unsettled day that ended quietly with a psalm.
levels.paragraph: This morning I was in great trouble to get passage, the rain making coaches scarce, so I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to White Hall. There the Duke of Yorke heard the dispute between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr. Wayth and resolved it with rare judgement, chiding both yet encouraging Wayth to keep captains honest for the King. The Court was full of news of Tom Cheffin's sudden death and the plague's increase, which frightened everyone. After missing the sermon in the Chappell, I used Lord Hinchingbroke's coach to carry Mrs. Hunt home for dinner, and we talked of the Protector and his family. Later I tried to hear a Jesuite preach but came too late, so I went home to business and ended with Mercer combing my head and a psalm.
levels.summary:
The day began with vexation: rain had driven away all coaches, so I walked to the Old Swan and took a scull to White Hall. There I witnessed the Duke of Yorke settle a quarrel between Sir Thomas Allen and Mr. Wayth with great order and judgement.

Allen's complaint about Wayth's usage at the pay of his ship seemed a sorry occasion, and the Duke chided both while encouraging Wayth to be a check on captains for the King's right. I had never seen the Duke do anything with more judgement.

The Court was heavy with news: Tom Cheffin, the King's closet-keeper, had died suddenly between six and seven that morning, apparently of an imposthume in his breast, and the plague was said to be increasing everywhere.

I had the pleasure of seeing an Archbishop in the pulpit at the Chappell, though I could not get in to hear well. Later I carried Mrs. Hunt home in Lord Hinchingbroke's coach and dined with her, discoursing on old matters of the Protector, who lives in France on about L500 a year.

After returning her, I missed the Jesuite's sermon at St. James's, and so went home to business. At night Mercer combed my head, I sang a psalm, and went to bed.

periods.label: May 1666

levels.sentence: My day ran from church and a noble dinner with my wife to a clandestine encounter at Mrs. Martin's, a disturbing bribe to Lord Ashly, ship inspections, Bacon's "Faber Fortunae," and my wife's happy return from standing godmother at Greenwich.
levels.paragraph: This morning I went to church with my wife, and at noon we dined mighty nobly alone. After she and Mercer left for Greenwich to be gossip at Mrs. Daniel's child's christening, I went to Mrs. Martin's and did what I would with her, but her loose company left me displeased. At Westminster Abbey I talked with Mr. Blagrave, a sober politique man, and then met Mr. Yeabsly, who told me he had given my Lord Ashly L100 to secure his friendship in our accounts—which makes me think as ill of Ashly as the world does. On the water I inspected Victualling ships and went to Deptford, reading Bacon's "Faber Fortunae" all the way, and returned to find my wife pleased with her afternoon as godmother; she had held the child at the font, and he is named John.
levels.summary:
This morning I went to church with my wife, and at noon we dined mighty nobly, just the two of us. Afterward my wife and Mercer rode by coach to Greenwich, where she was to be gossip at Mrs. Daniel's child's christening. I went to Westminster and called on Mrs.

Martin, who had stayed in all day for me; I took my pleasure with her, yet found myself not well pleased with her over-free and loose company, so I left for Westminster Abbey.

There I fell into discourse with Mr. Blagrave, whom I find a sober, politique man that gets money and increase of places. Then I met Mr.

Yeabsly, who told me he had presented my Lord Ashly with L100 to bespeak his friendship in the accounts now before us—and my Lord has received it, which makes me believe he is as bad, as to bribes, as the world says.

I called on all the Victualling ships and went to Deptford for a little business, and all the way coming and going I read my Lord Bacon's "Faber Fortunae," which I can never read too often.

When I came home, my wife was returned from Greenwich, much pleased with her reception. She was godmother and held the child at the font, and the child is called John. After putting my papers in order and supping, I went to bed, desirous to rise betimes in the morning.

periods.label: June 1666

levels.sentence: In June 1666 I swallowed the bitter truth of a naval defeat disguised as victory, wrote sad letters instead of triumphant ones, attended grand funerals, quarreled with commanders, and stole small pleasures from women, art, and my father's portrait to keep the disquiet at bay.
levels.paragraph: June 1666 began with my shock that the supposed victory was a defeat, leaving me to manage the Duke's letters and a sad letter to Lady Sandwich. The month mixed public gloom with private consolations: my father's portrait, a forgotten lobster, trysts with Mrs. Tooker and Mrs. Bagwell, prints from Faythorne's, and Mings's grand funeral. But discord between the Duke and Albemarle, the plague death at Mrs. Bagwell's, and Father's leaving all weighed on me. I ended the month with a colic, £20 given to my father, and a garden song before bed.
levels.summary:
At the start of June I woke expecting to celebrate a victory, but Lord Bruncker and Sir T. H. told me we had been beaten, losing The Prince and Sir G. Ascue. The town's mood sank, and Captain Page confirmed the Dutch had chased us for two hours.

At White Hall the Duke of York gave me letters for setting the fleet out again, and I worked late on abstracts, tallying losses: The Prince, Essex, Swiftsure, many captains, and Sir William Clerke. Albemarle said not above twenty officers behaved like men, forcing me to write a painful letter to Lady Sandwich.

The second week brought discord between the Duke of York and Albemarle over commanders, especially Du Tell, and my Tangier hopes collapsed while tallies at the Exchequer failed. But my father's portrait at Hales's lifted me; then a lobster forgotten at dinner made us laugh.

periods.label: August 1666

levels.sentence: I settled my accounts to a new high of £5,700, found all business stalled without me at St James's, learned from Sir W. Coventry of the Dutch defeat, and spent the afternoon in amorous play at Mrs Martin's before returning home to my wife's drawing and a pleasant bed.
levels.paragraph: This morning I settled my last month's accounts and blessed God to find myself worth £5,700, the most my book ever showed. I was delayed by Sir W. Pen and came too late to St James's, where everything stood still for want of me. Walking with Sir W. Coventry, I heard that the Dutch lost 5,000 men and De Ruyter is out of favour, though Coventry is not pleased with our Generals. After church I dined at the Swan on a rabbit, then at Mrs Martin's amused myself with Mrs Burroughs, the widow Mrs Eastwood, and Mrs Fenton. I towzed and tumbled the merry widow, then carried them home, fearful of being seen, and returned to find my wife at her drawing, going to supper and bed very pleasant.
levels.summary:
This day I rose early to settle my last month's accounts, and blessed God to find them very clear, my worth now £5,700, the most my book ever showed. I prepared to attend the Duke of York as usual, but Sir W.

Pen, just as I was going out, came home from Sheerness and held me in discourse about public business, so that I came by coach too late to St James's, where everything stood still and nothing was done for want of me.

Thence I walked over the Park with Sir W.

Coventry, who is not thoroughly pleased with the late management of the fight, nor with anything the Generals do; only he is glad to hear De Ruyter is out of favour, and that this fight cost the Dutch 5,000 men as they report, while we had not above 400 or 500 killed and wounded, and as many flag-officers on their side as ordinary captains on ours.

I left him going to chapel, it being the common fast day, and the Duke of York at chapel.

I went to Mrs Martin's, but she was abroad, so I sauntered to the Abbey and then to the parish church, fearful of being seen; after service I dined at the Swan upon a rabbit, then returned to Mrs Martin's, where I found Mrs Burroughs, a pretty widow, one Mrs Eastwood, and one Mrs Fenton, a maid.

There was merry kissing and looking on their breasts, and all the innocent pleasure in the world; the widow dissembled a faint at a jigg her late husband loved, but I made her as merry as possible and towzed and tumbled her as I pleased.

I carried her and her sober kinswoman Mrs Fenton home to their lodgings, mightily pleased with the afternoon's mirth yet in great pain to ride in a coach with them for fear of being seen. So home, where I was much pleased with my wife's drawing, and so to supper and to bed very pleasant.

periods.label: September 1666

levels.sentence: After the Great Fire, I tended to counsels and cargo, indulged a shameful desire, then found relief in settling the war's vast accounts and in fetching my wife's flowered tabby gown.
levels.paragraph: In mid-September I attended to business with the Duke and spoke with Michell and Howlett about their young ones, promising to counsel the young man whose unkindness to his wife was over. I visited Martin, dined with Balty and his wife, and helped Balty load goods onto the Bezan at Deptford. That night I stole to Bagwell, but my conquest turned to self-loathing, and I escaped when her husband returned. By late September, our first office meeting after the fire faced Sir W. Warren's evasions over the Scotch motion. I finished the Parliament lists, and with Sir W. Coventry rejoiced that our medium expenses came above L3,000,000, while extraordinaries justified our L320,000; then I fetched my wife's new best gown, and went to bed in good humour.
levels.summary:
After the fire, I was back at my rounds. With the Duke of Yorke, then with Michell and Howlett, I heard of the young man's unkindness to his wife being over and promised to counsel him; I was glad she would be near again.

I visited Martin, dined with Balty and his wife, and took Balty to Deptford to help load goods onto the Bezan. That night, I gave in to lust with Bagwell, and the pleasure soured into self-loathing; I made my escape when her husband returned, and went to Sir W. Pen's, where I found him in his usual simple humour.

Later in the month, our first office meeting since the fire found Sir W. Warren stumbling over the Scotch motion, and we parted without resolution. I finished the lists for the Parliament Committee and carried them to St James's, where Sir W. Coventry waited.

To our joy, the medium of wages, victuals, and wear and tear came above L3,000,000, and the extraordinaries would justify our L320,000; Coventry said if God sent us over this rub, we must take another course for a better Comptroller.

I fetched my wife from Unthanke's with her new best gown — coloured tabby, flowered — gave my clerks extra work in a new method, and went to bed in good humour, glad of the end we had brought this matter to.

periods.label: October 1666

levels.sentence: In October 1666, amidst the burned city and a failing war effort, I juggled pressing official duties, my growing family, and my secret dalliances, all while trying to secure my own fortune.
levels.paragraph: October 1666 brought a whirl of public anxiety and private indulgence. I faced cuts to naval funding, begged for Tangier money before a silent King, and heard grim reports of our fleet's condition. Yet I also found time for merriment with friends and for secret pleasures with Mrs. Martin and others, even as I worried over my new servant and moved my treasure to safety. Through it all, I kept my accounts and sought some comfort in reading.
levels.summary:
The month opened with a farewell to my father and a blow from the House, which cut £150,000 from our wear and tear, though they allowed 28,000 men. I tended to business, paid a ticket for little Michell, and then indulged with Mrs. Martin, who is big with child and insists I be godfather.

At home, my wife brought a poor, ordinary new girl from Mr. Falconbridge's, which disheartened me, and I spent the evening making up my accounts.

I attended the Cabinet to beg money for Tangier, but the King sat like an image, and I was referred to another meeting. Walking with Sir H. Cholmly, I learned of Killigrew's banishment for calling Lady Castlemayne a lecherous girl, and that Williamson and Bab May were rejected by voters.

Later, I read Stillingfleet on Purgatory and, for safety, carried two iron chests of money to my closet. Captain Guy then dined with me, declaring English valour spent and the June fight a defeat; he condemned Holmes and praised Smith. Afterward, I tumbled widow Burroughes and Doll at Mrs.

Martin's, and later supped merrily with the Wights, while noting more naval disasters.

periods.label: November 1666

levels.sentence: In November 1666 I balanced the King's financial troubles and gloomy talk of ruin with private pleasures—taking liberties with several women, feasting, and trying to shake off my own unease about the future.
levels.paragraph: This November I found myself pulled between the public decay and my private appetites. The office and Sir W. Coventry spoke of ruin and lost discipline, while I sought comfort in wine, women, and company. My wife and I quarreled over fashion, then made up; I heard of the French king's insult to our King, and learned of friends' losses in the fire. periods.label: December 1666

levels.sentence: At the close of 1666, I mix pleasure with business, mourn poor Batters, and settle my accounts, troubled by my lavish spending yet comforted by a growing estate.
levels.paragraph: I began the month with dinners and dalliances—Pegg, Mrs. Burroughs, then Sarah—but also heard ill news from Scotland and comforted Mrs. Turner in her plague losses. I grieved when Batters was drowned going to his ship, and that fear clung to me all day. I helped Mrs. Clerk's son-in-law seek a command, attended to my pictures and plate, and paid visits around town. On New Year's Eve I balanced my books: income down, spending up, yet my worth above L6,200, and I resolved to be more careful.
levels.summary:
This December I have been as busy in pleasure as in business. I dined nobly, visited Gresham College, and took my ease with Pegg, Mrs. Burroughs, and Sarah, feeling no great guilt even as I faced a dun and troubling news of Scotland. I comforted poor Mrs.

Turner, who lost everything in the plague and chid me for not writing.

Death shadowed the month: brave Batters, who brought his ship safely in, was drowned going back to her in the Thames, and I could not shake the fear it raised in me all day. Yet I went on—attending the Duke of York, meeting Mr. Thomas Andrews, helping Mrs.

Clerk's daughter about her husband's command, and carrying home more silver plate.

On the last day I settled all my accounts, paying every debt, and found I had spent L1,154—far too much—while my income fell to L2,986. Still, my whole estate now stands above L6,200, and I pray God to make me thankful and more frugal in the year ahead.

My household is well, save my sore eyes, and I can serve guests entirely on silver.
