periods.label: January 1667

levels.sentence: Amid January frost and French invasion fears, I grappled with Parliament's discontent and my own restless appetites—refusing a bribe, chasing pleasure with Betty, Mercer, and Knipp, and taking comfort in small savings.
levels.paragraph: Frost lay on London as I shuttled between White Hall and the office, hearing alarms of a French landing and grumbles from Parliament. I refused a golden bribe, enjoyed music with Mercer, and stole kisses and caresses from Betty Michell and Knipp wherever I could. I went home at night light-hearted from diligence, yet ashamed when I had neglected my wife.
levels.summary:
I began the month at White Hall, attending the Duke of York while the Court trembled at reports that the French had shipped landsmen at Brest, likely for Ireland. Orders came to send all ships to the Downes, but no ships can go without men, and no men without money; each day brought new mutinies.

The Houblons laughed at the invasion talk, saying it was only French West India plantations and that we at Court blew it up to make Parliament open its purse. I did not believe we had such a plot, yet Mr.

George Montagu told me all was going ill: the King was displeasing the Commons by turning their Accounts Bill into a commission, leaving out Coventry and me.

In the Painted Chamber I heard a conference on the Wine Patent, where Swinfen and Sir Thomas Meres far outdid the Lords, and I was glad. Afterwards Doll Lane and I drank good wine at the Rose Taverne, and I gave her twelve soldis for gloves.

I saw "The Custome of the Country" a second time; Knipp played the Widow well and sang a little song admirably, though the play itself was the worst I ever saw.

I went home displeased at losing so much time and disobliging my wife by being there without her, and walked through the cold, slippery frost thinking on establishing my vows.

The middle weeks were a tangle of duty and desire. I worked hard, dined with Lord Bruncker, and examined the loss of The Prince Royall with the Trinity House; at night I was troubled about the Prize Office's shameful candle sale of hemp and timber, knowing we would need those goods again. Yet I also kissed Mrs.

Burroughs, later touched her breasts, and after a great dancing party at my house, crept up to Knipp's bed and handled her breasts. With the Michells I had baisers with Betty, and one moonlit boat ride I got her hand under my cloak.

I refused a box of £100 in gold from the flaggmakers Young and Whistler because I wanted to be able to say I had refused it.

I settled my monthly accounts with relief, thanking God I had saved a little from my salary. I visited the Michells with my wife, sang with Mercer by moonlight until reminded it was a fast-day, and went ashamed to cards, then kissed Mercer several times before bed.

I heard the Prince was better, that Lord Sandwich had perfected peace with Spain, and that Lord Bellasses had taken near £2000 in gratuities and tried to undermine Sir H. Cholmly.

In the last dark ride home, a bruise on my testicle gave me occasion to shift sides with my wife; I sat by Betty, took her hand, and did what I pleased, to my great satisfaction. I set her at home, finished my office business, and went to bed glad of my success.

periods.label: February 1667

levels.sentence: I balanced my accounts and my lusts, dodging suspicion and court gossip while grasping at money, power, and pleasure in a February of narrow escapes.
levels.paragraph: This February I balanced my monthly accounts with relief, then gave myself over to pleasure and risk. I pursued Betty Michell while dreading my wife's suspicions, refused a bribe to keep my hands clean, and stood firm at the Duke's council despite Carteret's fury. Through it all, news of peace and war, princes and knaves, swirled around me, and I took my secret joys where I could.
levels.summary:
I began the month settling my accounts and thanking God for my savings, then visited little Michell and his wife with my own wife, Mercer, and Barker. That evening I sang with Mercer by moonlight until my wife reminded me it was a fast-day, and I felt ashamed — yet still kissed Mercer before bed.

Later I refused a box of gold from the flaggmakers, heard good news of the Prince and Lord Sandwich, and enjoyed a play with fine ladies. At the New Exchange I gave Betty Michell gifts, and on the ride home I took liberties with her to my great satisfaction, though a bruise made me shift sides with my wife.

The next week I went with Lord Bellasses about my Tangier warrant but found our hopes defeated by the Poll Bill. I heard Prince Rupert was better and that my Lord Sandwich was ordered home, and I bought the King's speech with words promising possible peace. At Povy's I saw the notorious knave Vernatty at work.

I met Betty Michell and bought her a dressing-box, but when I tried to get her into a drinking house she refused. On the way home I panicked, fearing her husband had gone to my house and would give my wife suspicions; by luck her maid came to my door and I told her Betty was home, and all was well.

At midmonth I stood firm at the Duke's council that without money no fleet could be expected, but only Sir W. Coventry seconded me, and Sir G. Carteret was furious. I walked with the King and Duke, galled by my ignorance about the St. Patrick and by the King's coarse jokes about marriage.

Betty Michell refused even my hand, and I went home troubled, resolved to mind my business. ' I was pleased to see my Navy accounts handsomely bound, had secret pleasure with Mrs Burrows in my closet, and at the playhouse a witty masked lady diverted me more than The Mayd's Tragedy itself.

Betty Michell refused even my hand, and I went home troubled, resolved to mind my business. ' I was pleased to see my Navy accounts handsomely bound, had secret pleasure with Mrs Burrows in my closet, and at the playhouse a witty masked lady diverted me more than The Mayd's Tragedy itself.

- January 30 week
  - Settled monthly accounts and thanked God for savings
  - Visited little Michell and his wife with my wife, Mercer, and Barker; enjoyed their charming house
  - Sang with Mercer by moonlight; felt ashamed on the fast-day and kissed her before bed
  - Refused £100 bribe from the flaggmakers Young and Whistler to remain above reproach
  - Heard the Prince was better and Lord Sandwich had perfected peace with Spain
  - Learnt of Lord Bellasses's underhand dealings in the Mole business
  - Saw a good play; Knipp sang 'All night I weepe'; admired Mrs. Middleton
  - Gave Betty two pairs of gloves and a dressing-box; groped her on the ride home, to my great satisfaction
- February 6 week
  - Went by water with Lord Bellasses and Creed about my Tangier warrant; hopes defeated by the Poll Bill
  - Heard Prince Rupert better and that Lord Sandwich was ordered home
  - Bought the King's speech with words promising possible peace
  - Met Vernatty, the cunningest knave, at Povy's over endless accounts
  - Took Betty Michell to a cabinet-maker's, bought her a dressing-box for twenty shillings
  - She refused to enter a drinking house; we were merry, and the shopkeeper took us for man and wife
  - Feared her husband had sought her and would give my wife strange thoughts
  - Escaped discovery as her maid came to my door; all was well within, and my joy was full
  - Taught Barker a little of my song before bed
- February 13 week
  - Stood firm at the Duke's council that without money no fleet could be expected; only Sir W. Coventry seconded me
  - Sir G. Carteret furious at me; walked with the King and Duke, galled by my ignorance and the King's coarse jokes
  - Betty Michell refused me even a touch of her hand; went home troubled and resolved to mind my business
  - Captain Cocke's night visit brought grave news of peace and fears of civil war; read a fine answer to 'The Apology for Papists'
  - Was pleased to see Navy expense accounts handsomely bound; handled tallies at the Exchequer
  - Had Mrs Burrows alone in my closet; kissed and touched her breasts, a secret pleasure

periods.sentence: I balanced my accounts and my lusts, dodging suspicion and court gossip while grasping at money, power, and pleasure in a February of narrow escapes.
periods.paragraph: This February I balanced my monthly accounts with relief, then gave myself over to pleasure and risk. I pursued Betty Michell while dreading my wife's suspicions, refused a bribe to keep my hands clean, and stood firm at the Duke's council despite Carteret's fury. Through it all, news of peace and war, princes and knaves, swirled around me, and I took my secret joys where I could.

periods.label: March 1667

levels.sentence: Amid fearful reports of war and the kingdom's want of victuals, I cling to my wife's music, stolen kisses, and the hope that my honest account may set things right.
levels.paragraph: I spent two weeks torn between duty and delight. I traveled to Deptford and Woolwich on business, suffered Sir W. Batten's unfortunate tumble into a tar-drain, and inspected a wharf we could not hire. At court I heard alarming news of peace and war, while merchants braced for ruin and the fleet lacked provisions, prompting my resolve to report the Victualler's true state. Yet I found pleasure in my wife's flageolet, in kissing Betty and Mis Tooker, and in Tom's teaching Barker to sing, though my tryst with Doll Lane came to naught and the shadows of coming troubles lingered.
levels.summary:
These weeks were full of anxiety. My trips to Deptford and Woolwich with Sir J. Minnes and Sir W. Batten brought both mishap and merriment: Batten sprained his foot falling into a stinking drain, and we dined joyously at the White Hart.

More troubling were the reports from the Exchange and the court: the Dutch and the King of France braved high terms, merchants feared for their goods, and I learned from Mr. Gawden that the Council doubted we could fit out a fleet for want of victuals.

Knowing I had failed to represent the provisions, I determined to draw up a true statement for the Duke of York.

Amid these dark clouds I seized small joys. My wife's first attempts on the flageolet delighted me, and I was pleased that Tom had been teaching Barker to sing a third part. I stole kisses from Betty Michell and little Mis Tooker, though my planned meeting with Doll Lane came to nothing.

Sir John Winter called me early about timber, and I heard of Buckingham's going to France and Carcasse's request that I stand godfather. Late nights spent preparing a speech for the King left me weary, but I finished my journals and went to bed, holding onto the cheerful moments as best I could.

periods.label: April 1667

levels.sentence: Amid fears of a bad peace and spreading hardship, I found my days crowded with office maneuvers, public spectacles, and guilty private pleasures, from Betty Michell's pretty face to Mrs Lowther's willing kisses.
levels.paragraph: The month opened with quarrels, false friends, and uneasy news: I clashed with Carcasse, saw through Sir W. Pen, and heard at the Exchange that the town cried out for peace while I feared we would make a bad one. I settled accounts with Viner, paid my poll money ashamed, and listened to Young's account of churches and Moorefields built for profit rather than people. My private hours were no steadier—I kissed a miss at the Swan, found Betty Michell so pretty that she haunted me, and later took willing liberties with Mrs Lowther. Yet there were quiet pleasures too: singing with my wife, the birth of Betty Michell's girl, and a book on Turkish policy.
levels.summary:
At the start of April I quarrelled with Carcasse, saw through Sir W. Pen's falseness, drank with Betty Michell without a kiss, settled accounts with Viner, and heard from Houblon that there was no hope of peace.

Young told me how the new churches and the Moorefields scheme served the great men rather than the people, and I paid my poll money ashamed that I had assessed myself so low.

At the Exchange the town cried for peace, but I feared a bad peace, with tenants flinging up lands, Buckingham losing six thousand pounds, and Jasper Trice leaving housekeeping. I saw the tame Tameing of a Shrew, missed Knipp, kissed a miss at the Swan, and found Betty Michell so pretty she haunted me.

I also heard of Lady Batten's jewels being found under a china cup, and read a book on Turkish policy.

The next week I blocked Pett's attempt to force Carcasse's business onto the agenda, sang alone with my wife, wrote to my father longing to have him in town, and enjoyed Mrs Lowther's willingness.

The third week opened with a grand feast for the Swedish ambassadors, and then came the news that my wife had helped deliver Betty Michell of a pretty girl. I called on Mrs Martin and did what I would with her, visited the Michells to see the baby, and openly opposed Sir W.

Warren as he now applies himself wholly to Lord Bruncker. So the month ran on between public fears and private indulgences.
levels.outline:
- April 1667: uneasy peace, office intrigue, and guilty pleasures
  - Week of Apr 3
    - Quarrelled with Carcasse; saw Pen's falseness while helping about Mrs Turner's son
    - Drank at the Old Swan with Betty and her husband; no kiss; saw Mrs Howlett recovered
    - Settled accounts with Sir Robert Viner; met James Houblon, who saw no hope of peace
    - Heard Young's account of churches placed for advantage and the Moorefields scheme
    - Paid poll money of L40 17s, ashamed it was so little
    - At the Exchange, town cried for peace but I feared a bad one; tenants, Buckingham, and Jasper Trice suffer
    - Saw The Tameing of a Shrew; mean fare, only Sawny by Lacy had any life
    - Sought Knipp but she was gone; kissed a miss at the Swan; Betty Michell haunted me
    - Heard Lady Batten's jewels found under a china cup after servant arraigned
    - Read a well-regarded book on Turkish policy
  - Week of Apr 10
    - At the office, blocked Pett's attempt to force Carcasse's business onto the agenda
    - Sang alone with my poor wife; eyes troubled me after candle-light
    - Wrote to my father, longing to have him in town and take pleasure in my doing well
    - Mrs Lowther came; I touched and kissed her breasts and mouth, and she was very willing
  - Week of Apr 17
    - Grand feast at White Hall to show jollity to the Swedish ambassadors
    - Young Michell summoned my wife to Betty's labour; wife and midwife delivered a pretty girl
    - Called on Mrs Martin and did what I would with her
    - Visited little Michell's, saw the child, asked after Betty
    - Opposed Sir W. Warren openly, as he applies himself wholly to Lord Bruncker
    - Came home to the office, then to my chamber, and so to bed

periods.label: May 1667

levels.sentence: In these two May weeks I swung between light pleasures—new tunes, flagelettes with my wife, stolen visits to Mrs. Martin—and heavier cares, for everyone doubted whether the peace would hold, and my father's sudden, patient suffering made me question my promises about Brampton.
levels.paragraph: This fortnight I went about my usual affairs—learning tunes on the flagelette, attending to business at Westminster, and hearing uncertain talk about the King's new Treasury commissioners and whether peace would come. I yielded to my old appetites, seeing Betty Michell's prettiness and paying visits to Mrs. Martin where I did what I would with her, though I was once ashamed when a girl's uncle caught us tumbling. My wife stayed at home with her cold, and we played flagelets together of an evening. But the deepest note was struck at the end, when my poor father suffered a fallen bowel and bore it with such patience that I was touched, and I began to doubt my promises about building at Brampton.
levels.summary:
At the start of the week I rose early to practice a new tune on my flagelette, then went to Westminster, where everyone was guessing at the King's Treasury commissioners and wondering whether we should have peace.

I heard a captain say the seamen of Holland cried out against peace, though the common people wished for it.

The afternoon was a broken day, so by my vows I could walk abroad; I went over the Hill to the postern-gate for the first time since the fire, spied my young mercer and his pretty little wife in their new place, and later saw Betty Michell, who had grown wonderfully pretty since her christening. I walked with Sir W.

Doyly and then called on Mrs. Martin, where I did what I would with her, and came home by coach, though I was ashamed in the morning at the Swan when her uncle found the little girl's neckcloth off while we tumbled.

The following Sunday was sweltering; I left off my waistcoat and walked in the garden before church, then dined at home with little Michell and his pretty wife. I went alone by water to Westminster to see Mrs. Martin, followed her to church, was placed in the gallery by Mr.

Howlett, and endured the sermon with my perspective glass, looking at the fine women and sleeping. Afterwards I stayed an hour or two with Mrs. Martin again. Rowing home I read Evelyn against Solitude, which I thought thin, and Boyle on Colours, which made me laugh.

At Barne Elmes I saw gallant ladies supping under the trees. But at home I found my father in an unexpected fit, his bowel fallen down; W. Hewer helped put it back, and my father's patience under affliction touched me deeply.

That night we talked of building at Brampton, and I felt fresh doubts about my engagement to Uncle Thomas and his son, and about being near Hinchingbroke.

  - Afternoon walk: postern-gate first time since fire; spied mercer and his wife
  - Old Swan: saw Betty Michell and her child; walked with Sir W. Doyly
  - Mrs. Martin: did what I would with her; drank; home by coach
  - Shame at the Swan: tumbling with a girl; her uncle found her neckcloth off

periods.label: June 1667

levels.sentence: Amid the mal-administration of the times and the threat of the Dutch, I attended to my office, wrote bold letters to Sir W. Coventry, and stole moments of private pleasure with Mrs. Martin, Nell, and Mrs. Markham.
levels.paragraph: I began the week at White Hall and St. James's, hearing that the Duke of Cambridge might live after all, and I made a point of visiting Sir W. Coventry to show my interest. I gave Lord Barkeley maps, saw the Duke of Monmouth's young Hectors, and later took a solitary boat ride to Barne Elmes, reading L'Estrange's "The Visions." But the times were troubled: we issued orders for fire-ships against the Dutch, and my cousin Roger Pepys came to talk of the kingdom's misery and mal-administration. Amid it all, I found time for dalliance with Mrs. Martin, my maid Nell, and Mrs. Markham.
levels.summary:
This week was full of business and anxiety. I went to White Hall and St. James's, learning the Duke of Cambridge might recover, and I visited Sir W. Coventry to be seen in his company.

I gave Lord Barkeley a set of maps, saw the Duke of Monmouth's young Hectors who I fear will debauch country women, and afterward attended church with Creed and dined with my father and wife. I saw Betty Michell at Westminster Church, had my way with Mrs. " Finding an order for fire-ships, I joined W. Batten and W.

Pen in issuing orders.

My cousin Roger Pepys came with his son Talbot, and we talked of the misery and mal-administration of the times, including Lord Arlington's taking up 12,000 pounds in gold. He promised to show me an old Chancery decree with many of our name. I wrote a bold letter to Sir W.

Coventry about the want of money, though I feared it might give offense. In quieter moments I showed dalliance to my maid Nell, and later dallied all alone with Mrs. Markham in the garden before reading and writing in my chamber.

    - Joined W. Batten and W. Pen to issue orders

  - Office work
    - Searched old letters for Sir W. Coventry
    - Wrote bold letter about want of money, feared offense
  - Cousin Roger Pepys
    - He brought son Talbot, meant for Temple, but took him back
    - Talked of misery and mal-administration
    - He told of Lord Arlington's 12,000 pounds in gold

periods.sentence: Amid the mal-administration of the times and the threat of the Dutch, I attended to my office, wrote bold letters to Sir W. Coventry, and stole moments of private pleasure with Mrs. Martin, Nell, and Mrs. Markham.
periods.paragraph: I began the week at White Hall and St. James's, hearing that the Duke of Cambridge might live after all, and I made a point of visiting Sir W. Coventry to show my interest. I gave Lord Barkeley maps, saw the Duke of Monmouth's young Hectors, and later took a solitary boat ride to Barne Elmes, reading L'Estrange's "The Visions." But the times were troubled: we issued orders for fire-ships against the Dutch, and my cousin Roger Pepys came to talk of the kingdom's misery and mal-administration. Amid it all, I found time for dalliance with Mrs. Martin, my maid Nell, and Mrs. Markham.

periods.label: July 1667

levels.sentence: Amid the Dutch war and our want of money, the concluded peace lifts me, and even an Epsom trip that ends with a sprained foot leaves me thanking God that no business was missed.
levels.paragraph: In July the long-expected peace arrived, and my heart was light, though our office still stood still for want of money. I was pleased to hear that everyone speaks mightily of me, even while the King and others speak ill of our office. At Epsom I drank the waters and walked with my wife and Mrs. Turner, but I sprained my right foot leaping down a bank. I ended in pain, yet thanked God that no business was missed.
levels.summary:
Our office met again while the Dutch were still on the coast, but money troubles made us helpless: the merchantmen would not be fitted, and even grapnells went unpaid. At home, Jane's old mistress wanted her back and Jane cried; I dallied with Nell. Mrs.

Turner assured me everyone speaks mightily of me, though the King and others speak ill of our office. Poor Tooker died, and Sir J. Minnes's illness kept us from singing.

Then Creed brought glorious news of peace. The King's letters said it was concluded, and Mr. Coventry was coming; I hurried to confirm it at White Hall, feeling that peace would save us from ruin. Mrs.

Martin was not with child, to my relief, though her sister Doll accused Captain Vandener of assaulting her—a story I doubted, knowing her freedom with me. Mr. Rolt's nose bled at parting, an ill omen; Lady Jemimah was delivered of a boy.

At Epsom with my wife and Mrs. Turner, I drank the waters, dined at the King's Head, and heard James Houblon call me the only happy man of the Navy. I sprained my foot leaping down a bank, but was charmed by a shepherd and his boy reading the Bible on the downs, and gave the boy money.

I returned by glow-worms, in great pain, yet thanked God that no business was missed.

periods.label: August 1667

levels.sentence: After church and dinner with Pelling, I wandered by water to Westminster, hoped in vain to spy Betty Michell at church, then took a leisurely walk to Barne-Elmes, reading Boyle's Hydrostatics with great delight before supping with W. Hewer.
levels.paragraph: I began the day at church, then hosted Pelling for dinner. Afterwards I went by boat to Westminster, where I kissed Frank at the Swan and attended church hoping to see Betty Michell, but mistook her mother for her. My boat's oar broke, but it was soon mended. I proceeded to Putney, admired the fine folk there, and walked on to Barne-Elmes, delighting in Boyle's Hydrostatics. In the evening I supped with W. Hewer and talked freely about office matters.
levels.summary:
I rose and went to church, then dined with Pelling, whose pleasant discourse made the meal agreeable.

Afterward, I set out by water, dropping Pelling at White Hall and continuing to Westminster, where I kissed Frank at the Swan and went to church in hopes of seeing Betty Michell—but the nose I spied belonged to her mother, which vexed me.

My boat had broken an oar, yet it was quickly repaired, so I rowed up to Putney, stepped into the church there to admire the young ladies, and then walked to Barne-Elmes, savoring Boyle's Hydrostatics as Russel carried it. I strolled among the elms, then returned home by boat with great pleasure, supped with W.

Hewer, and relished our good talk about the Office before going to bed.

periods.label: September 1667

levels.sentence: Amid secret indulgences and fair entertainments, I attend to navy business and council debates, then greet a new servant and look toward Brampton.
levels.paragraph: In early September I stole to the Swan with Doll Lane while my wife was away, then joined her at Walthamstow and the fair, where I pitied a crippled dancer and marveled at a clockwork show. Later in the month, after a dull Tangier committee, I spoke well at the Council while Lord Anglesey defeated a scheme to pledge the King's credit. I spent a lonely evening at home, then slipped off to Mrs Martin before returning to find the grave, pretty Willet arrived. Now I begin to think of my journey to Brampton.
levels.summary:
I began the month with secret business at the Exchequer and a private hour with Doll Lane at the Swan, a pleasure I kept from my wife. Finding she had gone with Sir W. Batten to Walthamstow, I followed with Mrs. Turner, and we talked of Sir W. Pen's baseness and the suspicion that his son Lowther has the pox.

At Batten's the dinner was plain but good; I admired the house but tired of the company. On the way home my wife and I stopped at Bartholomew Fair, where a poor fellow danced on hands and crutches and moved me to pity, and a clockwork piece showed the ages of man to a hundred years.

In the dirty night a man nearly took up my wife before we saw it was Sam Hartlib; he hurried off when another man came. We supped and went to bed.

Later in the month, at White Hall, the Tangier committee accomplished little, and I dropped my petition to the Duke of York. At the Council we considered discharging seamen by tickets, and I spoke in a way that pleased the King and Council.

Lord Ashly moved to give an assignment on the Act to the East India Company or the City, but Lord Anglesey opposed it handsomely, arguing it would teach Parliament not to trust the King and want a separate treasurer. Anglesey carried it, and I agreed it was mean for the King to borrow their credit.

I dined alone, then went back to hear there would be musique before the King tomorrow, and stopped at the Swan to visit Mrs. Martin, where I had my pleasure and promised my goddaughter her first coat.

Returning home, I found the pretty, grave Willet arrived, well-carriaged and almost too good for my family; I hope my wife will use her well. Mr. Turner and his wife told me they hope to place their son Franke with the East India Company through Sir Andr. Rickard, which I like.

Now I seriously think of my journey to Brampton next week.

periods.label: October 1667

levels.sentence: I attended the Council over Pett's neglect, dined cheaply, saw Mrs. Martin, worried over Lord Sandwich's ruinous expenses, and learned that Sir W. Batten is not expected to live till tomorrow.
levels.paragraph: I spent the morning at White Hall in the Council's long hearing on Commissioner Pett's neglect, where the Chatham attendants contradicted him and he struck me as a weak, silly man. After a hasty dinner and a brief business talk with Lord Ashly about Mr. Yeabsly's abatement, I slipped away to Mrs. Martin's, though her husband has come home sooner than I expected. In the evening I conferred with Lord Crew about Lord Sandwich's desperate state — he has spent prodigious sums and can get neither money nor recall. Returning home, I found Sir W. Batten so ill that it is believed he cannot live till to-morrow, which troubles me for kindness and for the money he owes me.
levels.summary:
At White Hall this morning, the Duke of York and the Navy officers met about Navy business, and Sir W. Coventry generously recommended Sir John Harman and my Lady Minnes for the King's bounty.

Then we attended the Council in a long hearing of Commissioner Pett, where the two Masters Attendant of Chatham denied his claim about bringing up the great ships; I thought him a weak, silly man guilty of horrid neglect. The matter was put off till Monday. , then went to Lord Ashly's to settle Mr.

Yeabsly's business, abating him L1000.

Afterwards I went to Mrs. Martin's lodging and heard her husband is come from sea, which is sooner than I expected; I stayed and drank and touched her, then left.

I spent an hour with Lord Crew, who is distressed that Lord Sandwich can neither be called home nor supplied with money — he has spent L20,000 of the King's money and best part of L10,000 of his own, and the Treasury demands an account. I offered to speak to Sir W.

Coventry, but my Lord would not advise it without Sir G. Carteret's consent. Coming home, I found Sir W. Batten asleep and dangerously ill; word came that he cannot live till to-morrow, which troubles me and my wife mightily, partly from kindness and partly because of the money he owes me from our prize bargain.

periods.label: November 1667

levels.sentence: Amidst the political turmoil over Lord Clarendon and the King's shifting alignments, I managed my own affairs, dealt with arrogant musicians, and learned of threats to my position.
levels.paragraph: This week was thick with political intrigue and personal vexations. At Backewell's, I arranged a large remittance for Tangier while he bragged of his financial resilience. Parliament clashed over Clarendon, and I heard fears that Buckingham and Bristol might turn on my Lord Sandwich. Meanwhile, the returned Monsieur Humphreys disparaged the King's musicians, and we made but mean music together. I also learned that a waterman had been summoned to testify against me about prize goods, though I remain untroubled.
levels.summary:
At Backewell's, I arranged a £6000 remittance to Tangier; he boasted of surviving the Sheerness crisis by paying the Swedes and lending the Treasury over £40,000.

Parliament was in conflict over the Earl of Clarendon, with the Lords refusing to commit him without a specific treason charge, and I heard that the King's quarrel is with his brother, not the Chancellor. Buckingham and Bristol now guide the King, and there is fear they may fall upon my Lord Sandwich.

I met the conceited Pelham Humphreys at my tailor's; he disparaged all the King's musicians and claimed he would supplant Grebus. We dined on venison pasty and played theorbo, French lute, and viol, but made mean music. Later, Mr. Moore shared his fears of ruin and read me treason law.

The next week, I learned from Cooling that the Lords' stiffness toward Clarendon is born of self-preservation, and that Clarendon might fare better before the Lords than by the King's commission. I also visited the Temple church and noted Selden's plain tomb compared with his executor's.

The waterman Poundy told me he was summoned to testify against me about prize goods; I bade him tell all. I drank my morning draught with Betty Michell but found no chance to kiss her. These threads of political danger and private vexation weigh on me.

levels.sentence: As the year ends, I find myself blessed in my family's health and my own affairs, yet deeply troubled by the kingdom's precarious state, with a discontented Parliament, a misguided King, and the threat of French invasion looming.
levels.paragraph: I spent the last day of 1667 at White Hall and then at my office, dealing with public matters and hearing of the seamen's discontent and their being lured into French service. I also enjoyed some personal pleasures, including a visit to Mrs. Martin, and dined with my uncle Thomas. As I reflect on the year, I am grateful for my family's health and happiness, but I am filled with anxiety about the nation's future—Parliament is dissatisfied, the King is led astray, and foreign dangers threaten us.
levels.summary:
I began the day by going to White Hall, where I waited with Creed for the Duke of York, hearing much talk about the expected removal of the great Lords from council, all stemming from their opposition to the King regarding the Chancellor. At the Tangier committee, I found Lord Middleton a dull but stout soldier.

Returning home, I dined with my uncle Thomas, who is in mourning for his daughter Mary, and we discussed the new Act for accounts, which grants extraordinary power to the people—a thing I have no mind to read for fear of troubling myself.

In the afternoon, I accompanied my wife to Unthanke's, then left her to visit Mrs. Martin, with whom I had my way, and chided her husband's extravagance.

Later, Captain Perryman told me how seamen are being enticed to the French King's service, and advised me on my vessel, the Maybolt, suggesting I sell her rather than engage in the coal trade.

As the year closes, I feel great happiness in my own health and family, but my mind is heavy with thoughts of the kingdom's peril: Parliament dissatisfied, the King misled, divisions with the Duke of York, and the ever-present threat of foreign invasion.

I also cannot shake my fears about being examined by the Parliamentary committee on Navy matters.

periods.label: January 1668

levels.sentence: In January 1668 I savored the delight of company and music one week, then turned to the sober satisfaction of putting my accounts and domestic life in order the next.
levels.paragraph: One week I threw myself into lively society — mistaken dinner plans, a costly box at The Tempest, and an evening of dancing with the Duke of Buckingham's own musicians. The next week I kept to a quieter, industrious rhythm: church, a plain dinner, and long hours reckoning my Tangier and East India accounts. In both I found contentment, though of different kinds. I reflected that social joys are the truest comfort I can expect, while careful work restores order to my affairs.
levels.summary:
The first week opened with a small comedy of errors: Mr. Pierce and his wife, and then Mr. Harris, arrived thinking they were invited to dinner when we expected them for supper. We made do with a modest meal, and I delighted in Harris's excellent conversation.

That evening I took everyone to The Tempest at the Duke's house, paying dearly for a box because the pit was full, and then brought the whole company home.

At home I had arranged for the Duke of Buckingham's own musicians, sent by Greeting, which made the night extraordinary. We danced, sang, feasted on a great supper and a cake from Jane, and our neighbours joined us. Mrs.

Hollworthy came in at last, and though I had long wanted to meet her, I found her conceited and not very intelligent. Still, the night was a great pleasure, and I went to bed reflecting that such social joys are the truest comfort I can expect in life, and I must enjoy them while I have health and means.

Late in the month I spent a steady, industrious day: after church with my wife and a quiet dinner with no strangers, I worked from afternoon until late evening on my Tangier accounts and examined my East India accounts with Mr. Poynter, whom I employed the whole day to transcribe them fair.

In the evening I had supper with W. Hewer, and finally had the girl comb my head until I fell asleep. It was a day of careful reckoning and simple domestic comfort — no great events, but a sense of order restored.

periods.label: March 1668

levels.sentence: In March 1668 I faced Parliament's suspicions over tickets, places, and victuals, defended my office at the Council, and still found room for stolen pleasures with Mrs. Martin and Doll Lane, anxious readings, and small domestic reconciliations.
levels.paragraph: March 1668 was a month of constant care. I rose early to prepare defences with Sir W. Coventry, attended Parliament and Council, and answered fresh complaints about victuals. Yet I also enjoyed many small pleasures: Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, a talking starling, Hyde Park, and a painted board that deceived my eyes. At home I quieted a squabble with my wife, and ended the month troubled by a new accusation from Carcasse and by Deb's tears.
levels.summary:
March 1668 kept me in a state of anxious watchfulness. With Sir W. Coventry I prepared our defence concerning tickets and the sale of places, while the old complaint about victuals in the 1666 fleet also fell to me to answer.

At Parliament's door cousin Roger warned me that the House suspected me, and the waiting weighed on me; but when the Commissioners of Accounts laid little blame on us, my mind was set at ease.

Later, at a Council meeting, I successfully defended my office's signing of certificates against the Treasury, though I angered Duncomb and Clifford, and the King jested that I would have to make another speech.

Amid these cares, I stole pleasures where I could: I had my way with Mrs. Martin more than once, gave Doll Lane 20s. as my Valentine, kissed Frank at the Swan, and delighted in a starling that had been the King's. I went to Hyde Park, dined in good company, and admired Hewer's painted board that looked like real wood.

At home I had a small squabble with my wife that taught me the worth of silence, and I bought pewter and struggled to find a cook. My eyes were very bad, yet I could not stop reading; I thought Lord Newcastle's wife ridiculous and him an ass to suffer her.

The month closed with fresh troubles: on the last day I was summoned to a Committee about victuals for Sir John Harman's fleet, where they were full of jealous suspicion and wanted to blame Brouncker for failing to improve the first victory.

I drove the women about the park, ashamed that they were undressed, yet pleased. That night Deb cried at her poor writing, her mistress thought it sullenness, and as she undressed me for bed I gave her good advice and kissed her, and she went on weeping.

I went to bed restless, knowing Carcasse's complaint against Sir W. Batten and Sir W. Pen hung over me.

periods.label: April 1668

levels.sentence: In April 1668, I balanced office duties, political maneuvering, and personal pleasures, all while navigating scandals and my own indiscretions.
levels.paragraph: April was a whirl of business and pleasure. I saw my wife off, kissed her maid Deb, and attended to pressing office matters. I heard gossip about Lady Castlemayne's affair with Hart, and I furthered my own dalliances with Knipp and Mrs. Martin. Politics swirled around Sir W. Pen's impeachment, and I kept my counsel to protect my reputation.
levels.summary:
The month opened with family and office. I sent my wife to my father's, managing a kiss with Deb and a shilling for her attendance. The office kept me busy, and I gave L40 to the new college at the Royal Society, fearing faction.

I also enjoyed plays, including 'The English Monsieur,' and visited Knipp, learning of Sir W. Davenport's death and Lady Castlemayne's love for Hart.

Mid-month brought political tension. I began learning the recorder, and heard of the move to impeach Sir W. Pen. The Coventrys tried to save him by blaming Lord Sandwich, and I stayed silent, thinking it the only way. I also spent time with Mrs.

Martin, and returned home to find my maid's brother lodging there, which displeased me.

Later, at White Hall, I learned of a petition against Sir W. Coventry, which grieved me. Brouncker feared Parliament's violence might force the King to dissolve them. My attempt to see a pretty woman came to nothing, and I visited Betty Michell without success.

The Duke of York spoke kindly of Pen, and I ended the month supper at Pen's, my eyes too bad to read.

periods.label: May 1668

levels.sentence: In May 1668 I balanced the Duke's business and Tangier accounts with music, plays, walks, and stolen favours, while old age, sudden death, a meteor over the City, and Lord Sandwich's gentle reproach reminded me how quickly time and reputation slip away.
levels.paragraph: All month I kept my public duties before me—attending the Duke, settling the Excise, and toiling over Tangier accounts—while my heart ran to music, plays, singing, and women. I met old Mrs. Washington and saw age in her face, heard that stout Sir Thomas Teddiman had died of a thrush, and shared the town's dread of a meteor that seemed to promise fire and Popish knives. Yet I still took my pleasures: a salmon pie for my wife, the first green peas from Mr. Gibson, new songs from Smith of Oxford, and stolen moments with Mrs. Martin and Bagwell's wife. Lord Sandwich's letter stung me for neglecting him, but I went to bed satisfied.
levels.summary:
All month I lived between the office and the town. I attended the Duke of York, consulted with Sir W. Coventry and Sir Stephen Fox about the Excise, and watched the Council throw money at Hemskirke's impossible ship. I heard that stout Sir Thomas Teddiman had died of a thrush, and when I met Mrs.

Washington after eight or nine years I saw age in her face and knew time was doing the same to me. The House passed the City Bill, but I grieved that churches were given to bishops and colleges rather than the convenience of the people.

Pleasure ran just as strongly. I heard music I love in 'The Virgin Martyr,' sang at Kensington and Fox Hall, bought song-books by Smith of Oxford and Marcennus's music book, and wore my new black bombazin suit to the theatre. Mrs.

Martin promised me the King's starling, and I took what liberties I could with her and with Bagwell's wife. I spent evenings with Knepp, Mrs. Turner, and Mercer, ate curds and cream and the first green peas, and packed a salmon pie home for my wife.

Dark threads ran through the month: a meteor over the City frightened people of another fire and Papist knives, and Lord Sandwich's gentle letter reminded me I had neglected him while he was abroad.

Dark threads ran through the month: a meteor over the City frightened people of another fire and Papist knives, and Lord Sandwich's gentle letter reminded me I had neglected him while he was abroad.

I balanced business and licence as best I could, telling myself that a man ought once to know the loose company's manner of talk and lives, yet making sure to do my office business before I slept.

periods.paragraph: All month I kept my public duties before me—attending the Duke, settling the Excise, and toiling over Tangier accounts—while my heart ran to music, plays, singing, and women. I met old Mrs. Washington and saw age in her face, heard that stout Sir Thomas Teddiman had died of a thrush, and shared the town's dread of a meteor that seemed to promise fire and Popish knives. Yet I still took my pleasures: a salmon pie for my wife, the first green peas from Mr. Gibson, new songs from Smith of Oxford, and stolen moments with Mrs. Martin and Bagwell's wife. Lord Sandwich's letter stung me for neglecting him, but I went to bed satisfied.

periods.label: June 1668

levels.sentence: Between Tangier business and a hungry appetite for pleasure, I sang and played, fell into bawdy company, and strayed with Mrs. Martin and Bagwell's wife, yet I still did my office work and ended the fortnight singing with Mercer in the garden.
levels.paragraph: This June I kept my official duties before me—Tangier accounts, the Council Chamber, Treasury meetings—while my heart was bent on pleasure. I sang at Fox Hall, bought Marcennus's music book, and wore my new black bombazin suit to the theatre, remembering the part of Arethusa I once meant to play; but darker threads ran beneath, from Lord Sandwich's letter about my neglected writing to bawdy company and Harris's account of the 'Ballets' at my Lady Bennet's. I did what I would with Mrs. Martin and stole to Deptford to finish my agreed design with Bagwell's wife, yet I still came home to my office business before bed. The later week closed more quietly: after seeing 'The Impertinents' with W. Hewer and supping at Spring Garden without much mirth, I sat with Mercer in the garden and sang myself to bed.
levels.summary:
Early in the month I balanced Tangier business with pleasure: I sang with Mercer and Gayet at Fox Hall, bought Marcennus's music book, and delighted in my new black bombazin suit at the theatre, recalling the part of Arethusa.

But Lord Sandwich's letter gently noticed how I had neglected to write to him, which put me in great difficulty. I fell into bawdy company, learned from Harris that the 'Ballets' meant naked dancing at Lady Bennet's, and spent a late merry supper at Mr. Mills's house. I also did what I would with Mrs.

Martin, and stole down to Deptford to complete my agreed design with Bagwell's wife, laughing with a bargeman about the old woman of Woolwich as I left at midnight.

Through it all I told myself that a man ought once to know the loose company's manner of talk and lives, yet I still returned home to do my office business before bed.

Later, Creed and Colonel Atkins came about coals for Tangier, and I went with Creed to Alderman Backewell's over money; on the way to Westminster I stopped at Michell's for a drink, though I did not kiss her. Since it was a holyday, no business was done at Westminster.

I went to Martin's and then home by water, took W. Hewer to see 'The Impertinents' at the Duke of York's playhouse, and supped at Spring Garden, but I was not very merry. Coming home, Mercer and I sang in the garden for a good while, and so I went to bed.

periods.label: July 1668

levels.sentence: After a busy morning at the office, I dined and went to my bookseller's, where a pretty woman caught my eye and I followed her until I lost her, then visited Lord Crew, saw my wife's nearly finished portrait, took the family to Spring Garden where rude gallants troubled me, and returned home to receive my four new plates that both vex and please me.
levels.paragraph: I spent the morning at my office, then dined and went to my bookseller's in Duck Lane, but his wife was not at home; as I stood there, a pretty woman with a wanton look passed by, and I followed her round the streets to Newgate Market until she turned back and I lost her. I then waited on my Lord Crew, whose face is sore but mending, and from there to Cooper's, where my wife's picture is almost done and mighty fine. Crossing the water with my wife, Deb., and Mercer to Spring Garden, we ate and walked, but I was troubled to see young gallants rudely forcing themselves into arbours where women were without men. We returned home by water with much pleasure, and that day my plate-maker brought four little plates of the four Yards, costing me L5, which troubles me yet pleases me too.
levels.summary:
I began the day with business at the office and after dining went to my bookseller in Duck Lane, but his wife was not at home. While there, a pretty woman with a wanton look passed by, and I followed her round about the street to Newgate Market, but she turned back and I lost her.

I then visited my Lord Crew, whom I found up, and his face is sore but he hopes to do well again.

At Cooper's, my wife's picture is almost done and mighty fine indeed. , and Mercer to Spring Garden, where we ate and walked.

I was troubled to see how rude some young gallants of the town are become, going into arbours where there are no men and almost forcing the women—a confidence in the vice of this age that disturbed me. We returned home by water with much pleasure.

That day my plate-maker came with my four little plates of the four Yards, costing me L5. They trouble me for the cost, yet they please me as well.

periods.label: August 1668

levels.sentence: In August 1668, I busied myself with visits to lords, a portrait sitting, and various amorous and theatrical delights, all while managing everyday affairs.
levels.paragraph: This month I moved between business and pleasure, from White Hall to the Exchange, from Cooper's studio to the Fair. I paid a dear price for my wife's portrait, yet found it imperfect. I pursued several women with mixed success, and enjoyed a fine performance of Hamlet. My days were full of small errands and social calls, ending each night at home with my wife and Deb.
levels.summary:
I began the month by seeking Sir W. Coventry at White Hall, only to find him gone, then called on Lord Arlington at Goring House, where he received me respectfully and I gave an account of my journey. Lord Orrery flattered me greatly, and I relished his praise.

Later, I attended to business at the Exchange and dined at home before heading to Duck Lane, hoping for a chance with the book vendor's wife, but she was unavailable.

That afternoon I watched Cooper finish my wife's portrait, paying £30 plus extra for the case—though I was not entirely satisfied with the likeness or the blue garment. In the evening, I fondled Deb while my wife read a ridiculous book, then went to bed.

On the last day of the month, after office and errands, I kissed a girl at the Swan, saw Hamlet with friends, and visited the Fair for Polichinelle. I saw the money-telling mare, which picked me out and earned me a kiss.

I also tried to see Betty Michell but her husband was home, and later rebuffed a naughty wench in a coach. Mrs. Martin dined with us earlier, and I accepted a spaniel bitch for my wife with some reservation.

periods.label: September 1668

levels.sentence: Though I sought pleasure in plays, fairs, and pretty women, I was pulled back by pressing duties — the Duke's commands, my Lord's need for money, and troubling court rumours.
levels.paragraph: In late August I savoured London's diversions, from Hamlet and Polichinelle to a money-telling mare and a stolen kiss, yet even then my appetite for a married woman was thwarted and a coach-side wench I dismissed. In late September, duty reasserted itself: the Duke of York tasked me with improving the Office, and I learned of my Lord's urgent need for money, which I felt bound to supply despite my own neglect in writing. I visited Lord Burlington's house, singed my periwig by candlelight, and heard Italian music with the Queen. But gossip that Sir W. Coventry was out of favour and Arlington might become Lord Treasurer troubled me deeply, and I clung to the Duke's firm support for Gawden.
levels.summary:
At the end of August, I mixed business with pleasure: I attended to my office and Exchequer duties, stopped at the Swan to kiss the girl there, and dined alone while my shoe was mended. That evening I saw Hamlet with Mary Mercer, Batelier, and W.

Hewer, and was mightily pleased with Betterton's acting; afterward we went to the Fayre to see Polichinelle, and I accepted a spaniel bitch for my wife with some reservation.

My attempt to see Betty Michell came to nothing because her husband was home, though the famous money-telling mare at the Fair picked me out and earned me a kiss from a pretty girl.

I found the bookseller's wife in tears but could not learn why, and later in a coach I gave a shilling to a naughty wench who tried to join me, then left her.

In late September, duty pressed upon me. Knepp's maid summoned me to the women's day at the playhouse, and I gave her half-a-crown and a kiss; then at St. James's the Duke of York asked me to prepare something for better managing the Office.

I visited Lord Burlington's house for the first time, where I saw Lord Hinchingbroke and his lady, met Sidney Montagu, and learned of my Lord's urgent need for money. I felt duty-bound to supply L500, though I regretted my remissness in writing to him during his voyage.

At that house I accidentally set my periwig on fire by a candle, causing a strange noise, and later I walked through Westminster, admired my vintner's handsome wife, and greeted the widow Mrs. Horsfall.

Evening brought mixed pleasures: I saw the silly play "The City Match" at the King's playhouse, full for the women's sake, and then attended the Queen, who came out with her ladies to hear Italian musicians in a barge, with Seignor Joanni's voice standing out.

I saw Sidney Montagu kiss the Queen's hand, and the King spoke with him. But troubling news reached me that Sir W. Coventry is out of favour, and there are designs to make my Lord Arlington Lord Treasurer, which I cannot believe.

Hewer, and was mightily pleased with Betterton's acting; afterward we went to the Fayre to see Polichinelle, and I accepted a spaniel bitch for my wife with some reservation.

My attempt to see Betty Michell came to nothing because her husband was home, though the famous money-telling mare at the Fair picked me out and earned me a kiss from a pretty girl.

I found the bookseller's wife in tears but could not learn why, and later in a coach I gave a shilling to a naughty wench who tried to join me, then left her.

In late September, duty pressed upon me. Knepp's maid summoned me to the women's day at the playhouse, and I gave her half-a-crown and a kiss; then at St. James's the Duke of York asked me to prepare something for better managing the Office.

I saw Sidney Montagu kiss the Queen's hand, and the King spoke with him. But troubling news reached me that Sir W. Coventry is out of favour, and there are designs to make my Lord Arlington Lord Treasurer, which I cannot believe.

The Duke of York also told me of the hot dispute over Gawden, and he stood firmly in his support.

periods.label: October 1668

levels.sentence: I spent the day pulling strings to get Turner's place for Hater and to settle other preferments, while hearing a sober discourse on the Dutch war from old Major-General Middleton.
levels.paragraph: This morning I got Lord Brouncker's ready assent for Hater to have Turner's place, and hoped for Sir J. Minnes's too, but at the Board we learned James Southern is petitioning for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford, which troubled us. We resolved to push for our own clerks, insisting that preferment follow seniority and merit. After dinner I went with Mr. Turner to see the Duke of Albemarle, who took kindly my speaking for Turner. Then I stopped at Brouncker's for his sign on a letter to the Duke of York, and at Lord Middleton's to report on his L1000 payment, where he talked well against the Dutch war.
levels.summary:
I began the day by securing Lord Brouncker's support for T. Hater to take Mr. Turner's place, and hoped for Sir J. Minnes's too, only to learn from Mr. Wren that James Southern is petitioning for the Storekeeper's place of Deptford — a move that troubled me and the whole Board.

We resolved to fight hard for our own clerks, arguing that preferment should follow seniority and merit.

After the Board rose I dined at home, then went with Mr. Turner to see the Duke of Albemarle, who took my speaking for Turner kindly. I got Lord Brouncker's hand to a letter for the Duke of York about Hater, and visited Lord Middleton to report about his L1000 being paid.

He discoursed at length against the Dutch war, and I was pleased to hear him, though I noted how even a man of knowledge can be undone by drink and pleasures.

periods.label: November 1668

levels.sentence: When my wife discovered I had secretly visited Deb, I confessed, swore never to see the girl again, and bought peace with a promise I intended to keep, though the shame left me praying alone and unable to enjoy my new hangings.
levels.paragraph: I lied to my wife about Deb, spent the day finding her, kissed her in a coach, and gave her counsel and money, then came home with a fair tale. The next day my wife knew everything and raged at me until W. Hewer helped make peace on my written oath never to see Deb again. We were reconciled in bed, but I was so ashamed that I began to pray on my knees, and even the finished hangings gave me no joy.
levels.summary:
On Monday I woke late to my wife's jealousy: she feared I meant to visit Deb, and I denied it, God forgive me. That afternoon I hunted for Deb through Somerset House, Lincoln's Inn Fields, White Hall, the Strand, and Hercules Pillars before a porter carried a message to her.

At nightfall I rode to her, kissed her in the coach, counseled her to guard her honour, gave her 20s. and a direction to leave word at Herringman's, and resolved to seek her no more. I went home and told my wife a fair tale.

On Tuesday she confronted me, calling me a false, rotten-hearted rogue, and I confessed the whole wicked business. She swore to slit the girl's nose, leave me, demand hundreds of pounds, or expose me. W.

Hewer came and cried like a child, but he obtained peace on condition I give it under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again.

Before late a durable peace was made. We went to supper with kind words and to bed, and I made love to her content. I resolved never to give her such occasion again, and I began to pray to God on my knees alone, though not yet heartily.

Even with my best chamber newly hung, my sorrow and trouble put me out of all joy in looking upon it.

periods.label: March 1669

levels.sentence: I rode to Maidstone with Gibson and Coney, enjoyed the sights along the way, and on my return spent an evening of free flirtation with Mrs. Jowles, taking liberties but leaving before the final act.
levels.paragraph: I set out for Maidstone with Gibson and Mr. Coney, eager to see a town I had never visited. The ride was cold and windy but the country was fine, and I enjoyed the sight of Sir John Bankes's abbey and later the Saxon stones near Aylesford. In Maidstone I walked the town, climbed the steeple, and watched an old man beating flax. On the way back I stopped again at Captain Allen's, where Mrs. Jowles proved very free with her kindness, allowing me to kiss her and touch her breast at the door, though I lacked time and place to carry her to Cobham.
levels.summary:
I took a coach with Gibson and Mr. Coney, surgeon, toward Maidstone, having a mighty desire to see that town. On the way I stopped at Captain Allen's to give the pretence of calling on him, but really to see if his daughter Mrs. Jowles was about; she was, but I took no notice and promised to return at night.

Riding on, I was pleased with the sight of the Medway and the fine country, and I turned aside to see Sir John Bankes's old abbey, though he was in London. At Maidstone I walked all over the town, climbed the steeple for a noble view, watched an old man beating flax, and bought fresh fish for our dinner at the Bell.

In the afternoon we set back, and I stopped to see a Saxon monument of three stones by Aylesford. Then I stopped again at Captain Allen's, sent the coach and Gibson home, and stayed with Mr. Coney. Mrs.

Jowles came to us, a fine, proper lady, and we talked over old stories while I took the liberty to salute her often, pull off her glove, and find her hand moist. She was very willing to go with me to Cobham, for I believe she is a whore, but a brave and comely one.

A pretty cousin of hers came to supper, and later I got Mrs. Jowles to the street door, where I touched her breasts and kissed her without force. I might have had all else, but it was neither the time nor the place.

We stayed till almost midnight, then walked over the fields in pitch darkness and snow to Chatham, where I went straight to bed.

periods.label: April 1669

levels.sentence: I spent the day pursuing secret meetings with Bagwell's wife and then Deb., while trying to attend to business and social obligations, leaving me both hopeful and guilt-ridden.
levels.paragraph: I rose and went to the office, but my thoughts were elsewhere. Following Deb.'s direction, I tried to visit her aunt in Jewen Street but found her not in town. Later, I met Bagwell's wife in Moorfields, but the holiday crowd forced us to part. Then I saw Deb. on Holborn Hill and led her into a blind alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she stayed coy. I gave her twenty shillings and arranged another meeting, but my mind was full of trouble. I rejoined my wife and friends at Povy's house, but the bad pictures and my own fears spoiled my pleasure.
levels.summary:
's directions to search for her aunt in Jewen Street, only to learn she was away. Back at the office, I found Bagwell's wife waiting, and she slipped me a note asking me to meet her in Moorfields.

I went there after the office rose, but because it was a holiday and crowded, we could only talk briefly and agreed to meet another time.

While riding through the city, I caught sight of Deb. on Holborn Hill. I followed her into a little alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she seemed modest and hesitant. I gave her twenty shillings and we agreed to meet again in Westminster Hall on Monday.

My heart was troubled by what I had done, and even at my cousin Turner's and then at Povy's house, among family and friends, I could not shake my unease. I took my wife and the Bateliers home by way of Islington, and after supper went to bed, carrying my secret with me.

  - Parted because of the holiday crowd, agreeing to meet another time

  - Saw Deb. on Holborn Hill and followed her
  - Led her into a blind alehouse and kissed/touched her
  - She was modest, but we agreed to meet on Monday at Westminster Hall
  - Gave her 20s. in paper
- Social and evening
  - Went to cousin Turner's, found they had gone to Povy's
  - Dined at Povy's and viewed the rooms and pictures

periods.sentence: I spent the day pursuing secret meetings with Bagwell's wife and then Deb., while trying to attend to business and social obligations, leaving me both hopeful and guilt-ridden.
periods.paragraph: I rose and went to the office, but my thoughts were elsewhere. Following Deb.'s direction, I tried to visit her aunt in Jewen Street but found her not in town. Later, I met Bagwell's wife in Moorfields, but the holiday crowd forced us to part. Then I saw Deb. on Holborn Hill and led her into a blind alehouse, where we kissed and touched, though she stayed coy. I gave her twenty shillings and arranged another meeting, but my mind was full of trouble. I rejoined my wife and friends at Povy's house, but the bad pictures and my own fears spoiled my pleasure.

periods.label: May 1669

levels.sentence: As my eyes fail and political winds shift, I am forced to hand my journal to others, mourning the end of my private candor.
levels.paragraph: This month I have been beset by unease, both from the Duke of York's contentious meetings and from my own failing eyesight. I found some pleasure in taverns, in Mrs. Martin's company, and in a kiss from Mrs. Michell, but the news that my sister is with child left me oddly cold. The greatest blow came when I realized I could no longer write in my own hand; I resolved to let my servants keep the journal in long-hand, reserving a margin for any secret notes. It feels like a kind of death, and I pray God to prepare me for the blindness that threatens.
levels.summary:
In the early days of May, I was troubled at night while my wife went for May-dew, and my unease followed me to White Hall, where the Duke of York fell into a hot dispute about Mr. Child.

I kept careful to show no side, fearing heart-burnings, and later dined with the decaying Lord Crew, who shared an old rule about country families. The Duke then told me the King was satisfied with the Navy, and that Sir Jeremy Smith would replace Pen; I was glad, though I dare not think myself secure.

My coach and gold-lace sleeves drew too much notice in the Park, so I resolved to have the lace taken off.

Mid-month, I met old friends at Westminster Hall, invited Sidney Montagu to dinner, and enjoyed the company of Mrs. Martin in her lodging, though she boasted of her husband's wealth. A play, 'The Roman Virgin,' proved old and ordinary, and the candlelight hurt my eyes.

Then my brother John arrived with the first news that my sister is with child; I was uncertain whether to be troubled or pleased, for I have never much cared to see my own friends have children.

By the end of the month, I spent a difficult morning stating my accounts with W. Hewer, plagued by my ill eyes. I stole a kiss from Mrs. Michell, and went merrily to the Park and The World's End with my wife and friends. But the real burden came: I can no longer keep my journal with my own eyes.

I have resolved that from now on my people shall keep it in long-hand, and I will only add short notes in the margin. It feels almost like going into my grave, and I pray God to prepare me.

levels.sentence: From January's doubtful clerkship to August's busy accounts, I record suspicions, secrets, and small family dealings.
levels.paragraph: In January, Mr. Downing told me he had made me Clerk of the Council, yet I feared he only wanted to avoid paying me. I spent my days at Whitehall and ordinaries, hearing that all clerks were turned out but my name was undecided. By August, I was settled at the Privy Seal, where Sir Samuel Morland revealed his royal service and his rewards, making me think better of him. I dined with my father at the Tower, paid for my brother's schooling and my own degree, and returned home to have my head combed by the servants.
levels.summary:
In January, Downing claimed to have made me Clerk of the Council, but I wasn't heartily thankful, suspecting he wanted to escape paying my current salary. I spent time with Sheply and Pierce, got lodgings at Whitehall, and dined at the French Ordinary where Downing feasted MPs.

At day's end, I learned the clerks were turned out except the Leighs, and my name had been mentioned but nothing decided.

In August, I settled accounts at the Privy Seal, including for a velvet coat. Sir Samuel Morland stayed with me and recounted his secret service to the King under the Protector, his discoveries, and his losses, which the King now repays with £500 a year and two baronets.

I dined at the Tower with my father and others, received a firkin of butter for my wife, gave money for my brother John, and paid for my Master of Arts degree. The day ended at home, where the servants combed my head before bed.

levels.sentence: A day of farewells, family dinner, a heated quarrel with Antony Joyce, and evening rope-dancing, all shadowed by my wife's mysterious appointment and a dying aunt's summons.
levels.paragraph: This morning I took leave of my mother, who set off for Brampton with my sister Pall, and saw them into the waggon, Pall crying bitterly. After a merry dinner at my uncle Fenner's, I was summoned to attend my dying aunt Kite, but instead found myself quarrelling with Antony Joyce, whose meddling made me very angry. Later I took my wife to the fair, where we watched Italian rope-dancers and women tumbling, yet my mind remained vexed by Antony's words and by the secret message my wife received from a French footman.
levels.summary:
I began the day by attending to business at the Privy Seal, then took leave of my mother as she set out for Brampton with my sister Pall, whom I had given twenty shillings and good counsel.

At my uncle Fenner's I found my wife and Pall, and I saw the two women off from Beard's, Pall crying bitterly as the waggon pulled away. We then drank with my aunt Bell and Charles Pepys before sitting down to a merry family dinner.

After dinner, word came that my aunt Kite, the butcher's widow, lay dying and asked my uncle and me to take charge of her affairs and her daughter.

Before I could respond, Antony Joyce picked a quarrel with me that grew into high words, and though he spoke even worse to his father, the whole company was offended and we parted angry.

I took my wife to the fair, where we saw Italian rope-dancers and women doing strange tumbling tricks, but I walked home vexed about Antony and troubled by a private message a French footman had delivered to my wife, who promised to go somewhere tomorrow morning without telling me what it was.

levels.sentence: From dunning tradesmen and court balls to my private oath against wine and plays, I ended 1662 balancing a growing purse against nagging cares at home and court.
levels.paragraph: I spent much of May vexed by debts and family dealings, yet noted the Queen's arrival and my own improving health and fortune, worth about £530. I cut off my beard, tried to go without powder, and took an oath against wine and plays. By December I was richer, worth £650, and ended the year in mirth with my wife, though troubled by servants and uncle Thomas's business.
levels.summary:
This year began with everyday vexations: Anthony Joyce came dunning me for tallow money, my father and I talked over our dealings with uncle Thomas, and I found my powdered hair so foul that I cut off my beard and resolved to keep my head dry.

I took an oath to abstain from wine and plays, and already felt its good effect. The Queen came to Hampton Court and was praised as handsome and discreet, which I feared would disturb Madam Castlemaine; peace was made with Algiers, and my Lord Sandwich arrived safely with the Queen.

By December my purse had grown to about £650, and I enjoyed a court ball crammed with fine ladies, watching the Duke of Monmouth's mistress, Lady Castlemaine, and Sir Harry de Vicke's daughter. Yet cares weighed on me: my maid Jane turning proud, my boy Wayneman to be turned away, Sarah going to live with Sir W.

Pen, and above all my uncle Thomas's business threatening my fortune. In public matters I noted the King's dalliance with Castlemaine, the splendour of Monmouth, danger to the Lord Chancellor, and the Bishops pressing uniformity.

Still, the nation being quiet and my own health good, I gave thanks to God, counting my blessings alongside my cares.

levels.sentence: In 1663 I balanced my accounts, my appetites, and my duty to the King, closing the year with £800 to my name and a head full of resolutions.
levels.paragraph: In 1663 I kept busy with Navy business, dalliances with Mrs. Lane, and quiet reckonings with myself. I watched the King prorogue Parliament and I argued with Sir W. Pen at the office, while at night I made up my accounts by candlelight. My wife and I ate our Christmas turkey alone, and I finished the year wealthier than I started, but conscious of my sins and my swelling. I resolved to stick to business, get a little money, and do better.
levels.summary:
In July I did business with Sir J. Minnes, ordered a timber rule, and dallied with Mrs. Lane at the Crown, towzing her freely and then vowing never to do it again. I rode to the Wells, heard a gallant catch of musique, and watched the King in the Lords' House give assent to four subsidies.

A swelling by my anus frightened me of rupture. In September I took my wife to Bartholomew Fair, but later lied to her and carried Mrs. Lane to Lambeth, where she would not consent to the main thing, and I thanked God and resolved again to reform.

At the office I defied Sir W. Pen over a purser's fine and felt no regret, though I let a pretty lodger at Unthank's melt my anger by the hand. Captain Taylor gave me a little plate to help his demurrage claim. In December Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W.

Batten at our table, and I sat up till four in the morning balancing my accounts, finding myself worth over £800 and £700 more in my Lord Sandwich's hand. My health is pretty good but costiveness troubles me.

My cares lie thick: my wife's brother is unhappy, cousin Angier's rogue son goes to sea, my brothers give little hope, and Pall grows old. The Queen is recovered, the King minds his mistress too much, and the Turk is far into Germany.

I bless God I am in a good way, and I resolve to stick to my business and serve the King.
levels.outline:
- July 1663
  - Business and pleasure
    - Did business with Sir J. Minnes; ordered a timber rule.
    - Met Mrs. Lane at Westminster; went to Crown, ate chicken, towzed her freely; ashamed and resolve against it.
    - Lingered at Mrs. Howlett's, bought gloves, flirted with her daughter (my wife).
  - Excursions and Parliament
    - Rode to the Wells seeking dog; heard fine part-singing by citizens.
    - At Lords' House heard Speaker, saw King assent to subsidies and smaller acts.
    - Spoke with Lord Sandwich; visited Spring Garden with Creed; watched tumbling.
  - Health worry
    - Swelling by anus, fear of rupture, to consult Mr. Hollyard.
- September 1663
  - Amusements and temptations
    - Bought news-books, found Mrs. Lane immodest.
    - Dined at Mr. Povy's magnificent house; took wife to Bartholomew Fair (monkeys, clockwork).
  - Navy and guilt
    - Met Sir Philip Warwick about Navy debt.
    - Lied to wife, met Mrs. Lane at Lambeth; she refused the main thing; thanked God; resolved to reform.
  - Home
    - Found wife hard at work, grieved; saw God's justice.
- November 1663
  - Office conflict
    - Showdown with Sir W. Pen over purser's fine; he left like a discontented ass; no regret.
  - Town errands
    - Followed Howlett's daughter but she escaped; dallied with a pretty lodger at Unthank's.
    - Consulted Dr. Turner about East India freight.
  - Evening
    - Wrote letters; supper; cold; Captain Taylor's plate and demurrage cause.
- December 1663
  - Office and Christmas
    - Sir W. Warren defied Sir W. Batten; quiet Christmas dinner with wife (turkey and mince pie).
  - Year-end accounting
    - Sat till four in morning making accounts; worth above £800 in money, £700 with Lord Sandwich.
  - State of affairs
    - Health costiveness; office envies from Batten, false knave Pen.
    - Family cares: brother-in-law, cousin Angier's son, brothers, Pall.
    - Public: Queen recovered, King minds mistress, Duchess sick, talk of French King, Turk into Germany.
  - Resolution
    - Stick to business, get money, serve King.

periods.brief: In 1663 I balanced my accounts, my appetites, and my duty to the King, closing the year with £800 to my name and a head full of resolutions.
periods.full:
In July I did business with Sir J. Minnes, ordered a timber rule, and dallied with Mrs. Lane at the Crown, towzing her freely and then vowing never to do it again. I rode to the Wells, heard a gallant catch of musique, and watched the King in the Lords' House give assent to four subsidies.

A swelling by my anus frightened me of rupture. In September I took my wife to Bartholomew Fair, but later lied to her and carried Mrs. Lane to Lambeth, where she would not consent to the main thing, and I thanked God and resolved again to reform.

At the office I defied Sir W. Pen over a purser's fine and felt no regret, though I let a pretty lodger at Unthank's melt my anger by the hand. Captain Taylor gave me a little plate to help his demurrage claim. In December Sir W. Warren openly defied Sir W.

Batten at our table, and I sat up till four in the morning balancing my accounts, finding myself worth over £800 and £700 more in my Lord Sandwich's hand. My health is pretty good but costiveness troubles me.

My cares lie thick: my wife's brother is unhappy, cousin Angier's rogue son goes to sea, my brothers give little hope, and Pall grows old. The Queen is recovered, the King minds his mistress too much, and the Turk is far into Germany.

I bless God I am in a good way, and I resolve to stick to my business and serve the King.
periods.outlineFull:
- July 1663
  - Business and pleasure
    - Did business with Sir J. Minnes; ordered a timber rule.
    - Met Mrs. Lane at Westminster; went to Crown, ate chicken, towzed her freely; ashamed and resolve against it.
    - Lingered at Mrs. Howlett's, bought gloves, flirted with her daughter (my wife).
  - Excursions and Parliament
    - Rode to the Wells seeking dog; heard fine part-singing by citizens.
    - At Lords' House heard Speaker, saw King assent to subsidies and smaller acts.
    - Spoke with Lord Sandwich; visited Spring Garden with Creed; watched tumbling.
  - Health worry
    - Swelling by anus, fear of rupture, to consult Mr. Hollyard.
- September 1663
  - Amusements and temptations
    - Bought news-books, found Mrs. Lane immodest.
    - Dined at Mr. Povy's magnificent house; took wife to Bartholomew Fair (monkeys, clockwork).
  - Navy and guilt
    - Met Sir Philip Warwick about Navy debt.
    - Lied to wife, met Mrs. Lane at Lambeth; she refused the main thing; thanked God; resolved to reform.
  - Home
    - Found wife hard at work, grieved; saw God's justice.
- November 1663
  - Office conflict
    - Showdown with Sir W. Pen over purser's fine; he left like a discontented ass; no regret.
  - Town errands
    - Followed Howlett's daughter but she escaped; dallied with a pretty lodger at Unthank's.
    - Consulted Dr. Turner about East India freight.
  - Evening
    - Wrote letters; supper; cold; Captain Taylor's plate and demurrage cause.
- December 1663
  - Office and Christmas
    - Sir W. Warren defied Sir W. Batten; quiet Christmas dinner with wife (turkey and mince pie).
  - Year-end accounting
    - Sat till four in morning making accounts; worth above £800 in money, £700 with Lord Sandwich.
  - State of affairs
    - Health costiveness; office envies from Batten, false knave Pen.
    - Family cares: brother-in-law, cousin Angier's son, brothers, Pall.
    - Public: Queen recovered, King minds mistress, Duchess sick, talk of French King, Turk into Germany.
  - Resolution
    - Stick to business, get money, serve King.
periods.sentence: In 1663 I balanced my accounts, my appetites, and my duty to the King, closing the year with £800 to my name and a head full of resolutions.
periods.paragraph: In 1663 I kept busy with Navy business, dalliances with Mrs. Lane, and quiet reckonings with myself. I watched the King prorogue Parliament and I argued with Sir W. Pen at the office, while at night I made up my accounts by candlelight. My wife and I ate our Christmas turkey alone, and I finished the year wealthier than I started, but conscious of my sins and my swelling. I resolved to stick to business, get a little money, and do better.

levels.sentence: In this year of stone and sin, I endured the torments of a fit, pursued my desires with Bagwell's wife, and heard grim news of Tangier, all while keeping to the endless round of office and obligation.
levels.paragraph: My year was a tangle of bodily misery and secret pleasure. In May, a terrible stone fit had me roaring and helpless until a chance posture brought relief. By October, I was back at the office, dining with my uncle, and growing bold with Bagwell's wife, whom I promised to help. In December, I stole to her house, sent her husband away, and took my full satisfaction. The day ended in bread and work, leaving me contented but weary.
levels.summary:
I suffered a violent stone fit in May, brought on by a cold, which left me unable to break wind or make water and, for two hours, writhing in extraordinary anguish until a change of posture on my knees brought merciful ease. I slept well that night, thankful for the respite, though the blockage remained.

By autumn, my attentions had turned to Bagwell's wife, and I caressed her in my office, promising her husband a place—a bargain I meant to keep. The same day, I learned from Mr. Cholmely that Tangier was in a bad state under Fitzgerald, a dishonourable man who slighted the English and achieved nothing.

In December, I went to the Bagwells' house, sent the husband on an errand, and pressed my advantage to full satisfaction, then returned to dinner and the office, content but weary.

    - Slept well, thankful

    - Promised to get her husband a place

    - Grieved me
  - Bought two silver tumblers

  - Sat at the office all afternoon and evening
  - Contented but weary
