levels.sentence: In 1665, amidst the plague's devastation and the vanities of Court, I chased my lusts and schemes, yet found myself pricked by jealousy, duty, and the fear of death.
levels.paragraph: This year was a tangle of pleasure and vexation. I pursued my lusts with Jane, Mrs. Martin, and others, while my wife's reading on jealousy gnawed at me. The plague bore down on London, driving me to draw my will and renew my vows. Yet I still took comfort in friendship, superstition, and my daily rounds, and even found joy in my Lord Sandwich's vindication.
levels.summary:
In January, I indulged my appetites with little restraint—sporting with women, passing off a ballad at Lord Brunker's, and meddling in Jane's marriage plans to keep her company. But my wife's reading on jealousy struck home, and I suspected worse of those around me. A hare's foot from Mr.

Batten eased my belly, and I proudly bought Hooke's book of microscopy.

February brought office business and Court gossip: Lady Sandwich told me of the Maids of Honour's mad freaks, and Lord Castlemayne's expected return. August saw the plague kill thousands, and I felt mortality everywhere. I nearly touched my little girle, caught myself, and resolved to stop.

I grieved over the rising bill, heard Alderman Bence's strange tale, and began drawing over my will. By October, at Chatham and Rochester, I mixed inspection with stolen pleasures, yet the hideous precipice spoiled my delight.

The plague bill fell, I renewed my vows, and I rejoiced that my Lord Sandwich was cleared of abuse—going home to bed content.

levels.sentence: In 1666 I navigated a London beset by plague, fire, and war, while yielding to lust, managing the Navy, and watching my estate grow to £6,200.
levels.paragraph: In 1666 I came to a London reviving from plague, only to face defeat at sea and the Great Fire. I pursued pleasure with Mrs. Martin, Bagwell, Burroughs, and others, yet kept my accounts and rose in fortune to over £6,200. The year was one of public calamity and private indulgence, ending with resolve to be more frugal.
levels.summary:
I returned to a London recovering from plague, but the year brought the Dutch War's defeats—the loss of The Prince and Sir Christopher Mings's death—and the Great Fire. I worked hard at the Navy Office, struggled with the Act's limits on money, and saw the Duke of York's judgement, while Sir W. Coventry despaired.

My personal life was full of women: Mrs. Martin, Mrs. Bagwell, Doll Lane, widow Burroughs, and little Mrs. Tooker, and I swung between pleasure and self-loathing.

My wife worked on her hangings and drew; I gave her money and reconciled after quarrels. I dined nobly, visited Gresham College, and read Bacon. I watched my accounts: by August my worth was £5,700, by December £6,200, though I spent too much.

I faced the plague's shadow, the fire's aftermath, and deaths like Batters's, and ended the year resolving to be more frugal and thankful.

levels.sentence: In 1667 I balanced White Hall and stolen kisses, peace and peril, ending the year grateful for my family yet fearful for the kingdom.
levels.paragraph: Throughout 1667 I was torn between duty and desire. I refused bribes and pursued secret joys, from Betty Michell to Mrs. Martin, while Parliament quarreled and the Dutch threatened. Peace came in July, but by December I feared for the nation even as my own household remained happy.
levels.summary:
In 1667 I shuttled between White Hall and the office, refusing bribes, hearing alarms of a French landing, and standing firm at the Duke's council despite Carteret's fury. I clashed with Carcasse, saw through Sir W.

Pen, and reported the Victualler's true state; in the autumn I spoke at the Council and listened to the Chatham inquiry condemn Commissioner Pett. Peace came at last in July, but our office still lacked money, and by December Parliament was dissatisfied, the King led astray, and seamen were lured into French service.

My private life was no steadier: I chased Betty Michell, took liberties with Mrs. Martin and Doll Lane, and yet felt ashamed when I neglected my wife. I found quiet joy in music with Mercer, my wife's flageolet, and a solitary boat to Barne Elmes with Boyle's Hydrostatics.

My father's patience in illness touched me, Lord Sandwich's desperate state troubled me, and Sir W. Batten's dying frightened me for the money he owed. As the year closed, I was grateful for my family's health but anxious for the nation's future.
levels.outline:
- 1667: a year of duty, dalliance, and disquiet
  - Public affairs
    - Refused bribes and held my ground at council despite Carteret's fury.
    - Reported the true state of the Victualler and the fleet.
    - Saw through Sir W. Pen and clashed with Carcasse.
    - Spoke at the Council while Lord Anglesey defeated a credit scheme.
    - Attended the Chatham inquiry where Commissioner Pett seemed a weak, silly man.
  - Private pleasures
    - Pursued Betty Michell, Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and others.
    - Enjoyed music with Mercer, my wife's flageolet, and singing at home.
    - Walked to Barne Elmes, reading Boyle's Hydrostatics.
    - Marveled at a crippled dancer and a clockwork show at Walthamstow fair.
  - Cares and fears
    - Endured my father's fallen bowel and questioned my Brampton promises.
    - Worried over Lord Sandwich's debts and possible ruin.
    - Saw Sir W. Batten mortally ill, troubled for kindness and for money owed me.
    - Ended the year anxious about Parliament, the King, and foreign dangers.

levels.sentence: In 1668 I balanced public duty and political suspicion against stolen pleasures and social joys, but my unwise pursuit of Deb led to a bitter quarrel with my wife and a fragile peace that left me resolved to reform.
levels.paragraph: In 1668 I balanced public duty and political suspicion against stolen pleasures and social joys, but my unwise pursuit of Deb led to a bitter quarrel with my wife. After she called me a false, rotten-hearted rogue and threatened to leave me, W. Hewer helped us make peace on condition I never see Deb again. Though we returned to contentment in bed, I could not find joy even in my newly hung chamber, and I resolved to reform and began to pray, however half-heartedly.
levels.summary:
In 1668 I wrestled with the duties of my office and the suspicions of Parliament. I defended the Navy Office over tickets, victuals, and certificates, and was cleared more than once, though the threat of impeachment hung over my colleagues.

I advised the Duke of York and served on committees, while letters from Lord Sandwich reminded me of neglected friendships.

Alongside these cares I stole what joy I could: music at Fox Hall and Spring Garden, plays like The Tempest and Hamlet, the King's starling, and the company of Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and Bagwell's wife. Yet my greatest folly was my pursuit of Deb, my wife's maid.

I kissed her, gave her money, and sought her out until my wife discovered it and confronted me with fury.

My wife called me a false, rotten-hearted rogue and threatened to leave me, and only the intercession of W. Hewer brought a durable peace, on condition I give under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again.

I made love to my wife contentedly, but my sorrow and trouble put me out of all joy, even in my newly hung chamber. I resolved never to give her such occasion again, and began to pray, though not yet heartily.
levels.outline:
- January 1668
  - Social missteps and pleasures
    - Mr. Pierce, his wife, and Mr. Harris arrived thinking they were invited to dinner
    - Took everyone to The Tempest at the Duke's house, paying dearly for a box
    - Buckingham's musicians sent by Greeting made the night extraordinary
    - Mrs. Hollworthy proved conceited and not very intelligent
  - A steady day of accounts
    - Worked on Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter
    - Supped with W. Hewer and had my head combed by the girl
- March 1668
  - Anxious watchfulness and defence
    - Prepared defence with Sir W. Coventry about tickets and sale of places
    - Old complaint about victuals in the 1666 fleet fell to me
    - Cousin Roger warned of Parliament's suspicion; cleared by Commissioners
    - Defended signing of certificates against the Treasury; angered Duncomb and Clifford; King jested
  - Stolen pleasures
    - Had my way with Mrs. Martin, gave Doll Lane 20s. as Valentine, kissed Frank at the Swan
    - Delighted in a starling that had been the King's
    - Admired Hewer's painted board
  - Domestic cares
    - Squabble with wife taught me the worth of silence
    - Bought pewter; eyes very bad
    - Summoned about victuals for Harman's fleet; Deb cried at her writing; I kissed her and gave advice
- April 1668
  - Family and office
    - Sent wife to my father's; managed a kiss with Deb and a shilling
    - Gave L40 to the new college at the Royal Society
    - Enjoyed plays; visited Knipp
  - Political tension
    - Began learning the recorder; heard of impeachment of Sir W. Pen
    - Coventrys tried to blame Lord Sandwich; I stayed silent
    - Petition against Sir W. Coventry grieved me; Brouncker feared Parliament
    - Duke of York spoke kindly of Pen
- May 1668
  - Between office and town
    - Attended Duke of York; consulted with Coventry and Fox about Excise
    - Heard of Teddiman's death; saw age in Mrs. Washington
    - Grieved that churches were given to bishops rather than people
  - Pleasure ran strongly
    - Heard music in The Virgin Martyr; sang at Kensington and Fox Hall
    - Bought song-books; wore new black bombazin suit
    - Took liberties with Mrs. Martin and Bagwell's wife
    - Ate first green peas, packed salmon pie for wife
  - Dark threads
    - Meteor frightened people of another fire
    - Lord Sandwich's gentle letter reminded me I had neglected him
- June 1668
  - Tangier and pleasure
    - Sang with Mercer and Gayet at Fox Hall; bought Marcennus's book
    - Fell into bawdy company; learned of naked dancing at Lady Bennet's
    - Did what I would with Mrs. Martin; stole down to Deptford for Bagwell's wife
    - Told myself a man ought once to know loose company, yet did office business before bed
  - Business and diversions
    - Creed and Colonel Atkins came about coals for Tangier; went with Creed to Backewell's
    - Stopped at Michell's but did not kiss her; no business at Westminster (holyday)
    - Saw The Impertinents; supped at Spring Garden, not merry; sang with Mercer in garden
- July 1668
  - Business and lost opportunity
    - At bookseller's in Duck Lane, but his wife not at home; followed a pretty woman and lost her
    - Visited Lord Crew; his face sore
    - Wife's picture at Cooper's almost done
  - Spring Garden and troubled gallants
    - Went to Spring Garden with wife and Mercer; ate and walked
    - Troubled by rude young gallants forcing women in arbours
    - Returned home by water with pleasure
  - New plates
    - Plate-maker brought four little plates of the Yards, costing L5; troubled by cost but pleased
- August 1668
  - Seeking favour and portraits
    - Sought Sir W. Coventry but he was gone; Lord Arlington received me respectfully
    - Lord Orrery flattered me greatly
    - Watched Cooper finish wife's portrait; paid £30 plus extra; not entirely satisfied
    - In evening fondled Deb while wife read a ridiculous book
  - Last day pleasures
    - Kissed a girl at the Swan; saw Hamlet with friends; visited Fair for Polichinelle
    - Money-telling mare picked me out; earned me a kiss
    - Tried to see Betty Michell but husband was home; rebuffed a naughty wench
    - Mrs. Martin dined; accepted a spaniel bitch for my wife
- September 1668
  - Mixed business and pleasure
    - Attended to office and Exchequer; kissed girl at Swan; dined alone while shoe mended
    - Saw Hamlet with Mercer, Batelier, and Hewer; pleased with Betterton

periods.brief: In 1668 I balanced public duty and political suspicion against stolen pleasures and social joys, but my unwise pursuit of Deb led to a bitter quarrel with my wife and a fragile peace that left me resolved to reform.
periods.full:
In 1668 I wrestled with the duties of my office and the suspicions of Parliament. I defended the Navy Office over tickets, victuals, and certificates, and was cleared more than once, though the threat of impeachment hung over my colleagues.

I advised the Duke of York and served on committees, while letters from Lord Sandwich reminded me of neglected friendships.

Alongside these cares I stole what joy I could: music at Fox Hall and Spring Garden, plays like The Tempest and Hamlet, the King's starling, and the company of Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and Bagwell's wife. Yet my greatest folly was my pursuit of Deb, my wife's maid.

I kissed her, gave her money, and sought her out until my wife discovered it and confronted me with fury.

My wife called me a false, rotten-hearted rogue and threatened to leave me, and only the intercession of W. Hewer brought a durable peace, on condition I give under my hand never to see or speak with Deb again.

I made love to my wife contentedly, but my sorrow and trouble put me out of all joy, even in my newly hung chamber. I resolved never to give her such occasion again, and began to pray, though not yet heartily.

    - Buckingham's musicians sent by Greeting made the night extraordinary
    - Mrs. Hollworthy proved conceited and not very intelligent
  - A steady day of accounts
    - Worked on Tangier and East India accounts with Mr. Poynter
    - Supped with W. Hewer and had my head combed by the girl
- March 1668
  - Anxious watchfulness and defence

    - Old complaint about victuals in the 1666 fleet fell to me
    - Cousin Roger warned of Parliament's suspicion; cleared by Commissioners
    - Defended signing of certificates against the Treasury; angered Duncomb and Clifford; King jested

    - Had my way with Mrs. Martin, gave Doll Lane 20s. as Valentine, kissed Frank at the Swan
    - Delighted in a starling that had been the King's
    - Admired Hewer's painted board

    - Squabble with wife taught me the worth of silence

periods.paragraph: In 1668 I balanced public duty and political suspicion against stolen pleasures and social joys, but my unwise pursuit of Deb led to a bitter quarrel with my wife. After she called me a false, rotten-hearted rogue and threatened to leave me, W. Hewer helped us make peace on condition I never see Deb again. Though we returned to contentment in bed, I could not find joy even in my newly hung chamber, and I resolved to reform and began to pray, however half-heartedly.

levels.sentence: In these last months of 1669, I chase flirtations and public applause even as my eyesight fails, until I am forced to lay down my own pen, a surrender that feels like a descent into the grave.
levels.paragraph: These spring months were a whirl of temptation and vexation. I took liberties with Mrs. Jowles, followed Mrs. Bagwell's wife and Deb into fleeting meetings, and could not shake my guilt even among friends. Yet the truest blow was physical: my eyes grew so weak that I could no longer write my journal by my own hand. I resolved to have my people keep it in long-hand, and that decision felt like my death.
levels.summary:
In March, I set out for Maidstone with Gibson and Mr. Coney, partly to see the town and partly to catch sight of Mrs. Jowles, the daughter at Captain Allen's. I did see her, and on my return I sent the coach away and stayed with Mr. Coney, where Mrs.

Jowles proved a willing partner in kisses and touches at the street door. We walked through pitch darkness and snow to Chatham, and I went to bed, but the memory lingered.

April brought more secret meetings: Bagwell's wife slipped me a note and we met briefly in Moorfields, and I spotted Deb on Holborn Hill, following her into an alehouse for kisses and twenty shillings. Though I was troubled by my behaviour, I could not stop myself, and even family dinners left me uneasy.

By May, my eyesight had become a constant torment. I struggled with my accounts, feared the loss of my writing, and finally made the painful resolution to have my servants keep this journal in long-hand while I only add short notes. It felt like going into my grave, and I prayed for God to prepare me.

periods.label: 1660s

levels.sentence: I served the King through plague, fire, and war, while wrestling with my own appetites and failing eyesight.
levels.paragraph: Through the 1660s I rose as a clerk to a man of substance, navigating the Restoration court, the Plague, the Great Fire, and the Dutch War. My days were filled with account-keeping, office politics, and the pursuit of pleasure—often at the cost of my vows and my peace. I loved my wife yet betrayed her with servants and strangers, and each time was wracked with shame. Still, I counted my blessings, grew my fortune, and resolved again and again to reform. By the decade's end, failing eyesight forced me to trust my pen to others, and I turned toward God.
levels.summary:
I began the decade as a clerk at the Privy Seal, anxious about my salary and my name among the Council, but by the mid-1660s my worth had grown into thousands of pounds. I served the Navy Office diligently, defending it against Parliament, and watched the King's court with a mixture of fascination and alarm.

The Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of 1666 shook London and my own soul, yet I kept working, dining, and dallying.

Alongside my public labors ran a turbulent private life. I pursued Mrs. Lane, Bagwell's wife, Mrs. Martin, Doll Lane, and most dangerously my wife's maid Deb, whose discovery nearly broke my marriage. My dear wife Elizabeth was often my comfort, but also my accuser.

I made vows to abstain from wine and plays, broke them, renewed them, and always fell again. Through it all I kept careful accounts, sought advancement, and worried over my father, brothers, and uncle Thomas's business.

As the decade closed, my eyesight decayed, and I feared losing my writing and my memory. I resolved to have my journal kept in longhand, feeling it like the approach of the grave. Yet I remained thankful for my health, my family, and the nation's recovery, and I prayed for God's preparation.
